Hedging out the HEDGE Bias:
Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV

Endong Wang11 1 Department of Economics, University of Mannheim, L7, 3–5, Mannheim, Germany, 68161. TEL: +49 621-181-1879; Email: endong.wang@uni-mannheim.de. Ren Zhang22 2 Department of Finance and Economics, McCoy College of Business, Texas State University, 601 University Drive, San Marcos, TX 78666. Email: r_z79@txstate.edu. Dept. of Economics, University of Mannheim McCoy College of Business, Texas State Univ.
This version: November 9, 2026

Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

Keywords: Cross-sectional identification, panel local projections, partial-equilibrium effects, portable elasticities, shift-share designs, two-way fixed effects.

JEL Classification: C13, C26, C33, E52, E62.

1.  Introduction

A growing body of literature relies on cross-sectional identification to recover dynamic partial-equilibrium effects, which measure the direct responses of unit outcomes to a treatment driven by an aggregate shock when the paths of the other aggregates that move with the shock (the confounders) are held fixed.11 1 In macroeconomics, applications include Huber (2018); Beraja et al. (2019); Chodorow-Reich (2019); Guren et al. (2021); Jeenas (2026). Outside macroeconomics, the same design is used to study trade shocks (Autor et al., 2013; Acemoglu et al., 2016) and, in finance and the broader business literature, the effects of common price, policy, or technology shocks on firms and markets that differ in their exposure. Estimating these effects is of particular importance because, as portable statistics in the sense of Nakamura and Steinsson (2018), the estimates discipline and test structural models. Specifically, these studies use panel data on units that differ in their exposure to the shock and estimate two-way fixed-effects instrumental-variables (TWFE-IV) local projections, which include unit and time effects. The design presumes that the time effects control for the influence of the confounders, which are common to all units, so that the estimated relative responses recover the dynamic partial-equilibrium effects.

The time effects absorb only the part of the confounders’ influence that is common to all units. A confounder may therefore bias the TWFE-IV estimate when the confounder responds to the treatment and units that are more exposed to the treatment are also more or less sensitive to the confounder (Chodorow-Reich et al., 2021; Guren et al., 2021; Arkhangelsky and Korovkin, 2024). A recent paper by Donaldson (2026) terms this bias the heterogeneous-exposure-to-dynamic-general-equilibrium (HEDGE) bias. The central contribution of this paper is to characterize the HEDGE bias under general aggregate dynamics and to develop a regression-based framework, heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV), which identifies the dynamic partial-equilibrium effects across a broad range of environments. We summarize these results in turn.

We start by deriving an explicit formula for the dynamic partial-equilibrium effect in a backward-looking environment and by characterizing in closed form the HEDGE bias of the TWFE-IV estimate, which contains an exposure-correlation component and an aggregate-feedback component. Intuitively, the effect is the outcome response divided by the impact response of the treatment, in the experiment that holds the confounder path fixed. The exposure-correlation component arises when exposures to the treatment and to the confounder are correlated and the treatment shock moves the confounder, so that the numerator of the TWFE-IV estimate also reflects the influence of the confounder. The aggregate-feedback component arises when the confounder shock also moves the treatment (two-way general equilibrium), so that holding the confounder path fixed changes the treatment path, and possibly its impact response in the denominator, whereas the TWFE-IV estimate follows the unrestricted treatment path. Thus, the TWFE-IV estimate is generally biased whenever either component is present.

To hedge out the HEDGE bias, we develop for this environment the benchmark HELP-IV design, which augments the TWFE-IV local projection with the path controls and instruments boxed below. At each horizon hh, HELP-IV regresses the outcome Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} of unit ii on the treatment GtG_{t} and on the confounder path Rt,…,Rt+hR_{t},\ldots,R_{t+h}, each interacted with the exposure si​gs_{ig} of the unit to the treatment, together with unit and time effects,

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhHELP​si​g​Gt+∑s=0hch,s​si​g​Rt+s+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h.\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\boxed{\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{h,s}s_{ig}R_{t+s}}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}. (1)

HELP-IV instruments these regressors with si​g​(zg,t,zr,t,…,zr,t+h)s_{ig}\bigl(z_{g,t},\boxed{z_{r,t},\ldots,z_{r,t+h}}\bigr), where zg,tz_{g,t} is a proxy for the treatment shock and zr,t+sz_{r,t+s} is a proxy for the confounder shock dated t+st+s. We prove that, with valid instruments, bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} identifies the dynamic partial-equilibrium effect. Intuitively, the regression identifies its h+2h+2 coefficients through h+2h+2 moment conditions, one for each instrument, and identifying bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} is equivalent to taking a linear combination of these conditions that eliminates the coefficients on the path controls. This elimination is possible exactly when the corresponding combination of instruments is uncorrelated with every value of the confounder path, so the combination mimics a treatment shock in the experiment that holds the confounder path fixed. This linear combination then expresses bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} as the response of the outcome to the combined instruments divided by the response of the treatment to them. The numerator and the denominator of this ratio therefore correspond to those that define the dynamic partial-equilibrium effect, so HELP-IV removes both components of the HEDGE bias simultaneously.

We then extend the benchmark HELP-IV design to four more general environments that arise frequently in empirical applications. First, when units are exposed to the treatment along multiple margins, we identify a separate partial-equilibrium effect for each margin by interacting the treatment, the path controls, and the instruments with each margin. Second, when multiple confounders are present, we develop three designs, each suited to a different class of applications. These designs, respectively, (i) instrument each value on every confounder path with its own proxy, (ii) combine all proxies into one instrument that leaves the confounder paths unchanged (composite HELP-IV), and (iii) combine the time-series identification of HELP-IV with the cross-sectional targeting rule of Manuel (2026) to accommodate confounders that lack proxies but do not move the treatment. Third, when outcomes also depend on expected future aggregates, we build the composite instrument with news shocks about future confounders and, when such news shocks are few, identify an information-constrained effect. Fourth, when the target is defined on unit-level treatments and outcomes that may span multiple dates, many applications instrument the treatment with the exposure-weighted aggregate treatment itself rather than its innovation. We show that this instrument introduces an omitted-history bias in addition to the HEDGE bias, because it also reflects shocks that predate the treatment shock. HELP-IV, which instruments with shock proxies, removes both biases. Although the four environments differ, the HELP-IV framework can be adapted to all of them because every adapted design retains the common logic that a combination of instruments mimics a treatment shock holding the relevant confounder paths fixed.

The HELP-IV method has the advantage that inference for these designs builds on standard panel IV methods. With available proxies, we follow Almuzara and Sancibrián (2025) and compute standard errors that are robust to the correlation that common shocks induce across units and over time. We also adapt this inference where our designs go beyond this setting. First, the instruments may be estimated in a first step, as in composite HELP-IV or when shocks from a structural vector autoregression (SVAR) replace unavailable proxies. We then stack the first-step moments with the IV moment, so that the standard errors also reflect the first-step estimation error. Second, under the targeting rule of Manuel (2026), the instruments are uncorrelated with exposure to the confounders without proxies only in the population, so their sample correlation adds variance across units. We characterize this variance as a cross-sectional term that adds to the time-series variance and that can be estimated when the exposures to these confounders are identified.

To assess the performance of HELP-IV in finite samples and its practical importance, we conduct a set of Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications. The simulations, which cover all our designs and environments, show that HELP-IV recovers the target effect, with confidence intervals whose coverage is generally close to the nominal level. Our first application re-estimates the state-level fiscal multiplier of Nakamura and Steinsson (2014) under different assumptions about the environment. When the interest rate is the only confounder, HELP-IV lowers the two-year cumulative multiplier from the conventional TWFE-IV estimate of 1.45 to 1.00 in the backward-looking environment and to 0.90 in the forward-looking one. When we allow for multiple confounders through the targeting rule, the two-year multiplier falls to 0.35, comparable to the estimates of Manuel (2026). We thus conclude that the TWFE-IV estimate is biased upward, whereas the partial-equilibrium multiplier itself depends on the assumptions about the environment and on which confounders are held fixed. Our second application re-estimates the effect of stock wealth on local employment and payroll in Chodorow-Reich et al. (2021). They address four aggregate confounders through a control-function approach that interacts exposure with these confounders, and they report that their estimates are robust to dropping these interactions. Applying composite HELP-IV, we find that the two-year response of nontradable payroll falls from their estimate of 3.24 to 0.83 basis points. When we use this portable estimate in their structural model, the implied marginal propensity to consume out of stock wealth and the aggregate labor-market effects are substantially lower. In contrast to their robustness claim, HELP-IV reveals that the confounders bias the TWFE-IV estimate upward, even though this estimate moves only from 2.62 to 3.24 basis points when Chodorow-Reich et al. (2021) add these interactions as controls.

1.1.  Related literature

Our paper contributes mainly to the literature that estimates dynamic partial-equilibrium effects with panel local projections, which combine cross-sectional differences in exposure to aggregate shocks with two-way fixed effects (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2014; Ottonello and Winberry, 2020; Jeenas, 2026). Much of this literature abstracts from aggregate confounders that move with the treatment and to which units respond differently. Chodorow-Reich et al. (2021) and Guren et al. (2021) are notable exceptions. They recognize that time fixed effects do not absorb such confounders, and they confront this identification threat by interacting exposure with the suspected confounders. These studies, however, neither derive the resulting bias nor formally prove that their interactions correct for it. We contribute to this literature by deriving the HEDGE and omitted-history biases of the TWFE-IV estimators used in this literature in closed form at all horizons, and by developing a new regression-based framework that corrects for them.

Our paper also contributes to a recently developed literature that proposes corrections for the HEDGE bias by exploiting either cross-sectional or time-series variation. On the cross-sectional side, Arkhangelsky and Korovkin (2024) reweight units to balance their exposure to unobserved confounders, but only in a static setting. Manuel (2026) instead controls for an observed targeting rule, the characteristics that govern the assignment of exposure. Although he targets a different object, we show that his method also identifies our partial-equilibrium effect when the confounders do not feed back into the treatment. By contrast, our framework allows for two-way confounders and requires no targeting rule. When such a rule is available, however, HELP-IV can complement his method by controlling for the rule, which combines cross-sectional and time-series identification in a single regression.

On the time-series side, Donaldson (2026) develops a multi-step method that decomposes the two-way fixed-effects estimate into the partial-equilibrium effect and a bias term, which she estimates by scaling the cross-sectional responses to confounder shocks by offsetting shock sizes obtained from a time-series policy counterfactual, as in Sims and Zha (2006) and McKay and Wolf (2023). Although benchmark HELP-IV and the decomposition method both rely on time-series variation for identification, they differ in two respects. On the one hand, HELP-IV applies to more general environments. The benchmark design allows the confounders to feed back into the treatment, whereas the closed-form analysis in the main text of Donaldson (2026) assumes one-way confounders.22 2 Donaldson (2026) shows that the decomposition method recovers the partial-equilibrium effect in two examples with two-way feedback, in which the treatment shock is observed and moves the treatment one for one when the confounder path is held fixed. In more general environments, however, the decomposition method no longer recovers this effect, as we show formally in Section 2.4. The extension of HELP-IV to multiple exposure margins, multiple confounders, and transformed treatments and outcomes broadens this scope further. On the other hand, most HELP-IV designs are one-step LP-IV regressions, so they can be estimated with standard statistical packages, and inference builds on standard IV methods. The benchmark design is therefore accessible to researchers who are not familiar with constructing policy counterfactuals. Taken together, these two differences make HELP-IV a general and accessible framework for estimating dynamic partial-equilibrium effects across economics, finance, and the broader business and social sciences.

Our paper also speaks to three further strands of research, namely policy counterfactuals, shift-share designs, and the empirical questions that our applications address. First, a growing body of work constructs policy counterfactuals directly from impulse responses in semi-structural time-series models (Sims and Zha, 2006; McKay and Wolf, 2023; Barnichon and Mesters, 2023; Caravello et al., 2024; Wang, 2026). Our framework extends these counterfactuals from the time series to cross-sectional data through a panel local-projection design. Second, our paper relates to the literature on shift-share designs (Goldsmith-Pinkham et al., 2020; Adão et al., 2019; Borusyak et al., 2022), in particular to the recentered instruments of Borusyak and Hull (2023), which purge a shift-share instrument of its expected value. The omitted-history bias in our paper is the time-series counterpart of the bias that recentering removes (Jaeger et al., 2018; Borusyak et al., 2025). HELP-IV corrects this bias together with the HEDGE bias. Third, our applications speak to the literatures on cross-sectional fiscal multipliers (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2014; Dupor and Guerrero, 2017; Pennings, 2021; Chodorow-Reich, 2019) and on stock wealth effects (Zhou and Carroll, 2012; Di Maggio et al., 2020; Chodorow-Reich et al., 2021). The resulting estimates are portable and offer structural models in their respective fields a firmer empirical anchor for calibration.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the partial-equilibrium effect, derives the HEDGE bias, and establishes identification by HELP-IV. Section 3 extends HELP-IV to more general environments, and Section 4 develops its inference. Section 5 evaluates the designs in Monte Carlo simulations, Section 6 presents the two applications, and Section 7 concludes.

2.  Backward-looking HELP-IV

This section studies the partial-equilibrium effect in a backward-looking environment where unit outcomes respond only to current and past aggregates. This isolates the identification problem in its simplest form. We first describe the model environment and define the partial-equilibrium effect we seek to identify (Section 2.1). We then show that the standard TWFE-IV design does not recover this effect and characterize the resulting bias in closed form (Section 2.2). We next introduce a novel local-projection design, HELP-IV, and establish that it identifies the partial-equilibrium effect (Section 2.3). Finally, in Section 2.4, we compare HELP-IV with the decomposition method of Donaldson (2026).

2.1.  Environment and the identification target

The object of interest in this section is the partial-equilibrium effect: the response of a unit-level outcome to a one-unit autonomous movement in the aggregate treatment, holding the path of the aggregate confounder fixed over the response horizon. For example, when a researcher studies how regional output responds to government spending, the outcome is regional output, the treatment is government spending, and a candidate confounder is the interest rate, which moves with spending and also affects output directly.

2.1.1.  Model setup

The model specifies the dependence of unit outcomes on the aggregate variables, the joint process of those aggregates, and the cross-sectional relation between the exposures to them. In the backward-looking environment, the outcome of unit ii, denoted Yi​tY_{it}, depends on its own lag Yi,t−1Y_{i,t-1} and on the current and lagged values of the treatment GtG_{t} and the confounder RtR_{t}:

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+ρ​Yi,t−1+∑ℓ=0p(βℓ​si​g​Gt−ℓ+γℓ​si​r​Rt−ℓ)+ui​t.\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\rho Y_{i,t-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\left(\beta_{\ell}s_{ig}G_{t-\ell}+\gamma_{\ell}s_{ir}R_{t-\ell}\right)+u_{it}. (2)

Here μi\mu_{i} and λt\lambda_{t} are unit and time effects, and ρ\rho, with |ρ|<1|\rho|<1, measures own persistence.33 3 A single own lag keeps the notation light. An own-lag polynomial of order qq may change the closed-form expression for the identification target, but leaves the identification propositions in this paper unchanged. The coefficients βℓ\beta_{\ell} and γℓ\gamma_{\ell} measure the dependence of the outcome on the two aggregates, si​gs_{ig} and si​rs_{ir} are unit ii’s exposures to them, and ui​tu_{it} is an idiosyncratic disturbance. The two exposures are predetermined, and their cross-sectional relation is

si​r\displaystyle s_{ir} =ϕ​si​g+uir​g.\displaystyle=\phi s_{ig}+u_{i}^{rg}. (3)

We maintain that si​gs_{ig} and uir​gu_{i}^{rg} are independent, 𝔼⁡[uir​g]=0\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{rg}]=0, and (μi,si​g,uir​g,{ui​t})(\mu_{i},s_{ig},u_{i}^{rg},\{u_{it}\}) is independent of the aggregate process. The coefficient ϕ\phi measures exposure correlation, and ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0 challenges the identification of the partial-equilibrium effect, because units with greater exposure to GtG_{t} then also have systematically different exposure to RtR_{t}. We restrict attention to a single confounder and extend the framework to multiple confounders in the next section.

We assume that the two aggregates admit the stable structural moving-average representation

𝐖t\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{t} =∑j=0∞Ψj​ϵt−j,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\Psi_{j}\bm{\epsilon}_{t-j}, (4)

where 𝐖t=(Gt,Rt)′\mathbf{W}_{t}=(G_{t},R_{t})^{\prime} and ϵt=(ϵg,t,ϵr,t)′\bm{\epsilon}_{t}=(\epsilon_{g,t},\epsilon_{r,t})^{\prime}. The sequence {Ψj}j≥0\{\Psi_{j}\}_{j\geq 0} is absolutely summable. The two structural shocks, which we call the treatment shock ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and the confounder shock ϵr,t\epsilon_{r,t}, have mean zero, are serially uncorrelated, and are mutually orthogonal. We leave the scale of these shocks unrestricted, because the effects below are ratios of responses and do not depend on it. Each aggregate can respond to the other’s shock, so the representation permits feedback in both directions between GtG_{t} and RtR_{t}, a case we refer to as two-way general equilibrium. When RtR_{t} responds to ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} while GtG_{t} does not respond to ϵr,t\epsilon_{r,t} at any horizon, the feedback runs in one direction, and we refer to this special case as one-way general equilibrium.

2.1.2.  The partial-equilibrium effect

To formalize the definition of the partial-equilibrium effect, let G˘ℓ\breve{G}_{\ell} denote the controlled response of Gt+ℓG_{t+\ell} to ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} when the path Rt,…,Rt+hR_{t},\ldots,R_{t+h} is held fixed, and let Y˘i,h\breve{Y}_{i,h} denote the corresponding response of the outcome. The path is held fixed by confounder shocks dated tt through t+ht+h, referred to as the offsets (Sims and Zha, 2006). The confounder path does not change, so its direct contribution to the outcome response is zero, and applying equation (2) under this experiment gives

Y˘i,h\displaystyle\breve{Y}_{i,h} =si​g​∑ℓ=0min⁡{p,h}βℓ​G˘h−ℓ+ρ​Y˘i,h−1.\displaystyle=s_{ig}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min\{p,h\}}\beta_{\ell}\breve{G}_{h-\ell}+\rho\breve{Y}_{i,h-1}. (5)

Normalizing by the impact movement in GtG_{t} that this experiment generates gives the partial-equilibrium effect βhP=Y˘i,h/(si​g​G˘0)\beta_{h}^{P}=\breve{Y}_{i,h}/(s_{ig}\breve{G}_{0}), which satisfies the recursion

βhP\displaystyle\beta_{h}^{P} =∑ℓ=0min⁡{p,h}βℓ​G˘h−ℓG˘0+ρ​βh−1P,β−1P=0.\displaystyle=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min\{p,h\}}\beta_{\ell}\breve{G}_{h-\ell}}{\breve{G}_{0}}+\rho\beta_{h-1}^{P},\qquad\beta_{-1}^{P}=0. (6)

The initial condition holds because outcomes do not respond before the shock, so that β0P=β0\beta_{0}^{P}=\beta_{0}. Both the numerator and the denominator of βhP\beta_{h}^{P} are measured in the same fixed-path experiment, so any structural model that runs this experiment yields a direct counterpart of βhP\beta_{h}^{P}. In this sense, βhP\beta_{h}^{P} is a portable statistic (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2018). Its value, however, varies with the controlled treatment path G˘0,…,G˘h\breve{G}_{0},\ldots,\breve{G}_{h}, so a model reproduces βhP\beta_{h}^{P} only if it generates the same controlled path.

2.2.  The HEDGE bias of the TWFE-IV design

A large empirical literature targets the partial-equilibrium effect with a TWFE-IV design, for example in fiscal policy (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2014; Chodorow-Reich, 2019), monetary policy and firm investment (Ottonello and Winberry, 2020), and household wealth (Mian and Sufi, 2014; Guren et al., 2021; Chodorow-Reich et al., 2021). Specifications differ in the definition of the treatment, in the horizon, and in the controls, but they share the interaction of predetermined exposure with the treatment. We write the design as the two-way fixed-effects local projection

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhTWFE​si​g​Gt+μi,h+λt,h+vi,t,h.\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+v_{i,t,h}. (7)

The exposure-weighted treatment si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} is instrumented by si​g​zg,ts_{ig}z_{g,t}, where the treatment proxy zg,tz_{g,t} is

zg,t\displaystyle z_{g,t} =κg​ϵg,t+ηg,t,\displaystyle=\kappa_{g}\epsilon_{g,t}+\eta_{g,t}, (8)

for κg≠0\kappa_{g}\neq 0, and the measurement error ηg,t\eta_{g,t} has mean zero and is orthogonal to the structural shocks at all leads and lags. We also maintain that the exposure-weighted proxies are uncorrelated with the unit-level disturbances at all leads and lags. We refer to this condition as panel exclusion. It must be imposed separately, because orthogonality of the proxy to the aggregate shocks does not imply it.

Proposition 1 provides a closed-form expression for the wedge between the TWFE-IV coefficient and βhP\beta_{h}^{P}.

Proposition 1 (HEDGE bias of TWFE-IV).

Suppose (2)–(4) and (8) hold, the proxy satisfies the panel exclusion, Var⁡(si​g)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})>0, G0g≠0G_{0}^{g}\neq 0, and G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0. Then the population TWFE-IV coefficient in (7) satisfies

bhTWFE−βhP\displaystyle b_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}-\beta_{h}^{P} =((G0g)−1​∑j=0hφj​Gh−jg−G˘0−1​∑j=0hφj​G˘h−j)⏟aggregate feedback+ϕ​(G0g)−1​∑j=0hγ¯j​Rh−jg⏟exposure correlation,\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left((G_{0}^{g})^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{h}\varphi_{j}G_{h-j}^{g}-\breve{G}_{0}^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{h}\varphi_{j}\breve{G}_{h-j}\right)}_{\text{aggregate feedback}}+\underbrace{\phi\,(G_{0}^{g})^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{h}\bar{\gamma}_{j}R_{h-j}^{g}}_{\text{exposure correlation}}, (9)

where

Ghg=𝔼⁡[Gt+h​ϵg,t]𝔼⁡[ϵg,t2],φj=∑ℓ=0min⁡{p,j}ρj−ℓ​βℓ,γ¯j=∑ℓ=0min⁡{p,j}ρj−ℓ​γℓ,\displaystyle G_{h}^{g}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[G_{t+h}\epsilon_{g,t}]}{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{g,t}^{2}]},\qquad\varphi_{j}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min\{p,j\}}\rho^{j-\ell}\beta_{\ell},\qquad\bar{\gamma}_{j}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min\{p,j\}}\rho^{j-\ell}\gamma_{\ell},

and GhrG_{h}^{r}, RhgR_{h}^{g}, and RhrR_{h}^{r} are defined analogously to GhgG_{h}^{g}.

The proof of Proposition 1 is in Appendix A.1. Proposition 1 shows that the HEDGE bias has two components. The first is the aggregate-feedback component. TWFE-IV measures the outcome response along the unrestricted treatment path per unit of its impact G0gG_{0}^{g}. The target βhP\beta_{h}^{P} instead measures it along the controlled path per unit of G˘0\breve{G}_{0}. The two normalized responses both equal β0\beta_{0} at h=0h=0, and at longer horizons they can differ only if confounder shocks feed back into the treatment. This component is therefore zero under one-way general equilibrium, where Gℓr=0G_{\ell}^{r}=0 for all ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 and hence G˘ℓ=Gℓg\breve{G}_{\ell}=G_{\ell}^{g}. The second is the exposure-correlation component. When ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0, the treatment shock generates cross-sectional variation through both si​g​Gt+ℓs_{ig}G_{t+\ell} and si​r​Rt+ℓs_{ir}R_{t+\ell}, ℓ=0,…,h\ell=0,\ldots,h, and time effects remove only their common components, so the coefficient on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} also picks up the response through si​r​Rt+ℓs_{ir}R_{t+\ell}. This component is therefore zero when ϕ=0\phi=0 or when the confounder does not respond to the treatment shock at any horizon up to hh.

2.3.  Identification by the HELP-IV design

Both components of the HEDGE bias arise because the TWFE-IV design leaves the confounder path unrestricted. To identify the partial-equilibrium effect, we design a heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) regression that holds this path fixed. It adds the realized values of the confounder path to the TWFE-IV regression as path controls and instruments these controls with dated proxies for the confounder shocks.

In particular, we estimate

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhHELP​si​g​Gt+∑s=0hch,s​si​g​Rt+s+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h,h≥0.\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{h,s}s_{ig}R_{t+s}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h},\qquad h\geq 0. (10)

We instrument the exposure-weighted treatment si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} and the path controls si​g​Rt,…,si​g​Rt+hs_{ig}R_{t},\ldots,s_{ig}R_{t+h} with the exposure-weighted proxies

𝐙i​t,h\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}_{it,h} =si​g​(zg,t,zr,t,zr,t+1,…,zr,t+h)′,\displaystyle=s_{ig}\left(z_{g,t},z_{r,t},z_{r,t+1},\ldots,z_{r,t+h}\right)^{\prime}, (11)

where zr,tz_{r,t} is a proxy for the confounder shock,

zr,t\displaystyle z_{r,t} =κr​ϵr,t+ηr,t,κr≠0,\displaystyle=\kappa_{r}\epsilon_{r,t}+\eta_{r,t},\qquad\kappa_{r}\neq 0, (12)

and ηr,t\eta_{r,t} has mean zero and is orthogonal to the structural shocks at all leads and lags.44 4 The regression can also include controls determined before date tt, such as the lagged outcome, without affecting identification, because the proxies are orthogonal to them.

2.3.1.  Why HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect

We start from the identifying moment conditions. Exogeneity of the proxies and panel exclusion imply that the coefficients of the HELP-IV regression solve the population moment system

𝔼⁡[𝐙~i​t,h​(Y~i,t+h−𝑿~i​t,h′​ϑh)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\left(\widetilde{Y}_{i,t+h}-\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{it,h}^{\prime}\bm{\vartheta}_{h}\right)\right] =𝟎,\displaystyle=\mathbf{0}, (13)

where

𝑿i​t,h\displaystyle\bm{X}_{it,h} =si​g​(Gt,Rt,…,Rt+h)′,ϑh=(bhHELP,ch,0,…,ch,h)′\displaystyle=s_{ig}\left(G_{t},R_{t},\ldots,R_{t+h}\right)^{\prime},\qquad\bm{\vartheta}_{h}=\left(b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}},c_{h,0},\ldots,c_{h,h}\right)^{\prime}

collect the endogenous regressors and their coefficients, and a tilde on panel variables denotes population residualization with respect to the unit and time effects. The HELP-IV regression is exactly identified, because the moment system has h+2h+2 equations, one for each instrument, in the h+2h+2 elements of ϑh\bm{\vartheta}_{h}.

To show how bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} identifies the partial-equilibrium effect, we solve the moment system (13) for bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} through a linear combination of its equations from which the path coefficients ch,0,…,ch,hc_{h,0},\ldots,c_{h,h} drop out. Premultiplying system (13) by a row vector (1,w0,…,wh)(1,w_{0},\ldots,w_{h}) adds the equations of the confounder proxies, weighted by w0,…,whw_{0},\ldots,w_{h}, to the equation of the treatment proxy. The combined equation is the moment condition of a single instrument, the exposure-weighted combined proxy si​g​(zg,t+∑j=0hwj​zr,t+j)s_{ig}(z_{g,t}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}w_{j}z_{r,t+j}). Up to the common factor Var⁡(si​g)\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig}), each coefficient in this equation is multiplied by the covariance of the combined proxy with the aggregate part of its regressor, which is GtG_{t} for bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} and Rt+sR_{t+s} for ch,sc_{h,s}. The path coefficients therefore drop out of the combined equation exactly when the combined proxy is uncorrelated with every value of the confounder path,

𝔼⁡[Rt+ℓ​(zg,t+∑j=0hwj​zr,t+j)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[R_{t+\ell}\Bigl(z_{g,t}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}w_{j}z_{r,t+j}\Bigr)\Bigr] =0,ℓ=0,…,h,\displaystyle=0,\qquad\ell=0,\ldots,h, (14)

in which case the combined equation reduces to a single equation in bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}},

𝔼⁡[s˙i​g​(zg,t+∑j=0hwj​zr,t+j)​Y~i,t+h]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\dot{s}_{ig}\Bigl(z_{g,t}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}w_{j}z_{r,t+j}\Bigr)\,\widetilde{Y}_{i,t+h}\Bigr] =Var⁡(si​g)​bhHELP​𝔼​[Gt​(zg,t+∑j=0hwj​zr,t+j)],\displaystyle=\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})\,b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[G_{t}\Bigl(z_{g,t}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}w_{j}z_{r,t+j}\Bigr)\Bigr], (15)

where s˙i​g=si​g−𝔼⁡[si​g]\dot{s}_{ig}=s_{ig}-\mathbb{E}[s_{ig}] denotes demeaned exposure.

Condition (14) holds the confounder path fixed. Since each proxy covaries only with the shock of its own type and date, condition (14) is equivalent to Rℓg+∑j=0ℓej​Rℓ−jr=0R_{\ell}^{g}+\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}e_{j}R_{\ell-j}^{r}=0 for ℓ=0,…,h\ell=0,\ldots,h, in the notation of Proposition 1, where eje_{j} is proportional to wjw_{j}. Each such sum is the response of Rt+ℓR_{t+\ell} to a unit treatment shock accompanied by confounder shocks of sizes e0,…,ehe_{0},\ldots,e_{h} at dates tt through t+ht+h. Because the path is held fixed, the confounder channel is shut down in the reduced form on the left side of condition (15), and the exposure-correlation component is removed.

Condition (15) equates the covariance of the exposure-weighted combined proxy with the outcome, the reduced form, to bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} times its covariance with the treatment, the first stage. Under condition (14) and up to the common factor Var⁡(si​g)​𝔼​[zg,t​ϵg,t]\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})\mathbb{E}[z_{g,t}\epsilon_{g,t}], the first stage is G˘0\breve{G}_{0}, the impact response of GtG_{t} in the fixed-path experiment, and the reduced form is the outcome response per unit of exposure, which equals G˘0​βhP\breve{G}_{0}\beta_{h}^{P} by the definition of βhP\beta_{h}^{P}. Condition (15) therefore reads G˘0​bhHELP=G˘0​βhP\breve{G}_{0}b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\breve{G}_{0}\beta_{h}^{P}, so that bhHELP=βhPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\beta_{h}^{P} whenever G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0. HELP-IV thus divides the controlled reduced form G˘0​βhP\breve{G}_{0}\beta_{h}^{P} by the controlled first stage G˘0\breve{G}_{0}, whereas TWFE-IV divides the unrestricted reduced form by the unrestricted first stage G0gG_{0}^{g}. Because the numerator and the denominator of HELP-IV are measured in the same fixed-path experiment, the aggregate-feedback component is removed as well.55 5 To see the logic in the simplest case, take h=0h=0. Condition (14) then gives w0=−𝔼[Rtzg,t]/𝔼[Rtzr,t]w_{0}=-\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{g,t}]/\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{r,t}] when 𝔼⁡[Rt​zr,t]≠0\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{r,t}]\neq 0. The combined proxy zg,t+w0​zr,tz_{g,t}+w_{0}z_{r,t} thus moves GtG_{t} only through the treatment shock accompanied by the confounder shock that keeps RtR_{t} unchanged, so its covariance with GtG_{t} is proportional to G˘0\breve{G}_{0}, and condition (15) yields b0HELP=β0P=β0b_{0}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\beta_{0}^{P}=\beta_{0}.

The following proposition formally establishes that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect.

Proposition 2 (HELP-IV identification).

Suppose (2)–(4), (8), (11), and (12) hold, the exposure-weighted proxies satisfy the panel exclusion restrictions, Var⁡(si​g)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})>0, 𝔼⁡[Rt​zr,t]≠0\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{r,t}]\neq 0, and G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0. Then (13) has a unique solution whose first element satisfies

bhHELP\displaystyle b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} =βhP.\displaystyle=\beta_{h}^{P}. (16)

The proof is in Appendix A.2. The two relevance conditions play distinct roles. The condition 𝔼⁡[Rt​zr,t]≠0\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{r,t}]\neq 0 requires the confounder proxy to move the confounder on impact, which guarantees that weights satisfying condition (14) exist and are unique. The condition G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0 requires the treatment to move in the fixed-path experiment, which allows condition (15) to determine bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}.

2.3.2.  Why ordinary controls are insufficient

Prior studies address aggregate confounders by interacting exposure with the suspected confounders and adding these interactions to the TWFE-IV regression as ordinary controls (Chodorow-Reich et al., 2021; Guren et al., 2021, e.g.,). A control for the current confounder si​g​Rts_{ig}R_{t}, however, falls short of the fixed-path experiment for two reasons. First, it restricts the confounder only at date tt, although the outcome at date t+ht+h responds to the entire path Rt,…,Rt+hR_{t},\ldots,R_{t+h}. Second, it restricts the realized value RtR_{t}, which reflects all aggregate shocks rather than the treatment shock alone, and therefore removes only the component of the later path that RtR_{t} predicts through the unconditional autocovariance of the confounder. Controlling only for the current confounder can thus still bias the estimate of the partial-equilibrium effect.

Controlling for the entire realized path si​g​Rt,…,si​g​Rt+hs_{ig}R_{t},\ldots,s_{ig}R_{t+h} resolves the first problem but not the second, since these controls are themselves realized values. The realized path responds also to shocks dated before tt and to subsequent treatment shocks, which affect the outcome through terms omitted from the regression, namely the lags in equation (2) and later values of the treatment. By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, the effective instrument for si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} is the exposure-weighted treatment proxy net of its projection on the realized path. Since the treatment shock moves the confounder, this projection is nonzero and transmits the omitted shocks to the instrument, so that the realized path becomes an endogenous control. Instrumenting the path controls is therefore necessary, and the dated confounder proxies are valid instruments for this purpose, as each is correlated only with the confounder shock of its date.

2.4.  Identification comparison with the decomposition of Donaldson (2026)

Donaldson (2026) also studies the HEDGE bias of the TWFE-IV design and proposes a decomposition method that targets the same partial-equilibrium effect as HELP-IV. This subsection compares the two methods. We first show that, under the backward-looking data-generating process of this section, the decomposition method removes the exposure-correlation component of the HEDGE bias but differs from the partial-equilibrium effect when the offsets change the treatment response used for normalization. We then discuss two further advantages of HELP-IV.

The decomposition method proceeds in three steps. The cross-sectional step regresses the outcome on the exposure-weighted proxies of both shocks,

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhDon​si​g​zg,t+chDon​si​g​zr,t+μi,h+λt,h+ei,t,h.\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}s_{ig}z_{g,t}+c_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}s_{ig}z_{r,t}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+e_{i,t,h}. (17)

The coefficient bhDonb_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}} is the unrestricted reduced-form response of the outcome to the treatment proxy, which contains the HEDGE bias because the treatment shock also moves the confounder path. The coefficient chDonc_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}} is the reduced-form response of the outcome to the confounder proxy. The time-series step, following Sims and Zha (2006), finds the sequence of confounder proxies that reproduces the confounder path generated by the treatment proxy. It chooses {νr,k}k=0h\{\nu_{r,k}\}_{k=0}^{h} such that

πR,ℓg\displaystyle\pi_{R,\ell}^{g} =∑k=0ℓπR,ℓ−krνr,k,ℓ=0,…,h,\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}\pi_{R,\ell-k}^{r}\nu_{r,k},\qquad\ell=0,\ldots,h, (18)

where πX,ℓj=𝔼⁡[Xt+ℓ​zj,t]/𝔼⁡[zj,t2]\pi_{X,\ell}^{j}=\mathbb{E}[X_{t+\ell}z_{j,t}]/\mathbb{E}[z_{j,t}^{2}] denotes the response of Xt+ℓX_{t+\ell} to the proxy zj,tz_{j,t}, for X∈{G,R}X\in\{G,R\} and j∈{g,r}j\in\{g,r\}, so that ℓ=0\ell=0 gives the impact response at date tt. The weight νr,k\nu_{r,k} applies to the confounder proxy dated t+kt+k. The final step subtracts the outcome effect of this sequence, Δh=∑k=0hch−kDon​νr,k\Delta_{h}=\sum_{k=0}^{h}c_{h-k}^{\mathrm{Don}}\nu_{r,k}, from bhDonb_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}, using the coefficients c0Don,…,chDonc_{0}^{\mathrm{Don}},\ldots,c_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}} from the regressions at each horizon. It then divides the result by the first-stage coefficient πG,0g\pi_{G,0}^{g}, which removes the unknown scale of the proxy,

βhDon\displaystyle\beta_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}} =(πG,0g)−1​(bhDon−Δh).\displaystyle=\left(\pi_{G,0}^{g}\right)^{-1}\left(b_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}-\Delta_{h}\right). (19)

The difference bhDon−Δhb_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}-\Delta_{h} is thus proportional to the controlled reduced form of Section 2.3.1, and the decomposition method normalizes it by the unrestricted first stage πG,0g\pi_{G,0}^{g} instead of the controlled one.

The partial-equilibrium effect of Section 2.1.2 instead divides the same outcome response by the impact movement of GtG_{t} under the experiment. Because offsetting confounder shocks dated after tt cannot move GtG_{t}, this movement is the unrestricted impact response less the impact movement induced by the offsetting proxy dated tt. Hence,

βhP\displaystyle\beta_{h}^{P} =(πG,0g−νr,0​πG,0r)−1​(bhDon−Δh).\displaystyle=\left(\pi_{G,0}^{g}-\nu_{r,0}\pi_{G,0}^{r}\right)^{-1}\left(b_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}-\Delta_{h}\right). (20)

The statistics in (19) and (20) share the numerator. Their denominators differ by νr,0​πG,0r\nu_{r,0}\pi_{G,0}^{r}, the impact response of GtG_{t} to the offsetting confounder proxy. Under one-way general equilibrium, the treatment does not respond to confounder shocks, so this term vanishes and the decomposition method recovers the partial-equilibrium effect. Under two-way general equilibrium, the term is nonzero when the confounder shock moves GtG_{t} on impact and the treatment shock moves RtR_{t} on impact. When either response arises only with a lag, the denominators of equations (19) and (20) coincide for the date-tt treatment of this section. When the term is nonzero, the decomposition method removes the exposure-correlation component of Proposition 1 and the part of the aggregate-feedback component that operates through the outcome response.66 6 Under two-way general equilibrium, the HEDGE bias given in Proposition 1 also differs from its counterpart in Donaldson (2026). It is derived in a more general environment, with an aggregate block that has an infinite-order moving-average representation and distributed lags in the outcome equation. It retains, however, the part that operates through the normalization, so the statistic in (19) is biased for the partial-equilibrium effect.77 7 Appendices A.1 and A.3.3 of Donaldson (2026) show that the decomposition method recovers the partial-equilibrium effect in specific two-way examples. There, the treatment shock enters the treatment equation with a unit coefficient, so a unit shock moves GtG_{t} by one when the confounder path is held fixed, and the corrected reduced form bhDon−Δhb_{h}^{\mathrm{Don}}-\Delta_{h} needs no normalization. Her application instead divides by the horizon-hh first stage of cumulative local defense spending, whereas the relevant denominator is the response of cumulative spending through t+ht+h to the proxy and the entire offsetting sequence, which lagged feedback also changes (Section 3.4).

HELP-IV has two further advantages over the decomposition method. First, HELP-IV imposes the fixed-path experiment and the normalization within a single IV regression, whereas the decomposition method combines a cross-sectional regression with a time-series step. This single regression can be estimated with standard statistical packages and delivers both the estimate and its standard error (Section 4). Second, HELP-IV can be extended to more general environments with multiple exposure margins (Section 3.1), multiple confounders (Section 3.2), forward-looking outcomes (Section 3.3), or transformed treatments and outcomes (Section 3.4). Together, these advantages widen the range of applications of HELP-IV.

3.  HELP-IV in more general environments

Many empirical applications target the partial-equilibrium effect in environments more general than that of Section 2. This section extends the HELP-IV design to multiple exposure margins, multiple confounders, outcomes that depend on expected future aggregates, and transformed treatments and outcomes, so that it can be implemented in such applications.

3.1.  Multiple exposure margins

Units are often exposed to the same aggregate treatment along multiple margins. For example, in estimating local spending multipliers, Park et al. (2026) distinguish counties’ exposure to prime-contract spending from their exposure to subcontract spending. They estimate separate prime-contract and subcontract multipliers, which capture economically distinct sources of local fiscal transmission. Motivated by this application, we extend HELP-IV to identify a separate partial-equilibrium effect for each exposure margin.

Consider an environment in which the aggregate treatment affects unit ii through MM predetermined exposure margins:

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+ρ​Yi,t−1+∑ℓ=0p∑m=1Mβm,ℓ​si​g,m​Gt−ℓ+∑ℓ=0pγℓ​si​r​Rt−ℓ+ui​t.\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\rho Y_{i,t-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\beta_{m,\ell}s_{ig,m}G_{t-\ell}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\gamma_{\ell}s_{ir}R_{t-\ell}+u_{it}. (21)

Here si​g,ms_{ig,m} denotes exposure along margin mm, and 𝐬i​g=(si​g,1,…,si​g,M)′\mathbf{s}_{ig}=(s_{ig,1},\ldots,s_{ig,M})^{\prime}. Confounder exposure may be correlated with each treatment-exposure margin: si​r=∑m=1Mϕm​si​g,m+uir​gs_{ir}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\phi_{m}s_{ig,m}+u_{i}^{rg}, where 𝐬i​g\mathbf{s}_{ig} is independent of uir​gu_{i}^{rg} and 𝔼⁡[uir​g]=0\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{rg}]=0. The aggregate dynamics are unchanged from Section 2. For each margin mm, the partial-equilibrium effect βm,hP\beta_{m,h}^{P} is the response of Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} per unit of exposure along margin mm, holding exposure along the other margins fixed. As in Section 2.1.2, this response is measured in the fixed-path experiment and normalized by the impact movement G˘0\breve{G}_{0}, so that

βm,hP\displaystyle\beta_{m,h}^{P} =G˘0−1​∑ℓ=0min⁡{p,h}βm,ℓ​G˘h−ℓ+ρ​βm,h−1P,βm,−1P=0.\displaystyle=\breve{G}_{0}^{-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\min\{p,h\}}\beta_{m,\ell}\breve{G}_{h-\ell}+\rho\beta_{m,h-1}^{P},\qquad\beta_{m,-1}^{P}=0. (22)

Because the confounder exposure loads on every margin, the path controls must be interacted with each margin. HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins therefore estimates the regression

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =∑m=1Mbm,hHELP​si​g,m​Gt+∑s=0h∑m=1Mcm,h,s​si​g,m​Rt+s+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h.\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{M}b_{m,h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}s_{ig,m}G_{t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}\sum_{m=1}^{M}c_{m,h,s}s_{ig,m}R_{t+s}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}. (23)

The endogenous variables are instrumented using 𝐬i​g⊗(zg,t,zr,t,zr,t+1,…,zr,t+h)′\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes(z_{g,t},z_{r,t},z_{r,t+1},\ldots,z_{r,t+h})^{\prime}.

Corollary 1 (Identification with multiple exposure margins).

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 2 hold for the model and instruments of this subsection, with Var⁡(si​g)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})>0 replaced by nonsingularity of Var⁡(𝐬i​g)\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{s}_{ig}). Then the population coefficients in (23) satisfy bm,hHELP=βm,hPb_{m,h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\beta_{m,h}^{P} for m=1,…,Mm=1,\ldots,M.

The proof is in Appendix A.3. Corollary 1 also applies to exposure transmitted through production or spatial networks. For example, Acemoglu et al. (2016) measure exposure to import competition both directly and through input–output linkages, while Adão et al. (2019) measure exposure to trade shocks through linkages across locations. One may then set si​g,1=si​gs_{ig,1}=s_{ig} for own exposure, si​g,2=∑jai​jU​sj​gs_{ig,2}=\sum_{j}a^{U}_{ij}s_{jg} for upstream exposure, and si​g,3=∑jai​jD​sj​gs_{ig,3}=\sum_{j}a^{D}_{ij}s_{jg} for downstream exposure, where aUa^{U} and aDa^{D} are input–output or spatial linkage weights. The corollary then identifies one partial-equilibrium effect for each margin.

3.2.  Multiple aggregate confounders

In many applications, multiple confounders are present. For example, Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate the effect of robot adoption on local labor markets and treat four aggregates as potential confounders: Chinese imports, Mexican imports, offshoring, and the decline in routine tasks. If commuting zones more exposed to robots are also more exposed to these aggregates, and their paths move with robot adoption, each aggregate generates HEDGE bias in the TWFE-IV design, which control variables alone do not remove (Section 2.3.2). This subsection therefore extends HELP-IV to hold all confounder paths fixed jointly.

We extend the data-generating process to KK confounders. The outcome satisfies

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+ρ​Yi,t−1+∑ℓ=0p(βℓ​si​g​Gt−ℓ+∑q=1Kγq,ℓ​si​rq​Rq,t−ℓ)+ui​t.\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\rho Y_{i,t-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\left(\beta_{\ell}s_{ig}G_{t-\ell}+\sum_{q=1}^{K}\gamma_{q,\ell}s_{ir_{q}}R_{q,t-\ell}\right)+u_{it}. (24)

Here R1​t,…,RK​tR_{1t},\ldots,R_{Kt} are the confounders and si​rqs_{ir_{q}} is unit ii’s exposure to Rq​tR_{qt}. Exposure to each confounder may be correlated with treatment exposure,

si​rq\displaystyle s_{ir_{q}} =ϕqsi​g+uirq,q=1,…,K,\displaystyle=\phi_{q}s_{ig}+u_{i}^{r_{q}},\qquad q=1,\ldots,K, (25)

where ϕq\phi_{q} measures that exposure correlation, and si​gs_{ig} and uirqu_{i}^{r_{q}} satisfy the conditions maintained for equation (3). Let 𝐑t=(R1​t,…,RK​t)′\mathbf{R}_{t}=(R_{1t},\ldots,R_{Kt})^{\prime} and ϵr,t=(ϵr1,t,…,ϵrK,t)′\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}=(\epsilon_{r_{1},t},\ldots,\epsilon_{r_{K},t})^{\prime}. The aggregate dynamics follow equation (4), with RtR_{t} and ϵr,t\epsilon_{r,t} replaced by 𝐑t\mathbf{R}_{t} and ϵr,t\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}, and with the same stability and orthogonality conditions.

The target is the response to a movement in GtG_{t} caused by ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} when 𝐑t,…,𝐑t+h\mathbf{R}_{t},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{t+h} are held fixed jointly. The partial-equilibrium effect therefore retains the form in equation (6), with {G˘ℓ}\{\breve{G}_{\ell}\} now denoting the treatment path under this joint fixed-path experiment. We consider three implementations: multiple-confounder HELP-IV, composite HELP-IV, and targeting-rule HELP-IV. All three identify the same target under their own conditions, but each is suited to a different empirical application.

3.2.1.  Multiple-confounder HELP-IV

The direct extension of HELP-IV adds the full path of every confounder as path controls and instruments these controls jointly with the corresponding proxies. We refer to this design as multiple-confounder HELP-IV. At horizon hh, consider

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhHELP​si​g​Gt+∑q=1K∑s=0hcq,h,s​si​g​Rq,t+s+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h.\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\sum_{q=1}^{K}\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{q,h,s}s_{ig}R_{q,t+s}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}. (26)

The endogenous variables si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} and si​g​Rq,t+ss_{ig}R_{q,t+s}, for q=1,…,Kq=1,\ldots,K and s=0,…,hs=0,\ldots,h, are instrumented by

𝐙i​t,h\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}_{it,h} =si​g​(zg,t,𝒛r,t′,𝒛r,t+1′,…,𝒛r,t+h′)′,\displaystyle=s_{ig}\left(z_{g,t},\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime},\bm{z}_{r,t+1}^{\prime},\ldots,\bm{z}_{r,t+h}^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}, (27)

where 𝒛r,t=(zr1,t,…,zrK,t)′\bm{z}_{r,t}=(z_{r_{1},t},\ldots,z_{r_{K},t})^{\prime} collects the proxies for the confounder shocks, each defined as in equation (12). The system is exactly identified, with 1+K⁡(h+1)1+K(h+1) instruments for as many endogenous variables.

Let Σr​z,0=𝔼⁡[𝐑t​𝒛r,t′]\Sigma_{rz,0}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}]. Joint relevance requires Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0} to be nonsingular. Because a confounder proxy dated t+st+s does not move the confounders dated before t+st+s, the first-stage system for 𝐑t,…,𝐑t+h\mathbf{R}_{t},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{t+h} is block triangular with Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0} on each diagonal block, so the confounder-path block has full rank, while G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0 supplies the remaining rank condition for the treatment.

Corollary 2 (Identification with multiple confounders).

Suppose (4), (8), (12), (24), (25), and (27) hold, the exposure-weighted proxies satisfy the panel exclusion restrictions, Var⁡(si​g)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})>0, Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0} is nonsingular, and G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0. Then the population coefficient on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} in (26) satisfies bhHELP=βhPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\beta_{h}^{P}.

The proof is in Appendix A.4. Although multiple-confounder HELP-IV identifies βhP\beta_{h}^{P} at any horizon and for any number of confounders, it uses K⁡(h+1)K(h+1) path controls, a count that grows with both. Each path control is instrumented by its own proxy, so the estimate is precise only if the proxies separate the treatment from every path value. These controls are aggregate series interacted with a common exposure, so the variation that separates them is time-series variation. When the proxies measure the confounder shocks with substantial error, the matrix of sample cross moments between the instruments and the regressors can be nearly singular in a given sample, and this risk rises with the number of path controls. This motivates an alternative design that does not need to separate the path values one by one.

3.2.2.  Composite HELP-IV

We construct this alternative by replacing the instrumented control for each confounder at each date with a single instrument that moves GtG_{t} but leaves the confounder path unchanged. The idea follows Sims and Zha (2006), who hold a policy variable on a given path through a sequence of policy shocks. Here the instrument combines the treatment proxy with dated confounder proxies that offset every movement the treatment shock causes in the confounder path. Because the path does not move with the instrument, the first stage and the reduced form are the movements in GtG_{t} and in Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} along the fixed path, so the regression needs no path control. Their ratio is therefore βhP\beta_{h}^{P}. We refer to this design as composite HELP-IV, because its instrument is a composite of the treatment proxy and the dated confounder proxies.

To implement this design, we form, for each horizon hh, the instrument

zg,t,hC\displaystyle\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C} =zg,t+∑s=0h𝒘s′​𝒛r,t+s,\displaystyle=z_{g,t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}\bm{w}_{s}^{\prime}\bm{z}_{r,t+s}, (28)

where zg,tz_{g,t} is the treatment proxy of equation (8), 𝒛r,t+s\bm{z}_{r,t+s} collects the confounder proxies of equation (12) dated t+st+s, and 𝒘s\bm{w}_{s} is the K×1K\times 1 vector of offset weights on them. The weights are chosen so that the instrument leaves the joint confounder path 𝐑t,h=(𝐑t′,…,𝐑t+h′)′\mathbf{R}_{t,h}=(\mathbf{R}_{t}^{\prime},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{t+h}^{\prime})^{\prime} unchanged,

𝔼⁡[𝐑t,h​zg,t,hC]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{R}_{t,h}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}\right] =𝟎.\displaystyle=\mathbf{0}. (29)

With a single confounder, this instrument is the exposure-weighted combined proxy of Section 2.3.1 without the factor si​gs_{ig}, and requirement (29) is condition (14). Since each confounder proxy dated t+st+s covaries only with the confounder shock dated t+st+s, and that shock does not move the confounders realized before t+st+s, requirement (29) is a triangular linear system in the weights. Specifically, its KK equations for date t+ℓt+\ell involve only 𝒘0,…,𝒘ℓ\bm{w}_{0},\ldots,\bm{w}_{\ell}, and the weights 𝒘ℓ\bm{w}_{\ell} on the proxies dated t+ℓt+\ell enter them only through the impact covariance Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0}. Because Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0} is nonsingular, this system has a unique solution, obtained recursively from the impact horizon,

𝒘ℓ\displaystyle\bm{w}_{\ell} =−Σr​z,0−1(𝐯ℓ+∑s=0ℓ−1Σr​z,ℓ−s𝒘s),ℓ=0,…,h,\displaystyle=-\Sigma_{rz,0}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{\ell}+\sum_{s=0}^{\ell-1}\Sigma_{rz,\ell-s}\bm{w}_{s}\right),\qquad\ell=0,\ldots,h, (30)

where 𝐯ℓ=𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​zg,t]\mathbf{v}_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}z_{g,t}] is the covariance of the confounders at horizon ℓ\ell with the treatment proxy and Σr​z,ℓ=𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​𝒛r,t′]\Sigma_{rz,\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}] is their covariance with their own proxies.

The weight 𝒘ℓ\bm{w}_{\ell} therefore offsets, across all KK confounders at once, the movement in 𝐑t+ℓ\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell} that remains after the treatment proxy and the offsets at earlier dates. With these weights, composite HELP-IV estimates

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhHELP​-​C​si​g​Gt+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,hC,\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}^{C}, (31)

using si​g​zg,t,hCs_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C} as the instrument for si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t}. The weights are determined by the moments 𝐯ℓ\mathbf{v}_{\ell} and Σr​z,ℓ\Sigma_{rz,\ell}, which can be estimated in two ways. With proxies, these moments are the sample cross moments of the aggregates and the proxies. When proxies are unavailable, shocks estimated from an SVAR replace the proxies in instrument (28), and these moments are implied by the estimated impulse responses and shock variances. In both cases, the estimated weights define the instrument z^g,t,hC\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C}. Section 4.2 derives its inference with proxies, and Appendix B.3 derives it with SVAR shocks.

The following proposition establishes that bhHELP​-​Cb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}} identifies the partial-equilibrium effect.

Proposition 3 (Composite HELP-IV).

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 2 hold for (24) and (25), with 𝔼⁡[Rt​zr,t]≠0\mathbb{E}[R_{t}z_{r,t}]\neq 0 replaced by detΣr​z,0≠0\det\Sigma_{rz,0}\neq 0. Then the weights satisfying (29) exist and are unique. If, in addition, 𝔼⁡[Gt​zg,t,hC]≠0\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}]\neq 0, the population coefficient on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} in (31) satisfies

bhHELP​-​C\displaystyle b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}} =βhP.\displaystyle=\beta_{h}^{P}. (32)

The proof is in Appendix A.5. The condition 𝔼⁡[Gt​zg,t,hC]≠0\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}]\neq 0 in the proposition is implied by G˘0≠0\breve{G}_{0}\neq 0, because this covariance is proportional to G˘0\breve{G}_{0}. Composite HELP-IV and multiple-confounder HELP-IV use the same weights in population and differ only in how they estimate them. The argument of Section 2.3.1 extends to KK confounders and applies equally to sample moments, so the sample coefficient of multiple-confounder HELP-IV equals the IV coefficient obtained with si​gs_{ig} times an instrument of the form in equation (28). The weights of this instrument set its sample cross moment with every path control to zero, after the unit and time effects are partialed out, and in population they solve requirement (29).

The two designs differ in finite samples. Multiple-confounder HELP-IV performs the offsetting implicitly, estimating the weights jointly with the effect of interest, so its instrument is exactly uncorrelated with the path controls in the sample. Composite HELP-IV instead estimates the weights in a separate first step, from recursion (30). This recursion imposes the causality restrictions 𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​𝒛r,t+s′]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\bm{z}_{r,t+s}^{\prime}]=\mathbf{0} for s>ℓs>\ell in place of their sample counterparts, so the composite instrument remains correlated with the path controls in the sample. The composite estimate therefore absorbs part of the dependence of the outcome on the confounder path, in proportion to the path coefficients cq,h,sc_{q,h,s} and to this remaining correlation. This part vanishes as the number of periods grows.

Each design has its own advantages. Composite HELP-IV is more stable when the proxies are noisy and the number of path controls K⁡(h+1)K(h+1) is large. Because composite HELP-IV estimates the offset weights in a separate first step, it keeps a single endogenous regressor for any KK and hh and inverts only the K×KK\times K impact covariance Σr​z,0\Sigma_{rz,0} in recursion (30). Multiple-confounder HELP-IV instead inverts the [1+K⁡(h+1)]×[1+K⁡(h+1)][1+K(h+1)]\times[1+K(h+1)] matrix of cross moments between its instruments and its regressors, which can then be nearly singular, so that some estimates take extreme values. By contrast, when the proxies are accurate and this matrix is well conditioned, multiple-confounder HELP-IV is more precise. Multiple-confounder HELP-IV sets the sample cross moments of its instrument with the path controls exactly to zero and thus avoids the finite-sample error that the composite estimate incurs by absorbing part of the dependence of the outcome on the confounder path. Multiple-confounder HELP-IV is also a standard one-step IV regression. Therefore, the two designs complement each other.

3.2.3.  Targeting-rule HELP-IV

Multiple-confounder HELP-IV and composite HELP-IV hold the path of every confounder fixed and therefore require a proxy for each confounder shock. This requirement is difficult to meet in some applications. This subsection relaxes it by requiring shock proxies only for the two-way confounders, whose shocks move the treatment. The one-way confounders, whose shocks move neither the treatment nor a two-way confounder (Assumption 1 below), require no proxies and can remain unspecified. By Proposition 1, a one-way confounder can generate only the exposure-correlation component of the HEDGE bias, which arises when exposure to the confounder is correlated with exposure to the treatment and the treatment shock moves the confounder. To correct this component, we draw on the targeting-rule approach of Manuel (2026), which removes the first of these two conditions and was originally developed for general-equilibrium biases in shift-share regressions.88 8 The target of Manuel (2026) is the direct effect of the treatment along its equilibrium path, an object that is well defined whether the general-equilibrium aggregates are one-way or two-way. Our target βhP\beta_{h}^{P} is instead evaluated along the treatment path obtained when the confounder paths are held fixed. The two treatment paths coincide for one-way confounders but generally differ for two-way ones, so the targeting rule serves our target only for one-way confounders.

We partition the confounders into a two-way block and a one-way block. We index the two-way confounders by q=1,…,K1q=1,\ldots,K_{1} and the one-way confounders by q=K1+1,…,Kq=K_{1}+1,\ldots,K. Equation (25) is maintained only for the two-way block, and we impose two assumptions, the first on the one-way block.

Assumption 1 (One-way confounders).

For q>K1q>K_{1}, j≤K1j\leq K_{1}, and ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0,

Gℓrq=0,Rj,ℓrq=0,G_{\ell}^{r_{q}}=0,\qquad R_{j,\ell}^{r_{q}}=0,

where Gℓrq=𝔼⁡[Gt+ℓ​ϵrq,t]/𝔼⁡[ϵrq,t2]G_{\ell}^{r_{q}}=\mathbb{E}[G_{t+\ell}\epsilon_{r_{q},t}]/\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{r_{q},t}^{2}] and Rj,ℓrq=𝔼⁡[Rj,t+ℓ​ϵrq,t]/𝔼⁡[ϵrq,t2]R_{j,\ell}^{r_{q}}=\mathbb{E}[R_{j,t+\ell}\epsilon_{r_{q},t}]/\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{r_{q},t}^{2}]. The matrix (Rq′,0rq)q,q′>K1(R_{q^{\prime},0}^{r_{q}})_{q,q^{\prime}>K_{1}} is nonsingular.

In words, the shocks of the one-way block affect neither the treatment nor any two-way confounder at any horizon, so offsetting them cannot change the controlled treatment path, either directly or through the two-way confounders. Because the impact matrix of this block is nonsingular, its paths can be offset without changing the two-way block.

The second assumption is a targeting rule, which governs the cross-sectional allocation of treatment exposure.

Assumption 2 (Targeting rule).

Let 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} be a vector of observed, predetermined, time-invariant characteristics that includes a constant and is independent of the aggregate process, with 𝔼⁡[𝐚i​𝐚i′]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}] nonsingular, and let si​g⟂=si​g−𝐚i′​𝔼​[𝐚i​𝐚i′]−1​𝔼​[𝐚i​si​g]s_{ig}^{\perp}=s_{ig}-\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}s_{ig}]. The residual satisfies Var⁡(si​g⟂)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig}^{\perp})>0 and 𝔼⁡[si​g⟂​si​rq]=0\mathbb{E}[s_{ig}^{\perp}s_{ir_{q}}]=0 for q=K1+1,…,Kq=K_{1}+1,\ldots,K.

Adapting the identifying condition of Manuel (2026), we obtain a sufficient condition for Assumption 2. Consider the conditional expectation of treatment exposure given 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} and the unit characteristics that determine exposure to the confounders. If this expectation is linear in 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} and does not depend on the other characteristics, then si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} is orthogonal to any function of those characteristics, including exposure to each one-way confounder. The assumption therefore holds for all one-way confounders simultaneously, without requiring the researcher to specify them.

Building on these assumptions, we identify βhP\beta_{h}^{P} by combining HELP-IV for the two-way block with the targeting rule of Manuel (2026) for the one-way block. At horizon hh, we estimate

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhHELP​-​T​si​g​Gt+∑q=1K1∑s=0hcq,h,s​si​g​Rq,t+s+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,hT,\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}T}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\sum_{q=1}^{K_{1}}\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{q,h,s}s_{ig}R_{q,t+s}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}^{\mathrm{T}}, (33)

and instrument si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} and {si​g​Rq,t+s}q≤K1,s=0,…,h\{s_{ig}R_{q,t+s}\}_{q\leq K_{1},\;s=0,\ldots,h} by si​g⟂​zg,ts_{ig}^{\perp}z_{g,t} and {si​g⟂​zrq,t+s}q≤K1,s=0,…,h\{s_{ig}^{\perp}z_{r_{q},t+s}\}_{q\leq K_{1},\;s=0,\ldots,h}, respectively. We refer to this design as targeting-rule HELP-IV, which requires no confounder proxy when K1=0K_{1}=0, because the path-control block is then empty. Because the instruments use only si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp}, Assumption 2 removes the one-way confounders from every IV moment. The design thus reduces to multiple-confounder HELP-IV for the two-way block, with si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} in place of si​gs_{ig} in the instruments, and its identification follows from Corollary 2. Assumption 1, in turn, ensures that holding the paths of the one-way confounders fixed would not alter the treatment path, so the reduced design still identifies βhP\beta_{h}^{P}. The following corollary formalizes this result, and its proof is in Appendix A.6.

Corollary 3 (Targeting-rule HELP-IV).

Suppose (4) and (24) hold for all KK confounders and the remaining conditions of Corollary 2 hold for the first K1K_{1} confounders, with si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} in place of si​gs_{ig} in the instruments, and the exposures si​rqs_{ir_{q}}, q>K1q>K_{1}, are predetermined and independent of the aggregate process. Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the population IV coefficient in (33) satisfies bhHELP​-​T=βhPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}T}}=\beta_{h}^{P}.

Using si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} in the instruments is equivalent in population to controlling for 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} interacted with time effects. With K1=0K_{1}=0, targeting-rule HELP-IV is therefore the method of Manuel (2026), applied with a treatment shock proxy as the instrument, and Corollary 3 shows that this method identifies βhP\beta_{h}^{P} when no confounder feeds back into the treatment, because the equilibrium treatment path then coincides with the controlled path.

3.3.  Forward-looking environment

The preceding sections maintain a backward-looking outcome equation in the data-generating process, in which the outcome depends only on current and lagged aggregates. In many macroeconomic and finance models, however, current outcomes can depend on expected future aggregates. Identifying the partial-equilibrium effect then requires holding the confounder path fixed both in expectation and ex post. In this subsection, we develop this extension for a single exposure margin and a single confounder, which isolates the role of expectations.99 9 The method extends to multiple confounders by stacking their paths and their contemporaneous and news shocks. It extends to multiple exposure margins by interacting the composite instrument introduced below with each margin, since the offset is common to all margins. We first state how the data-generating process changes and define the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect. We then show how composite HELP-IV can be extended to this environment.

The forward-looking environment differs from the backward-looking environment of Section 2.1 in the outcome equation and in the evolution of the aggregate process, while the exposure restriction in equation (3), which relates confounder exposure si​rs_{ir} to treatment exposure si​gs_{ig}, is unchanged. First, the outcome also responds to anticipated future values of both aggregates,

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+ρ​Yi,t−1+si​g​(∑ℓ=0pβℓ​Gt−ℓ+∑f=1Fζfg​𝔼t​Gt+f)\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\rho Y_{i,t-1}+s_{ig}\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\beta_{\ell}G_{t-\ell}+\sum_{f=1}^{F}\zeta_{f}^{g}\mathbb{E}_{t}G_{t+f}\right)
+si​r​(∑ℓ=0pγℓ​Rt−ℓ+∑f=1Fζfr​𝔼t​Rt+f)+ui​t,|ρ|<1,\displaystyle\quad+s_{ir}\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{p}\gamma_{\ell}R_{t-\ell}+\sum_{f=1}^{F}\zeta_{f}^{r}\mathbb{E}_{t}R_{t+f}\right)+u_{it},\qquad|\rho|<1, (34)

where 𝔼t​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{t}[\cdot] denotes the expectation conditional on aggregate information at date tt. Second, the aggregates are also driven by news shocks about the confounder, so that 𝐖t=(Gt,Rt)′\mathbf{W}_{t}=(G_{t},R_{t})^{\prime} satisfies

𝐖t\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{t} =∑j=0∞Ψjϵt−j,ϵt=(ϵg,t,ϵr,tE′,ϵo,t′)′,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\Psi_{j}\bm{\epsilon}_{t-j},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{t}=\left(\epsilon_{g,t},\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E\prime},\bm{\epsilon}_{o,t}^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}, (35)

where ϵr,tE=(ϵr,t,ϵr,t,1E,…,ϵr,t,dE)′\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}=(\epsilon_{r,t},\epsilon_{r,t,1}^{E},\ldots,\epsilon_{r,t,d}^{E})^{\prime} collects the contemporaneous shock ϵr,t\epsilon_{r,t} and dd news shocks for which proxies are available, and ϵo,t\bm{\epsilon}_{o,t} collects the remaining shocks. The news shocks are realized at date tt and move expectations of future values of RR. The shocks satisfy the conditions of equation (4), with G0g=1G_{0}^{g}=1 and each element of ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E} normalized to move RtR_{t} one for one on impact or, for a news shock that does not move RtR_{t} on impact, to move contemporaneously an observed variable one for one.

The forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect is the response of Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} to a movement in GtG_{t} caused by ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} when the confounder path is held fixed both ex post and in the expectations formed at dates tt through t+ht+h. As in equation (20) of Section 2.4, we express this effect in terms of shock responses. It divides the outcome response to an experiment that combines the treatment shock with offsetting shocks to RR by the impact movement of GtG_{t} under the same experiment. Relative to the backward-looking case, the experiment must satisfy two additional requirements. First, because Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} depends on expectations formed at date t+ht+h, the offset must cover Rt,…,Rt+HR_{t},\ldots,R_{t+H} for H≥h¯+FH\geq\bar{h}+F, where h¯\bar{h} is the largest horizon of interest. Second, because shocks realized after tt cannot alter the expectations formed at tt, the offsetting shocks must be dated tt, as in McKay and Wolf (2023). A single contemporaneous shock moves the path along one impulse response and therefore cannot offset an arbitrary path response over H+1H+1 dates. The experiment therefore also requires news shocks, which are realized at date tt but move the expected confounder at later dates. Let 𝐫Hg\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g} and 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} denote the responses of the path Rt,…,Rt+HR_{t},\ldots,R_{t+H} to ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and to the elements of ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}. The offsetting combination 𝐞HE\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E} of the date-tt shocks then holds this path fixed, 𝐫Hg+𝐑HE​𝐞HE=𝟎\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}+\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}=\mathbf{0}, when such a combination exists. Otherwise, it minimizes the remaining movement of the path, as we make precise below.

Under this experiment, the outcome moves by bh+(𝐞HE)′​𝐜hEb_{h}+(\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E})^{\prime}\mathbf{c}_{h}^{E}, where bhb_{h} and 𝐜hE\mathbf{c}_{h}^{E} are the outcome responses to ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and to ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}, defined by the population projection

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bh​si​g​ϵg,t+(𝐜hE)′​si​g​ϵr,tE+μi,h+λt,h+ei,t,h.\displaystyle=b_{h}s_{ig}\epsilon_{g,t}+\left(\mathbf{c}_{h}^{E}\right)^{\prime}s_{ig}\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+e_{i,t,h}. (36)

The treatment moves on impact by G˘0,HE=1+(𝐠0E)′​𝐞HE\breve{G}_{0,H}^{E}=1+(\mathbf{g}_{0}^{E})^{\prime}\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}, where 𝐠0E\mathbf{g}_{0}^{E} collects the impact responses of GtG_{t} to ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}. For given weights 𝐞HE\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}, the experiment therefore yields the ratio of the outcome response to the impact movement of the treatment,

βhE\displaystyle\beta_{h}^{E} =(G˘0,HE)−1​[bh+(𝐞HE)′​𝐜hE].\displaystyle=\left(\breve{G}_{0,H}^{E}\right)^{-1}\left[b_{h}+\left(\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}\right)^{\prime}\mathbf{c}_{h}^{E}\right]. (37)

We extend composite HELP-IV of Section 3.2.2 to identify βhE\beta_{h}^{E}. For each h=0,…,h¯h=0,\ldots,\bar{h}, the extension estimates the same regression as in that section,

Yi,t+h\displaystyle Y_{i,t+h} =bhE​-​HELP​si​g​Gt+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,hE,\displaystyle=b_{h}^{\mathrm{E\text{-}HELP}}s_{ig}G_{t}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}^{E}, (38)

and differs only in the instrument for si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t}. Let zg,t\mathrm{z}_{g,t} be a proxy for the treatment shock ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t}, and let 𝐳r,tE\bm{\mathrm{z}}_{r,t}^{E} collect proxies for the contemporaneous shock and the dd news confounder shocks in ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}. Each proxy is relevant for its own shock and exogenous, in the sense that it is orthogonal to all other shocks at all leads and lags, as in equations (8) and (12) and analogously for the news proxies. We write these proxies upright, because each is also normalized to have unit covariance with its own shock, by dividing it by its covariance with the variable that its shock moves one for one on impact. The composite instrument weights these proxies by the offsetting combination,

zg,tE\displaystyle\mathrm{z}_{g,t}^{E} =zg,t+(𝐞HE)′​𝐳r,tE,\displaystyle=\mathrm{z}_{g,t}+\left(\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}\right)^{\prime}\bm{\mathrm{z}}_{r,t}^{E}, (39)

and regression (38) instruments si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} by si​g​zg,tEs_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t}^{E}. Because each proxy has unit covariance with its own shock, 𝔼⁡[(Rt,…,Rt+H)′​zg,tE]=𝐫Hg+𝐑HE​𝐞HE\mathbb{E}[(R_{t},\ldots,R_{t+H})^{\prime}\mathrm{z}_{g,t}^{E}]=\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}+\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}. Holding the path fixed is therefore the forward-looking counterpart of requirement (29). This instrument reflects both requirements of the target experiment. First, its weights offset the confounder path through t+Ht+H. Second, it combines only proxies dated tt, including news-shock proxies. Unlike the backward-looking composite instrument, which holds the path fixed only ex post, this instrument also offsets the path in the expectations formed at tt. We refer to this design as E-HELP-IV.

The composite instrument in equation (39) is fully specified once its weights 𝐞HE\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E} are determined. Holding the path fixed requires 𝐫Hg+𝐑HE​𝐞HE=𝟎\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}+\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}=\mathbf{0}, a system of H+1H+1 equations in d+1d+1 weights, so the solution depends on the number of available news shocks. If this number equals the number of future dates to be offset, d=Hd=H, and 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} is nonsingular, the system has the unique solution 𝐞HE=−(𝐑HE)−1​𝐫Hg\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E}=-(\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E})^{-1}\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}. In most applications, however, the news shocks are fewer, d<Hd<H, and the system has more equations than weights. It then generically has no solution, so we instead take the weights that minimize the remaining movement of the path, given by the Moore–Penrose solution (Auclert et al., 2021),

𝐞HE\displaystyle\mathbf{e}_{H}^{E} =−(𝐑HE)+​𝐫Hg,\displaystyle=-\left(\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}\right)^{+}\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}, (40)

which reduces to the unique solution when 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} is nonsingular. In practice, 𝐫Hg\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g} and 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} are estimated, either from sample cross moments of the aggregates with the proxies or from an SVAR, and rescaling a proxy only rescales its weight. Composite HELP-IV treats the cases d=Hd=H and d<Hd<H within one framework. The benchmark HELP-IV design of Section 2.3 could also handle the case d=Hd=H, with the path controls si​g​Rt,…,si​g​Rt+Hs_{ig}R_{t},\ldots,s_{ig}R_{t+H} instrumented by the date-tt proxies, and is then exactly identified. With d<Hd<H, however, that design has fewer instruments than endogenous regressors and is under-identified. A pseudo-inverse solution of its moment conditions then depends on the units of the path controls. We therefore refer to the case d=Hd=H with 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} nonsingular and the case d<Hd<H as the exactly identified and the under-identified case of the offset.

As in the backward-looking case, the instrument applies the same shock combination to the treatment and the outcome, so bhE​-​HELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{E\text{-}HELP}} equals βhE\beta_{h}^{E} in equation (37) for any weights. Whether βhE\beta_{h}^{E} is the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect, however, depends on whether the weights hold the path fixed. In the exactly identified case, the offset is complete, so βhE\beta_{h}^{E} is that effect. In the under-identified case, the weights generally leave part of the path unabsorbed, and βhE\beta_{h}^{E} is then the effect of an experiment that offsets only the Euclidean projection of the path response on the column space of 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}, the part that the available date-tt shocks can offset. We refer to βhE\beta_{h}^{E} in both cases as the information-constrained effect, because it is constrained by the news shocks for which proxies are available, and it equals the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect when the offset is complete. We report the share of the path response left unabsorbed, ‖[𝐈H+1−𝐑HE​(𝐑HE)+]​𝐫Hg‖2/‖𝐫Hg‖2\|[\mathbf{I}_{H+1}-\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}(\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E})^{+}]\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}\|^{2}/\|\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g}\|^{2}, as a diagnostic of how far this experiment departs from the fixed-path experiment.1010 10 The share is zero if and only if 𝐫Hg\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g} lies in the column space of 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E}, in which case βhE\beta_{h}^{E} is the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect. The share alone does not bound the difference between the two effects, because that difference also depends on the outcome loadings and on the controlled first-stage denominator. The following proposition, whose proof is in Appendix A.7, covers both cases.

Proposition 4 (Forward-looking E-HELP-IV).

Suppose (3), (34), and (35) hold, the proxies satisfy the relevance, exogeneity, and normalization conditions above, the exposure-weighted proxies satisfy the panel exclusion restrictions, Var⁡(si​g)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{ig})>0, and the weights in (39) are (40). If G˘0,HE≠0\breve{G}_{0,H}^{E}\neq 0, the population coefficient on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} in (38), with instrument si​g​zg,tEs_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t}^{E}, satisfies bhE​-​HELP=βhEb_{h}^{\mathrm{E\text{-}HELP}}=\beta_{h}^{E}, where βhE\beta_{h}^{E} is given by (37).

The decomposition method of Donaldson (2026) has an analogous ex ante form for this environment, which also offsets the expected confounder path with date-tt shocks but, like its backward-looking form, normalizes by the unrestricted treatment response rather than the controlled one.

3.4.  Transformed treatments and outcomes

Sections 2–3.2 focus on the identification target βhP\beta_{h}^{P}, the ratio of the response of Yi,t+hY_{i,t+h} to that of si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} under the fixed-path experiment. In many applications, however, the treatment of interest is a unit-level variable rather than the exposure-weighted aggregate si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t}, and both the outcome and the treatment may be transformations that combine multiple dates within the window. The target is then the ratio of the response of a transformed outcome 𝒴i,t+h\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h} to that of a transformed unit-level treatment 𝒢i,t+h𝒢\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h_{\mathcal{G}}}, with h𝒢≤hh_{\mathcal{G}}\leq h, under the same fixed-path experiment, and we denote it by ℬhP\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P}.
