For example, the state-level cumulative fiscal multiplier of Donaldson (2026), which applies the cumulative definition of Ramey and Zubairy (2018) to the design of Nakamura and Steinsson (2014), is the ratio of state output cumulated from tt through t+ht+h to state government spending cumulated over the same window.

The data-generating process retains the outcome equation, the aggregate process, and the exposure restriction of Section 2, with a single exposure margin and a single confounder. To define ℬhP\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P}, we complete it with a transformed outcome and a unit-level treatment process. The transformed outcome is a linear combination of the outcomes Yi,t,…,Yi,t+hY_{i,t},\ldots,Y_{i,t+h},

with weights υi,j\upsilon_{i,j} that may differ across units and a predetermined term 𝒴i,t−10\mathcal{Y}^{0}_{i,t-1}. The weights and the predetermined term are measurable with respect to the information ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} available at date t−1t-1, which contains the history of the aggregates, the shocks, and the unit outcomes, together with the predetermined unit loadings. The treatment process 𝒢i,t+h𝒢\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h_{\mathcal{G}}} is specified in Assumption 3, under which it is determined by the shocks dated tt through t+h𝒢t+h_{\mathcal{G}}, by the state inherited from before the window, and by unit-specific disturbances. The horizon h𝒢≤hh_{\mathcal{G}}\leq h records when the treatment is measured, ranging from zero for a treatment dated tt to hh for a treatment that spans the outcome window.

The proof is in Appendix A.8. Intuitively, under Assumption 3 and the specification of 𝒴i,t+h\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h}, each transformation combines realizations at dates within the response window, with unit-specific weights and loadings, and adds components determined before the window opens. The dated path instruments fix the confounder path throughout the window, so the design recovers the controlled response of the within-window combination, including a cumulative sum. The weights υi,j\upsilon_{i,j} enter the numerator and the loadings 𝐝i,j\mathbf{d}_{i,j} the denominator of each unit’s ratio, and the common ratio in equation (43) ensures that the ratio does not vary across units. The design also removes the components 𝒴i,t−10\mathcal{Y}^{0}_{i,t-1} and 𝒢i,t−10\mathcal{G}^{0}_{i,t-1}, because they are orthogonal to the instruments, which are unpredictable from pre-window information. The same design extends to the environments of Sections 3.1–3.3 once its instruments are replaced. With multiple exposure margins or confounders, the instruments of Sections 3.1 and 3.2 apply. In the forward-looking environment of Section 3.3, the composite instrument in equation (39) replaces the dated proxies, as in the fiscal application of Section 6.1.

3.4.1.  Aggregate shifters and omitted-history bias

Previous applied work estimates targets defined on transformed treatments and outcomes with a shift-share IV regression (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2014; Chodorow-Reich, 2019; Donaldson, 2026),

𝒴i,t+h\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h} =ℬh​𝒢i,t+h𝒢+μi,h+λt,h+vi,t,h,\displaystyle=\mathcal{B}_{h}\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h_{\mathcal{G}}}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+v_{i,t,h}, (46)

in which the transformed treatment is instrumented by the shift-share variable si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} and the path controls are omitted. We denote the resulting IV coefficient by ℬhSS\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}. This regression is a TWFE-IV local projection, but its treatment instrument is the exposure-weighted aggregate treatment itself rather than the exposure-weighted proxy of Section 2.2. In what follows, we first characterize the bias of ℬhSS\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}, which in addition to the HEDGE bias contains a component that arises because the shifter GtG_{t} is not an innovation. We then explain why the HELP-IV design in regression (44) removes both components and how a treatment instrument that is unpredictable from pre-window information can be obtained in practice.

To characterize the bias of ℬhSS\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}, we compare it with ℬhTWFE\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}, the coefficient in regression (46) when the treatment is instead instrumented by the proxy si​g​zg,ts_{ig}z_{g,t} of equation (8), as in the TWFE-IV design of Section 2.2. Because the proxy is a date-tt innovation, the bias of ℬhTWFE\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}} is the HEDGE bias alone. The comparison therefore isolates the additional bias from the shift-share variable, the omitted-history bias. Write Gt=∑ς∈{g,r}∑s≥0ψς,sG​ϵς,t−sG_{t}=\sum_{\varsigma\in\{g,r\}}\sum_{s\geq 0}\psi^{G}_{\varsigma,s}\epsilon_{\varsigma,t-s}, with ψς,sG=[Ψs]G,ς\psi^{G}_{\varsigma,s}=[\Psi_{s}]_{G,\varsigma} from equation (4) and σς2=Var⁡(ϵς,t)\sigma_{\varsigma}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{\varsigma,t}), let 𝒮ς,ℓ𝒴=𝔼⁡[s˙i​g​∂𝒴i,t+h/∂ϵς,t+h−ℓ]\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{Y}}_{\varsigma,\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\dot{s}_{ig}\,\partial\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h}/\partial\epsilon_{\varsigma,t+h-\ell}] and 𝒮ς,ℓ𝒢=𝔼⁡[s˙i​g​∂𝒢i,t+h𝒢/∂ϵς,t+h−ℓ]\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{\varsigma,\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\dot{s}_{ig}\,\partial\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h_{\mathcal{G}}}/\partial\epsilon_{\varsigma,t+h-\ell}] denote the exposure-weighted responses of the transformed outcome and treatment to ϵς,t+h−ℓ\epsilon_{\varsigma,t+h-\ell} without holding the confounder path fixed. The index ℓ\ell is the distance from the shock date to t+ht+h, so ℓ=h+s\ell=h+s refers to the shock dated t−st-s. Define

ΦhG\displaystyle\Phi_{h}^{G} =∑ς∈{g,r}∑s≥0ψς,sG​σς2​𝒮ς,h+s𝒢.\displaystyle=\sum_{\varsigma\in\{g,r\}}\sum_{s\geq 0}\psi^{G}_{\varsigma,s}\sigma_{\varsigma}^{2}\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{\varsigma,h+s}. (47)
Proposition 6 (HEDGE and omitted-history bias).

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 5 hold, the exposure-weighted shifter si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} satisfies the exclusion restrictions of Assumption 3(iii), ΦhG≠0\Phi_{h}^{G}\neq 0, 𝒮g,h𝒢≠0\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{g,h}\neq 0, and ψr,0G=0\psi^{G}_{r,0}=0. Then ℬhTWFE=𝒮g,h𝒴/𝒮g,h𝒢\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}=\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{Y}}_{g,h}/\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{g,h} and

ℬhSS−ℬhP\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P} =ℬhTWFE−ℬhP⏟HEDGE bias\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P}}_{\text{HEDGE bias}}
+(ΦhG)−1​∑ς∈{g,r}∑s≥1ψς,sG​σς2​(𝒮ς,h+s𝒴−ℬhTWFE​𝒮ς,h+s𝒢)⏟omitted-history bias.\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{(\Phi_{h}^{G})^{-1}\sum_{\varsigma\in\{g,r\}}\sum_{s\geq 1}\psi^{G}_{\varsigma,s}\sigma_{\varsigma}^{2}\left(\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{Y}}_{\varsigma,h+s}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{\varsigma,h+s}\right)}_{\text{omitted-history bias}}. (48)

The proof is in Appendix A.9. The condition ψr,0G=0\psi^{G}_{r,0}=0 means that GtG_{t} contains no contemporaneous confounder shock, which rules out impact feedback from the confounder to the treatment. Without it, ℬhSS\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}} contains a third term, (ΦhG)−1​ψr,0G​σr2​(𝒮r,h𝒴−ℬhTWFE​𝒮r,h𝒢)(\Phi_{h}^{G})^{-1}\psi^{G}_{r,0}\sigma_{r}^{2}(\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{Y}}_{r,h}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{G}}_{r,h}), from the contemporaneous confounder shock, which HELP-IV also removes. The omitted-history bias arises because GtG_{t} carries shocks dated before the window opens. These shocks reach the transformed treatment through 𝒢i,t−10\mathcal{G}^{0}_{i,t-1} and the transformed outcome through 𝒴i,t−10\mathcal{Y}^{0}_{i,t-1}, the lagged aggregates in equation (2), the persistence of Yi,t+jY_{i,t+j}, and the aggregates dated tt through t+ht+h, which also carry them, so the coefficient mixes their effects with the response to the current shock. The bias therefore vanishes generically only if 𝔼⁡[Gt∣ℱt−1]=0\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0, that is, only if GtG_{t} is itself an innovation. The term 𝔼⁡[Gt∣ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] is the expected value of the shifter given pre-window information, so the omitted-history bias is the time-series counterpart of the bias that recentering removes in shift-share designs (Borusyak and Hull, 2023). This requirement is the condition that the shifter be unpredictable, under which Manuel (2026) shows that shift-share regressions, with controls for the rule that assigns exposure, recover the units’ direct responses to the treatment path. Proposition 6 goes one step further, because it quantifies the bias when this condition fails. It also shows that the HEDGE bias remains even when GtG_{t} is an innovation, so that the bias must be removed separately by holding the confounder path fixed.

HELP-IV removes both biases simultaneously. On the one hand, its treatment instrument si​g​zg,ts_{ig}z_{g,t} is unpredictable from pre-window information, which excludes the past shocks behind the omitted-history bias ℬhSS−ℬhTWFE\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}. On the other hand, its path instruments si​g​zr,t,…,si​g​zr,t+hs_{ig}z_{r,t},\ldots,s_{ig}z_{r,t+h} hold the confounder path fixed, which removes the HEDGE bias ℬhTWFE−ℬhP\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{TWFE}}-\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P}.

The remaining practical question is how to obtain a treatment instrument with this property. When an external proxy satisfying equation (8) is available, it serves this role directly. When no external proxy is available, a treatment shock identified from an SVAR has the same property if the moving-average representation is invertible and the identifying restrictions separate the treatment shock from the contemporaneous confounder shock (Barnichon and Mesters, 2020). Appendix B accounts for its estimation.

Section summary. The extensions in this section differ in their environments but rest on one identification principle. As in Section 2.3, the treatment coefficient of each design equals the coefficient obtained with a single instrument, the exposure-weighted combined proxy. Its weights render it uncorrelated with every value of the relevant confounder paths, or with as much of the expected path as the available news shocks allow, and it is unpredictable from information before the treatment shock. This instrument therefore moves the treatment while holding those paths fixed, so that the reduced form and the first stage are measured under the same fixed-path experiment and their ratio identifies the partial-equilibrium effect, or the information-constrained effect when the news shocks are few. Each extension tailors the design to the environment that a class of empirical applications faces, yet every such adaptation preserves this principle. An advantage of this shared foundation is that every design remains an IV regression, so that estimation and inference for all designs share a common framework, which the next section develops.

4.  Inference for HELP-IV designs

This section develops inference for the HELP-IV designs of Sections 2 and 3. We focus our discussion on the benchmark HELP-IV design of Section 2, whose sampling uncertainty arises, with proxies, only from the IV moment, and composite HELP-IV, whose sampling uncertainty arises from both the IV moment and the estimated offset weights on the confounder proxies. Inference for the designs with multiple exposure margins, multiple confounders, the targeting rule, forward-looking outcomes, and transformed treatments and outcomes is discussed briefly in this section and developed in detail in Appendix C. The section closes with shocks estimated from an SVAR.

4.1.  Benchmark HELP-IV

The sample analogue of the HELP-IV moment system in Section 2.3 delivers the estimator

ϑ^h=Σ^h−1​1N​T​∑t,i𝐙~i​t,h​Y~i,t+h,Σ^h=1N​T​∑t,i𝐙~i​t,h​𝑿~i​t,h′,\widehat{\bm{\vartheta}}_{h}=\widehat{\Sigma}_{h}^{-1}\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{t,i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widetilde{Y}_{i,t+h},\qquad\widehat{\Sigma}_{h}=\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{t,i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{it,h}^{\prime}, (49)

where NN is the number of units, TT is the number of dates, 𝐙i​t,h\mathbf{Z}_{it,h} collects the exposure-weighted proxies, 𝑿i​t,h\bm{X}_{it,h} collects the exposure-weighted treatment and confounder path, and a tilde now denotes sample residualization on the unit and time effects and on any included controls, such as the lagged outcome. The coefficient on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t}, b^hHELP=e1′​ϑ^h\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=e_{1}^{\prime}\widehat{\bm{\vartheta}}_{h}, estimates the partial-equilibrium effect βhP\beta_{h}^{P}, where e1e_{1} is the first unit vector.

To characterize the asymptotic variance of this estimator, we define the population counterpart Σh\Sigma_{h} of Σ^h\widehat{\Sigma}_{h} and the long-run variance Ωh\Omega_{h} of the date-level IV moment N−1​∑i𝐙~i​t,h​ξ~i,t,hN^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h},

Σh=𝔼⁡[limN→∞1N​∑i𝐙~i​t,h​𝑿~i​t,h′],Ωh=limN,T→∞Var⁡(1T​∑t1N​∑i𝐙~i​t,h​ξ~i,t,h),\Sigma_{h}=\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{it,h}^{\prime}\right],\qquad\Omega_{h}=\lim_{N,T\to\infty}\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h}\right), (50)

where ξi,t,h\xi_{i,t,h} is the error of the local projection at the population coefficients. The date-level IV moment provides one observation per date, because all units share the same aggregate proxies at a given date. The estimator therefore converges at rate T\sqrt{T} rather than N​T\sqrt{NT} (Almuzara and Sancibrián, 2025), and Ωh\Omega_{h} normalizes the sum over dates by 1/T1/\sqrt{T}.

We estimate the long-run variance with a kernel estimator

Ω^h=1T​∑t=1T∑τ=1Tk⁡(t−τbT)​(1N​∑i𝐙~i​t,h​ξ^i,t,h)​(1N​∑i𝐙~i​τ,h​ξ^i,τ,h)′,\widehat{\Omega}_{h}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}k\Bigl(\frac{t-\tau}{b_{T}}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{it,h}\widehat{\xi}_{i,t,h}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i\tau,h}\widehat{\xi}_{i,\tau,h}\Bigr)^{\prime}, (51)

where ξ^i,t,h\widehat{\xi}_{i,t,h} denotes the fitted residuals, kk is a kernel with k⁡(0)=1k(0)=1, such as the Bartlett kernel k⁡(x)=(1−|x|)+k(x)=(1-|x|)_{+}, and bTb_{T} is the bandwidth. The kernel estimator is consistent for Ωh\Omega_{h} when bT→∞b_{T}\to\infty with bT=o⁡(T)b_{T}=o(\sqrt{T}) and the date-level IV moment has finite fourth moments and summable fourth-order cumulants (see Proposition C.5 for the proof). Because the estimator first averages the moment over units at each date and then weights the dates by the kernel, the resulting standard errors are robust to any correlation across units at a given date, provided the cross-sectional approximation error is negligible (Assumption C.1), and to serial correlation across dates, which the common shocks induce.

The following proposition establishes the asymptotic distribution of b^hHELP\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}, which rests on a central limit theorem for the date-level IV moment under regularity conditions on its serial dependence, the rank of the first stage, and the cross-sectional approximation error (Assumption C.1 in the appendix).

Proposition 7 (Inference for HELP-IV).

Under the regularity conditions in Assumption C.1, the conditions of Proposition 2, and Ω^h→𝑝Ωh\widehat{\Omega}_{h}\xrightarrow{p}\Omega_{h},

TV^h−1/2(b^hHELP−βhP)→𝑑N(0,1),\sqrt{T}\,\widehat{V}_{h}^{-1/2}\bigl(\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}-\beta_{h}^{P}\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1), (52)

where V^h=e1′Σ^h−1Ω^hΣ^h−1′e1\widehat{V}_{h}=e_{1}^{\prime}\widehat{\Sigma}_{h}^{-1}\widehat{\Omega}_{h}\widehat{\Sigma}_{h}^{-1\prime}e_{1}, V^h→𝑝Vh\widehat{V}_{h}\xrightarrow{p}V_{h}, and Vh=e1′Σh−1ΩhΣh−1′e1V_{h}=e_{1}^{\prime}\Sigma_{h}^{-1}\Omega_{h}\Sigma_{h}^{-1\prime}e_{1}.

The proof is in Appendix C.5. The normal approximation requires a controlled first stage that is strong relative to its sampling error. With weak proxies, the approximation can be poor, and Appendix C.11 gives an Anderson–Rubin-type confidence set for bhHELPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}} that remains valid when the controlled first stage is weak.

Proposition 7 extends to multiple-confounder HELP-IV and to HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins, because both designs keep the date-level IV moment and only add regressors and instruments, which enlarges Σh\Sigma_{h} and Ωh\Omega_{h}. The treatment coefficient remains a scalar with multiple confounders, so Proposition 7 holds with these larger matrices under the conditions of Corollary 2 in place of those of Proposition 2. The treatment coefficient becomes a vector with multiple exposure margins, because each regressor is interacted with each margin. This vector, identified under the conditions of Corollary 1, requires a matrix that selects it in place of e1e_{1}, and VhV_{h} becomes its covariance matrix, which also delivers inference on contrasts among these coefficients (Proposition C.2).

Proposition 7 also extends to targeting-rule HELP-IV (Section 3.2.3), but inference must then account for a sample imbalance in its instruments. This imbalance arises because the residual exposure si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} is orthogonal to exposure to the one-way confounders in the population but only up to order N−1/2N^{-1/2} in a sample. The imbalance leaves a component of the one-way confounders in the IV moment, and this component does not average out because the imbalance is fixed over time. The component therefore generally adds a cross-sectional sampling term to the variance. This term is zero in every sample when exposure to each one-way confounder lies in the span of the characteristics 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i}, and it is negligible under population balance when T/N→0T/N\to 0 (Proposition C.4). When the exposures to the one-way confounders and their path coefficients are identified, the term has a sample analogue, which we add to the time-series variance (Appendix C.8). When they are not, the time-series standard error is complete only in these two cases, and it understates the uncertainty when balance holds only in the population and T/NT/N does not vanish.

4.2.  Composite HELP-IV

Composite HELP-IV offers an alternative design for multiple confounders and for forward-looking partial-equilibrium effects. Its inference, however, differs from that in Section 4.1, because the design first estimates the weights on the confounder proxies and then constructs the instrument from these estimates. With the composite instrument, the regression in Section 3.2.2 delivers the estimator

b^hHELP​-​C=(∑t,isi​g​z^g,t,hC~​si​g​Gt~)−1​∑t,isi​g​z^g,t,hC~​Y~i,t+h,\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}}=\Bigl(\sum_{t,i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C}}\,\widetilde{s_{ig}G_{t}}\Bigr)^{-1}\sum_{t,i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C}}\,\widetilde{Y}_{i,t+h}, (53)

where z^g,t,hC=zg,t+∑s=0h𝒘^s′​𝒛r,t+s\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C}=z_{g,t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}\widehat{\bm{w}}_{s}^{\prime}\bm{z}_{r,t+s} is the estimated composite instrument.

The estimated weights 𝒘^ℓ\widehat{\bm{w}}_{\ell} solve the sample analogue of the recursion in Section 3.2.2,

𝒘^ℓ=−Σ^r​z,0−1(𝐯^ℓ+∑s=0ℓ−1Σ^r​z,ℓ−s𝒘^s),ℓ=0,…,h,\widehat{\bm{w}}_{\ell}=-\widehat{\Sigma}_{rz,0}^{-1}\Bigl(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\ell}+\sum_{s=0}^{\ell-1}\widehat{\Sigma}_{rz,\ell-s}\widehat{\bm{w}}_{s}\Bigr),\qquad\ell=0,\ldots,h, (54)

with the sample cross moments

𝐯^ℓ\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\ell} =1T​∑t(𝐑t+ℓ−𝐑¯ℓ)​(zg,t−z¯g),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}(\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}-\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell})(z_{g,t}-\bar{z}_{g}), (55)
Σ^r​z,ℓ\displaystyle\widehat{\Sigma}_{rz,\ell} =1T​∑t(𝐑t+ℓ−𝐑¯ℓ)​(𝒛r,t−𝒛¯r)′,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}(\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}-\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell})(\bm{z}_{r,t}-\bar{\bm{z}}_{r})^{\prime},

where bars denote sample means. These sample cross moments suffice for the recursion, because covariance stationarity makes the covariance of 𝐑t+ℓ\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell} with 𝒛r,t+s\bm{z}_{r,t+s} depend only on ℓ−s\ell-s and the causality restrictions set it to zero for s>ℓs>\ell.

The estimation error in the weights is governed by the weight equations, the stacked form of this recursion,

Σ¯^r​z,h​𝒘¯^h+𝐯¯^h=𝟎,\widehat{\underline{\Sigma}}_{rz,h}\widehat{\underline{\bm{w}}}_{h}+\widehat{\underline{\mathbf{v}}}_{h}=\mathbf{0}, (56)

whose population counterpart is Σ¯r​z,h​𝒘¯h+𝐯¯h=𝟎\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}\underline{\bm{w}}_{h}+\underline{\mathbf{v}}_{h}=\mathbf{0}. Here, 𝒘¯h=(𝒘0′,…,𝒘h′)′\underline{\bm{w}}_{h}=(\bm{w}_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,\bm{w}_{h}^{\prime})^{\prime} stacks the weights, 𝐯¯h=(𝐯0′,…,𝐯h′)′\underline{\mathbf{v}}_{h}=(\mathbf{v}_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{h}^{\prime})^{\prime} stacks the cross moments of the confounders with the treatment proxy, and Σ¯r​z,h=(Σr​z,ℓ−s𝟏{s≤ℓ})ℓ,s=0h\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}=(\Sigma_{rz,\ell-s}{\bf 1}\{s\leq\ell\})_{\ell,s=0}^{h} is the block lower-triangular matrix of their cross moments with the confounder proxies, whose zero blocks reflect the causality restrictions.

To characterize the asymptotic variance of the composite estimator, we define the population cross moment ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C} of the instrument and the treatment and the derivative D𝒘s,hD_{\bm{w}_{s},h} of the composite IV moment N−1​∑isi​g​zg,t,hC~​ξ~i,t,hCN^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}}\,\widetilde{\xi}^{C}_{i,t,h} with respect to the weights,

ΣhC=𝔼⁡[limN→∞1N​∑isi​g​zg,t,hC~​si​g​Gt~],D𝒘s,h=𝔼⁡[limN→∞1N​∑isi​g​𝒛r,t+s′~​ξ~i,t,hC],\Sigma_{h}^{C}=\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}}\,\widetilde{s_{ig}G_{t}}\right],\qquad D_{\bm{w}_{s},h}=\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\bm{z}_{r,t+s}^{\prime}}\,\widetilde{\xi}^{C}_{i,t,h}\right], (57)

where ξi,t,hC\xi^{C}_{i,t,h} is the error of the composite regression at the population coefficient, and D𝒘,h=(D𝒘0,h,…,D𝒘h,h)D_{\bm{w},h}=(D_{\bm{w}_{0},h},\ldots,D_{\bm{w}_{h},h}) collects these derivatives. The derivative is generally nonzero, because the composite error ξi,t,hC\xi^{C}_{i,t,h} contains the omitted path terms ∑q∑scq,h,s​si​g​Rq,t+s\sum_{q}\sum_{s}c_{q,h,s}s_{ig}R_{q,t+s}, which are correlated with the confounder proxies. It vanishes when the confounder path does not affect the outcome (Proposition C.1). The asymptotic variance of b^hHELP​-​C\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}} combines the long-run variance Ωg​g,hC\Omega_{gg,h}^{C} of the composite IV moment, the long-run variance Ωw​w,hC\Omega_{ww,h}^{C} of the weight equations, and their long-run covariance Ωg​w,hC\Omega_{gw,h}^{C},

VhC=(ΣhC)−2{Ωg​g,hC−2Ωg​w,hCΣ¯r​z,h−1′D𝒘,h′+D𝒘,hΣ¯r​z,h−1Ωw​w,hCΣ¯r​z,h−1′D𝒘,h′}.V_{h}^{C}=(\Sigma_{h}^{C})^{-2}\bigl\{\Omega_{gg,h}^{C}-2\,\Omega_{gw,h}^{C}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1\prime}D_{\bm{w},h}^{\prime}+D_{\bm{w},h}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1}\Omega_{ww,h}^{C}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1\prime}D_{\bm{w},h}^{\prime}\bigr\}. (58)

With known weights, the variance reduces to (ΣhC)−2​Ωg​g,hC(\Sigma_{h}^{C})^{-2}\Omega_{gg,h}^{C}, the first term in braces. Estimating the weights adds the other two terms, because Σ¯r​z,h−1\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1} maps the error in the weight equations into an error in the weights, and D𝒘,hD_{\bm{w},h} maps that error into the IV moment. The last term, D𝒘,hΣ¯r​z,h−1Ωw​w,hCΣ¯r​z,h−1′D𝒘,h′D_{\bm{w},h}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1}\Omega_{ww,h}^{C}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1\prime}D_{\bm{w},h}^{\prime}, is the variance of this transmitted error. The middle term, −2Ωg​w,hCΣ¯r​z,h−1′D𝒘,h′-2\,\Omega_{gw,h}^{C}\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1\prime}D_{\bm{w},h}^{\prime}, is twice its covariance with the IV moment, which can take either sign, so estimating the weights can raise or lower the variance.

To estimate this variance, we collect its three long-run objects in one matrix, the long-run variance of the composite IV moment stacked with the weight equations,

ΩhC=limN,T→∞Var⁡(1T​∑t(N−1​∑isi​g​zg,t,hC~​ξ~i,t,hC𝐑t​zg,t+𝐑t​𝒛r,t′​𝒘0𝐑t+h​zg,t+∑s=0h𝐑t+h−s​𝒛r,t′​𝒘s)).\Omega_{h}^{C}=\lim_{N,T\to\infty}\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t}\begin{pmatrix}N^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{s_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}}\,\widetilde{\xi}^{C}_{i,t,h}\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{R}_{t}z_{g,t}+\mathbf{R}_{t}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}\bm{w}_{0}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{R}_{t+h}z_{g,t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}\mathbf{R}_{t+h-s}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}\bm{w}_{s}\end{pmatrix}\right). (59)

The first row of the vector is the composite IV moment, and the remaining rows are the date-tt terms of the weight equations. Accordingly, Ωg​g,hC\Omega_{gg,h}^{C} is the first diagonal element of ΩhC\Omega_{h}^{C}, Ωw​w,hC\Omega_{ww,h}^{C} is its lower-right block, and Ωg​w,hC\Omega_{gw,h}^{C} is the remainder of its first row. We estimate ΩhC\Omega_{h}^{C} by applying the kernel estimator in equation (51) to this vector, evaluated at the estimated instrument, the fitted residuals, and the estimated weights. Replacing the blocks of ΩhC\Omega_{h}^{C}, and ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C}, D𝒘,hD_{\bm{w},h}, and Σ¯r​z,h\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}, in equation (58) with their sample counterparts then yields V^hC\widehat{V}_{h}^{C}.

The following proposition establishes the asymptotic distribution of b^hHELP​-​C\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}}, which rests on a central limit theorem for this vector.

Proposition 8 (Inference for composite HELP-IV).

Under Assumption C.1, the conditions of Proposition 3, and Ω^hC→𝑝ΩhC\widehat{\Omega}_{h}^{C}\xrightarrow{p}\Omega_{h}^{C},

T(V^hC)−1/2(b^hHELP​-​C−βhP)→𝑑N(0,1),\sqrt{T}\,(\widehat{V}_{h}^{C})^{-1/2}\bigl(\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C}}-\beta_{h}^{P}\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1), (60)

where V^hC→𝑝VhC\widehat{V}_{h}^{C}\xrightarrow{p}V_{h}^{C} and VhCV_{h}^{C} is given by (58).

The proof is in Appendix C.5. Proposition 8 extends to three further environments. First, with multiple exposure margins (Section 3.1), composite HELP-IV instruments 𝐬i​g​Gt\mathbf{s}_{ig}G_{t} with 𝐬i​g​zg,t,hC\mathbf{s}_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C} and identifies the margin-specific effects (Proposition C.1). The weights depend only on aggregate moments, so a single composite instrument serves all margins. With the exposure vector 𝐬i​g\mathbf{s}_{ig} in place of si​gs_{ig}, the composite IV moment, ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C}, and D𝒘s,hD_{\bm{w}_{s},h} become M×1M\times 1, M×MM\times M, and M×KM\times K, and the matrix counterpart of equation (58) is the covariance matrix of the margin-specific coefficients. Second, with forward-looking outcomes (Section 3.3), the weights change, because E-HELP-IV confines the composite instrument to proxies dated tt. These weights are estimated from sample cross moments of the confounder path with the date-tt proxies. The unit-covariance normalization of Section 3.3 is not imposed, because rescaling the proxies rescales the weights and leaves the composite instrument unchanged (Appendix C.3). The estimated weights are differentiable in these moments, with Jacobian WEW^{E}, when 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} has full column rank (Lemma C.2). Accordingly, WEW^{E} replaces −Σ¯r​z,h−1-\underline{\Sigma}_{rz,h}^{-1}, the derivative with respect to these weights replaces D𝒘,hD_{\bm{w},h}, and the cross moments that determine these weights replace the weight equations. Proposition 8 then holds with the information-constrained effect βhE\beta_{h}^{E} in place of βhP\beta_{h}^{P}, under the conditions of Proposition 4. Third, with transformed treatments and outcomes (Section 3.4), the regression changes, because 𝒴i,t+h\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h} replaces the outcome and 𝒢i,t+h𝒢\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h_{\mathcal{G}}} replaces the treatment regressor, with the same instruments and weights. Propositions 7 and 8 then hold with the generalized partial-equilibrium effect ℬhP\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P} of equation (43) in place of βhP\beta_{h}^{P}, under the conditions of Proposition 5, with Σh\Sigma_{h}, Ωh\Omega_{h}, ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C}, D𝒘,hD_{\bm{w},h}, and ΩhC\Omega_{h}^{C} computed from the transformed regression. The extensions combine. For example, E-HELP-IV for a cumulative multiplier uses the transformed regression with the forward-looking weights.

Shocks estimated from an SVAR can also serve as instruments in place of the proxies, as in both applications (Barnichon and Mesters, 2020). This step assumes that the aggregates follow a correctly specified SVAR of finite order whose shocks can be recovered from current and past aggregates, an assumption that the identification results of Sections 2 and 3 do not require. The sampling error of the SVAR then propagates to the coefficient through the instruments and, for composite HELP-IV, through the weights, which the fitted responses now determine. We therefore further generalize Propositions 7 and 8 by stacking the SVAR estimating equations with the IV moment (Propositions B.1 and B.2). The variance then also contains the variance of this sampling error and its covariance with the IV moment, so this correction, as with the weights, can raise or lower the standard error. The three extensions in the previous paragraph carry over, because in each case the estimated SVAR enters through the instruments and the weights (Appendix B.4).

5.  Monte Carlo simulations

This section uses Monte Carlo simulations to assess the identification and inference performance of the HELP-IV designs. We first consider a single confounder, for which we evaluate HELP-IV in the backward-looking environment and E-HELP-IV in the forward-looking environment and benchmark both designs against TWFE-IV and the decomposition method of Donaldson (2026). We then consider multiple confounders, for which we compare the performance of multiple-confounder HELP-IV, composite HELP-IV, and targeting-rule HELP-IV.

5.1.  A single confounder

5.1.1.  Data-generating process

The outcome equation is

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+0.37​Yi,t−1+si​g​(0.62​Gt+0.28​Gt−1−0.13​Gt−2+ζ1g​𝔼t​Gt+1+ζ2g​𝔼t​Gt+2)\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+0.37\,Y_{i,t-1}+s_{ig}\bigl(0.62\,G_{t}+0.28\,G_{t-1}-0.13\,G_{t-2}+\zeta^{g}_{1}\mathbb{E}_{t}G_{t+1}+\zeta^{g}_{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}G_{t+2}\bigr)
+si​r​(−0.45​Rt+0.21​Rt−1+0.09​Rt−2+ζ1r​𝔼t​Rt+1+ζ2r​𝔼t​Rt+2)+ui​t.\displaystyle\quad+s_{ir}\bigl(-0.45\,R_{t}+0.21\,R_{t-1}+0.09\,R_{t-2}+\zeta^{r}_{1}\mathbb{E}_{t}R_{t+1}+\zeta^{r}_{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}R_{t+2}\bigr)+u_{it}.

In the backward-looking environment, the coefficients on expectations are zero. In the forward-looking environment, (ζ1g,ζ2g,ζ1r,ζ2r)=(0.30,0.12,−0.25,0.10)(\zeta^{g}_{1},\zeta^{g}_{2},\zeta^{r}_{1},\zeta^{r}_{2})=(0.30,0.12,-0.25,0.10), so the outcome has a forward-looking horizon of F=2F=2 periods. The exposures si​gs_{ig} and si​rs_{ir} are related by

si​r=0.8​si​g+uir​g,s_{ir}=0.8\,s_{ig}+u_{i}^{rg},

so exposure to the confounder rises with exposure to the treatment. The aggregate block is an SVAR(2) with two-way general equilibrium,

Gt\displaystyle G_{t} =0.5​Rt+0.70​Gt−1+0.03​Rt−1−0.10​Gt−2+ϵg,t,\displaystyle=0.5\,R_{t}+0.70\,G_{t-1}+0.03\,R_{t-1}-0.10\,G_{t-2}+\epsilon_{g,t},
Rt\displaystyle R_{t} =0.5​Gt+0.05​Gt−1+0.10​Rt−1−0.05​Rt−2+ϵr,t+∑ℓ=16ϵr,t−ℓ,ℓE,\displaystyle=0.5\,G_{t}+0.05\,G_{t-1}+0.10\,R_{t-1}-0.05\,R_{t-2}+\epsilon_{r,t}+\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{6}\epsilon^{E}_{r,t-\ell,\ell},

where ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and ϵr,t\epsilon_{r,t} are the structural shocks to the treatment and to the confounder, and the news shock ϵr,t,ℓE\epsilon^{E}_{r,t,\ell}, ℓ=1,…,6\ell=1,\ldots,6, is realized at date tt and shifts Rt+ℓR_{t+\ell}. The news shocks are present only in the forward-looking environment. We assume that the instruments are proxies that measure the shocks with error, generated by zx,t=ϵx,t+ηx,tz_{x,t}=\epsilon_{x,t}+\eta_{x,t} for x∈{g,r}x\in\{g,r\} and by zr,t,ℓE=ϵr,t,ℓE+ηr,t,ℓEz^{E}_{r,t,\ell}=\epsilon^{E}_{r,t,\ell}+\eta^{E}_{r,t,\ell} for the news shocks. All primitive random variables are mutually independent and normal with mean zero. The measurement errors have standard deviation 0.50.5, and all other primitive random variables are standard normal, including the unit and time effects μi\mu_{i} and λt\lambda_{t}, the exposure si​gs_{ig}, the disturbances uir​gu_{i}^{rg} and ui​tu_{it}, and the shocks.

5.1.2.  Results

We simulate N=200N=200 units over T=200T=200 periods in each of 2,0002{,}000 replications and report the results at horizons h=0h=0, 22, and 44. We consider the backward-looking environment (Panel A of Table 1) and the forward-looking environment (Panel B). In the forward-looking environment, we assume that the researcher observes the instruments of only the first two of the six news shocks. This assumption corresponds to the case of under-identification, which is the common case in applications. Appendix D.2 reports the case of exact identification, in which the researcher observes the instruments of all six news shocks, so that E-HELP-IV holds the expected confounder path fixed completely. For each estimator, we report the median bias and the root mean squared error (RMSE) of its estimates across replications. For HELP-IV, we also show its inference performance by the share of replications in which the nominal 90 percent confidence interval covers the target and by the median length of that interval.1212 12 Every panel regression includes unit and time effects, the lagged outcome Yi,t−1Y_{i,t-1}, and si​g​Gt−1s_{ig}G_{t-1}, si​g​Gt−2s_{ig}G_{t-2}, si​g​Rt−1s_{ig}R_{t-1}, and si​g​Rt−2s_{ig}R_{t-2}, which the outcome equation contains. The cross-sectional step of the decomposition method includes the same controls. When the weights or the instruments are estimated, the standard error of HELP-IV uses the sandwich covariance of Section 4 or Appendix B, which stacks the first-step moments with the IV moment.

Table 1 shows that the bias of TWFE-IV changes sign across horizons in both environments. The bias is negative on impact, at −0.18-0.18 in the backward-looking environment and −0.10-0.10 in the forward-looking environment, and positive thereafter, reaching 0.590.59 and 0.800.80 at h=4h=4. This pattern reflects the two components of the HEDGE bias, which Proposition 1 derives for the backward-looking environment and which carry opposite signs under our data-generating process. The exposure-correlation component is negative, because a treatment shock raises the confounder, and the confounder lowers the outcome most in the units that are most exposed to the treatment. The aggregate-feedback component is positive, because the confounder feeds back into the treatment and prolongs its response. The former dominates on impact and the latter from h=2h=2 on.

HELP-IV, by contrast, is centered on the target in both panels, with a median bias of at most 0.040.04 in absolute value and an RMSE of at most 0.290.29. In the forward-looking environment, its target is the information-constrained effect, because the available instruments do not fully offset the expected confounder path. The outcome up to h=4h=4 depends on this path from tt to t+6t+6, and the instruments, zr,tz_{r,t} and the first two news instruments, leave 2.0 percent of its response to the treatment shock unabsorbed (Section 3.3). At these horizons, the target differs from the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect by at most 0.030.03.

The coverage of the intervals of HELP-IV differs between the two environments. In the backward-looking environment, the intervals cover the target in 88--89 percent of replications, close to the nominal 90 percent. In the forward-looking environment, they cover it in 92--95 percent of replications and are therefore mildly conservative.1313 13 The over-coverage stems from the first step, which estimates the composite weights. The estimated weights offset the confounder path in the sample and not only in the population, so the estimates are less dispersed than with the population weights. With the first-step term, the median length of the intervals is close to the range of the estimates, but the tt-statistic remains less dispersed than a standard normal variable (Appendix D.2).

The decomposition method is biased in this design, in which the confounder moves the treatment on impact, and its bias is negative at every horizon in both panels. It shares the numerator of the target, the outcome response with the confounder path held fixed, and therefore removes the exposure-correlation component. It divides, however, by the unrestricted impact response of the treatment; compare (19) with (20). Under our data-generating process, the controlled impact response is about 0.750.75 times the unrestricted one, so the decomposition method converges to about 0.750.75 times the target.

5.1.3.  Further designs and environments

Five further exercises are reported in Appendix D. First, when the measurement error of zg,tz_{g,t} or of zr,tz_{r,t} in the backward-looking environment has a standard deviation of 22 or 33 instead of 0.50.5, HELP-IV remains centered on the target, with a median bias of at most 0.040.04 in absolute value and coverage of 89–94 percent, although its estimates are less precise (Appendix D.1). Second, when the instruments are shocks estimated from a correctly specified aggregate SVAR (Appendix B), HELP-IV and composite HELP-IV still perform well, with median biases of at most 0.020.02 in absolute value and coverage of 87–90 percent (Appendix D.3). Third, when RR does not enter the equation for GtG_{t}, which confines general equilibrium to one direction, HELP-IV and the decomposition method are both centered on the target, with similar RMSEs (Appendix D.4). Fourth, when the data-generating process has a second exposure margin, as in Section 3.1, HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins recovers both margin-specific partial-equilibrium effects, with coverage of 85–89 percent (Appendix D.5).

The fifth exercise evaluates E-HELP-IV with transformed treatments and outcomes (Section 3.4) in a setting closer to applications. Instead of a stylized data-generating process, we simulate data from the forward-looking two-region New Keynesian model of Donaldson (2026), which Appendix D.6 describes. The target is the cumulative fiscal multiplier when the expected path of the real interest rate is held fixed. We first consider one-way general equilibrium, in which government spending does not respond to the real rate, as in the specification of Donaldson (2026). Both E-HELP-IV and her ex ante decomposition method are then centered on the target, but the intervals of E-HELP-IV are 32–39 percent shorter. We then relax this restriction and let spending respond to the lagged real rate. To keep this feedback empirically plausible, we calibrate its strength to the local-projection estimate of the response of US defense spending to a monetary policy shock, relative to that of the federal funds rate. This calibration is not a precise estimate of that response in US data. It shows the size of the bias of the decomposition method when the feedback from the real rate to spending is of this strength. E-HELP-IV remains centered on the target, and its intervals cover the target in 92–93 percent of replications. The decomposition method, by contrast, overstates the target, because a higher real rate lowers spending and thereby shrinks the unrestricted spending response by which the method normalizes. As this reduction accumulates, the overstatement widens with the horizon, from 8 percent one year after the shock to 19 percent after two years (Appendix D.7).

5.2.  Multiple aggregate confounders

5.2.1.  Data-generating process

We now turn to a data-generating process with K=8K=8 confounders, R1,t,…,R8,tR_{1,t},\ldots,R_{8,t}, of which the first K1=2K_{1}=2 are two-way and the other K−K1=6K-K_{1}=6 are one-way. The outcome equation is

Yi​t\displaystyle Y_{it} =μi+λt+0.8​Yi,t−1+si​g​Gt+∑q=18si​rq​Rq,t+ui​t.\displaystyle=\mu_{i}+\lambda_{t}+0.8\,Y_{i,t-1}+s_{ig}G_{t}+\sum_{q=1}^{8}s_{ir_{q}}R_{q,t}+u_{it}.

The lagged outcome has the coefficient 0.80.8, so that the effect of the treatment remains sizable at long horizons. Treatment exposure is si​g=0.6​ai+si​g⟂s_{ig}=0.6\,a_{i}+s_{ig}^{\perp}, where aia_{i} is the targeting characteristic of Assumption 2, and si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} has variance 0.640.64. Exposure to confounder qq is si​rq=0.8​si​g+uirqs_{ir_{q}}=0.8\,s_{ig}+u_{i}^{r_{q}} for the two-way confounders and si​rq=0.8​ai+uirqs_{ir_{q}}=0.8\,a_{i}+u_{i}^{r_{q}} for the one-way confounders, so si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} is orthogonal to exposure to every one-way confounder, as Assumption 2 requires.

We assume that the aggregate block follows the SVAR(1)

Gt\displaystyle G_{t} =0.5​Gt−1+0.1​∑q=1K1Rq,t−1+ϵg,t+ϖ​∑q=1K1ϵrq,t,\displaystyle=0.5\,G_{t-1}+0.1\textstyle\sum_{q=1}^{K_{1}}R_{q,t-1}+\epsilon_{g,t}+\varpi\textstyle\sum_{q=1}^{K_{1}}\epsilon_{r_{q},t},
Rq,t\displaystyle R_{q,t} =0.5Rq,t−1+0.1Gt+ϵrq,t,q=1,…,8,\displaystyle=0.5\,R_{q,t-1}+0.1\,G_{t}+\epsilon_{r_{q},t},\qquad q=1,\ldots,8,

where ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and ϵrq,t\epsilon_{r_{q},t} are the structural shocks to the treatment and to confounder qq. Each confounder responds to the treatment within the period with the coefficient 0.10.1, smaller than the 0.50.5 of Section 5.1.1 because eight confounders respond at once. The two-way confounders feed back into the treatment with a lag, and when ϖ>0\varpi>0 their shocks also move the treatment within the period. The one-way confounders feed back into neither the treatment nor the two-way confounders, as Assumption 1 requires. We assume that the instruments are proxies that measure the shocks with error, zg,t=ϵg,t+ηg,tz_{g,t}=\epsilon_{g,t}+\eta_{g,t} and zrq,t=ϵrq,t+ηrq,tz_{r_{q},t}=\epsilon_{r_{q},t}+\eta_{r_{q},t}, where ηg,t\eta_{g,t} has standard deviation 0.50.5 and ηrq,t\eta_{r_{q},t} has standard deviation ση\sigma_{\eta}. All primitive random variables are mutually independent and normal with mean zero, and all except the measurement errors and si​g⟂s_{ig}^{\perp} are standard normal.

We consider two settings of the data-generating process, which vary the measurement error of the confounder proxies, ση\sigma_{\eta}, and the within-period response of the treatment, ϖ\varpi. The first setting has a large measurement error and no within-period response, (ση,ϖ)=(1,0)(\sigma_{\eta},\varpi)=(1,0) (Panel A of Table 2). The second setting has a small measurement error and a within-period response, (ση,ϖ)=(0.5,0.5)(\sigma_{\eta},\varpi)=(0.5,0.5) (Panel B). The confounder shock accounts for half of the variance of its proxy in the first setting and for 80 percent in the second. The two settings serve two purposes. They verify that the three HELP-IV designs recover the target under different conditions, and they show when multiple-confounder or composite HELP-IV is preferable.

5.2.2.  Results

We simulate N=200N=200 units over T=200T=200 periods in each of 2,0002{,}000 replications and report the results at horizons h=2h=2, 44, 66, and 88. We study horizons longer than those of Section 5.1 to show how each design performs as the number of path controls of multiple-confounder HELP-IV, 8​(h+1)8(h+1), grows.

Table 2 shows that TWFE-IV is biased, with a median bias of 0.520.52 to 1.121.12, whereas the three HELP-IV designs recover the partial-equilibrium effect βhP\beta_{h}^{P} up to a finite-sample bias. The median bias of multiple-confounder HELP-IV is −0.10-0.10 to −0.05-0.05, and those of composite and targeting-rule HELP-IV lie between −0.09-0.09 and −0.02-0.02 (Appendix D.8). In finite samples, the bias arises from both the lagged outcome Yi,t−1Y_{i,t-1}, whose coefficient is 0.80.8, and the large number of parameters to estimate with eight confounders. The bias vanishes as TT grows.

The three HELP-IV designs differ, however, in their precision, stability, and interval coverage. Targeting-rule HELP-IV is the most precise design. At every horizon and in both panels, the design has the smallest RMSE, 0.160.16 to 0.290.29, and the shortest intervals. Because the characteristic aia_{i} absorbs the six one-way confounders through a moment across units, the design needs to hold fixed only the paths of the two two-way confounders, whereas multiple-confounder HELP-IV holds fixed the paths of all eight confounders.

When no targeting rule is available, the choice between multiple-confounder and composite HELP-IV depends on the setting. In Panel A, where the confounder proxies are noisy and the treatment does not respond to the confounders within the period, composite HELP-IV has the advantage at long horizons. The intervals of the two designs have similar median lengths at every horizon, but the RMSEs diverge at long horizons. The RMSE of multiple-confounder HELP-IV rises to 1.41.4 at h=6h=6 and exceeds 900900 at h=8h=8, whereas that of composite HELP-IV stays at or below 0.60.6. This large RMSE is due to extreme estimates in a few replications. For example, 88 of the 2,0002{,}000 estimates of multiple-confounder HELP-IV at h=6h=6 and 6161 at h=8h=8 deviate from the target by more than eight times the target, whereas no estimate of composite HELP-IV does. In Panel B, where the proxies are precise and the treatment responds within the period, multiple-confounder HELP-IV has the advantage, and the RMSE of composite HELP-IV is 1.41.4 to 1.51.5 times larger. The intervals of composite HELP-IV, however, cover the target in 88–92 percent of replications, whereas those of multiple-confounder HELP-IV cover it in only 80–85 percent.

The two designs hold the confounder paths fixed in different ways, and this difference explains the ranking in each panel. On the one hand, multiple-confounder HELP-IV instruments each of the 8​(h+1)8(h+1) confounder values on the paths with the proxy of the corresponding shock, so it must invert a large cross-moment matrix of instruments and regressors. When the proxies are noisy, as in Panel A, they carry little information about the path values, so in some replications this matrix is nearly singular, and a nearly singular matrix produces extreme estimates. Composite HELP-IV avoids this problem, because its IV step has a single endogenous regressor and its offset recursion imposes the causality restrictions, although noisy estimated offsets can still weaken its first stage in other samples. On the other hand, composite HELP-IV computes its weights from the recursion (30) of Section 3.2, which relies on causality restrictions that hold only in population. Because the corresponding sample moments are not exactly zero, the composite estimate absorbs part of the dependence of the outcome on the confounder paths, a term that multiple-confounder HELP-IV does not have. When the proxies are precise, as in Panel B, multiple-confounder HELP-IV produces no extreme estimates, so this additional term dominates the comparison and makes composite HELP-IV the less precise design.1414 14 Varying the measurement error and the within-period response one at a time (Appendix D.8) shows that the measurement error alone determines whether multiple-confounder HELP-IV produces extreme estimates. The within-period response widens the gap in precision. With a small measurement error, the RMSE of composite HELP-IV is 1.11.1 to 1.21.2 times that of multiple-confounder HELP-IV without the response and 1.41.4 to 1.51.5 times with it. Composite HELP-IV is thus the more reliable choice when the proxies are noisy and the horizon is long, whereas multiple-confounder HELP-IV is more precise when the proxies are accurate.

6.  Empirical applications

We consider two applications in which we use the HELP-IV framework developed in this paper to re-estimate partial-equilibrium effects reported in the existing literature. The first application (Section 6.1) revisits the state-level fiscal multiplier that Nakamura and Steinsson (2014) and Dupor and Guerrero (2017) estimate with a shift-share design. Donaldson (2026) and Manuel (2026) use this multiplier as a leading example and correct it for general-equilibrium bias from one-way confounders. We re-estimate the same multiplier but treat the interest rate as a two-way confounder. This application therefore permits a direct comparison with the decomposition method of Donaldson (2026). We also combine HELP-IV with the targeting rule of Manuel (2026) to address the one-way confounders for which no proxy is available.

The second application (Section 6.2) features multiple two-way confounders. It revisits the regional stock-wealth design of Chodorow-Reich et al. (2021, henceforth CNS). The target parameter is the partial-equilibrium effect of a stock-wealth gain on county employment and payroll, holding fixed the paths of other aggregate wealth and income variables. CNS identify it from cross-county variation in stock-market exposure and control for four confounders with a control-function method. We instead hold their paths fixed with composite HELP-IV and carry the estimate through the CNS model to its implications for the marginal propensity to consume out of stock wealth and for the aggregate labor-demand response.

6.1.  The cross-sectional fiscal multiplier

The object of interest in this application is the partial-equilibrium multiplier, the partial-equilibrium effect of state defense spending on state output. Nakamura and Steinsson (2014) estimate the cross-sectional multiplier with state and time fixed effects, arguing that the time fixed effects absorb the effects of aggregate confounders such as monetary policy. Following Donaldson (2026), we estimate its cumulative version,

𝒴i,t+h=ℬhSS​𝒢i,t+h+ιh​Δ​yi,t−1+μi,h+λt,h+vi,t,h,\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h}=\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}}\,\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h}+\iota_{h}\Delta y_{i,t-1}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+v_{i,t,h}, (61)

where 𝒴i,t+h=∑j=0h(Yi,t+j−Yi,t−1)/Yi,t−1\mathcal{Y}_{i,t+h}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}(Y_{i,t+j}-Y_{i,t-1})/Y_{i,t-1} and 𝒢i,t+h=∑j=0h(Gi,t+j−Gi,t−1)/Yi,t−1\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}(G_{i,t+j}-G_{i,t-1})/Y_{i,t-1} are the cumulative output and spending of Section 3.4, as in Ramey and Zubairy (2018), with Yi,tY_{i,t} real per capita gross state product and Gi,tG_{i,t} real per capita defense-contract spending. Both variables are therefore measured relative to the same pre-shock level of state output. The control Δ​yi,t−1\Delta y_{i,t-1} is lagged output growth, μi,h\mu_{i,h} and λt,h\lambda_{t,h} are horizon-specific state and time fixed effects, and ℬhSS\mathcal{B}_{h}^{\mathrm{SS}} is the shift-share IV multiplier.

We use the panel of Donaldson (2026), which contains real defense-contract spending and gross state product for 4646 states at annual frequency over 19691969–20072007.1515 15 Donaldson (2026) excludes North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Alaska because their gross state product changes by more than twenty percent in multiple years. She reports that retaining these small states leaves the point estimates similar but increases their variance. We use her sample so that our estimates and hers are computed on the same states. We instrument 𝒢i,t+h\mathcal{G}_{i,t+h} with the shift-share variable si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} of Section 3.4.1, where Gt=(GtUS−Gt−1US)/Yt−1USG_{t}=(G^{\mathrm{US}}_{t}-G^{\mathrm{US}}_{t-1})/Y^{\mathrm{US}}_{t-1} is the one-year change in real per capita national defense spending relative to real per capita national output, and si​gs_{ig} is the average of (Gi,t/Yi,t)/(GtUS/YtUS)(G_{i,t}/Y_{i,t})/(G^{\mathrm{US}}_{t}/Y^{\mathrm{US}}_{t}) over the five years before the estimation sample, 1964–1968, following Donaldson (2026).

The first row of Table 3 reports the shift-share IV multiplier. It rises from 1.061.06 in year 1 to 2.352.35 in year 4, close to the estimates in Donaldson (2026). If more exposed states are less sensitive to the interest rate, the monetary tightening that follows a defense-spending expansion depresses their output less, and the shift-share design attributes this smaller decline to defense spending, which overstates the multiplier. We therefore treat the interest rate as a two-way confounder. We first hold its path fixed with backward-looking HELP-IV and E-HELP-IV and then add one-way confounders through the targeting rule.

The single-confounder rows of Table 3 treat the interest rate as the only confounder. Backward-looking HELP-IV (Section 2), applied to the cumulative outcome and treatment as in Section 3.4, uses instruments constructed from a bivariate proxy-SVAR in national defense spending and the federal funds rate. In this proxy-SVAR, the Romer and Romer (2004) series identifies the monetary policy shock, and the defense-spending shock is orthogonalized against it. The resulting multiplier rises from 0.660.66 in year 1 to 1.691.69 in year 4, which indicates that the output response builds up more slowly than the spending response, and it lies 0.400.40 to 0.660.66 below the shift-share IV multiplier.

To facilitate comparison, we also estimate the decomposition method of Donaldson (2026), implemented as in her paper (Appendix E.2), which yields a multiplier rising from 0.970.97 to 1.851.85. The decomposition lies above HELP-IV, by between 0.160.16 and 0.310.31. Part of this gap arises because the decomposition divides by the unrestricted spending response (Section 2.4). To measure this part, we apply the decomposition to the proxy-SVAR shocks that HELP-IV uses and replace the unrestricted spending response by the controlled one. This replacement, which removes the feedback of monetary policy shocks into defense spending, lowers the multiplier by 0.050.05 in year 1 and by between 0.120.12 and 0.150.15 in years 2 to 4, about half of the gap in years 2 and 3 and most of it in year 4. The rest reflects the different shock measures of the two procedures.

We also estimate the fiscal multiplier with E-HELP-IV, introduced in Section 3.3, which allows outcomes to respond to the anticipated interest-rate path. We use the monetary proxies of Romer and Romer (2004) and Gertler and Karadi (2015) in a four-variable SVAR that also contains national defense spending, ordered first, and the federal funds rate. The SVAR delivers the identified shocks and the interest-rate responses from which the weights of the composite instrument are constructed. Combining the two monetary policy shocks with the defense-spending shock holds the interest-rate path almost fixed, leaving 2.92.9 percent of the response of the rate through t+5t+5 unabsorbed (the diagnostic of Section 3.3). The first-stage FF statistic lies between 16.916.9 and 33.133.1 across years. The resulting multiplier rises from 0.600.60 in year 1 to 1.651.65 in year 4 and differs from backward-looking HELP-IV by at most 0.110.11 in every year. Because the two monetary proxies do not offset the rate path completely, this estimate measures the information-constrained effect rather than the forward-looking partial-equilibrium effect.

Finally, we estimate the fiscal multiplier allowing for unspecified one-way confounders in addition to the interest rate, using the targeting-rule HELP-IV of Section 3.2.3. Following Manuel (2026), we project defense exposure on predetermined state characteristics that govern its allocation and use the residual from that projection in the instruments. The first characteristic is the state-level marginal propensity to consume MPCi\mathrm{MPC}_{i} of Bellifemine et al. (2023), which, due to data availability, we measure in 20112011 and assume to be a persistent state characteristic. The second is the state income-tax share Taxi\mathrm{Tax}_{i}, tax revenue relative to personal income over 19641964–19681968, the years over which exposure is measured. We select it from a set of economic, fiscal, and demographic characteristics in the Correlates of State Policy database as the characteristic, observed for every state, that adds most to the explanatory power of the MPC.1616 16 Manuel (2026) builds his rule from the same MPC measure together with trade openness and per capita income. Neither of these two characteristics predicts defense exposure in our sample once the MPC is included. The estimates reported below are similar when we target on the MPC alone, which carries most of the predictive power of the rule. The estimated targeting rule is

si​g\displaystyle s_{ig} =4.69(1.25)−9.93(3.16)​MPCi−0.123(0.068)​Taxi,R2=0.23,N=46,\displaystyle=\underset{(1.25)}{4.69}-\underset{(3.16)}{9.93}\,\mathrm{MPC}_{i}-\underset{(0.068)}{0.123}\,\mathrm{Tax}_{i},\qquad R^{2}=0.23,\quad N=46, (62)

with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors in parentheses and pp-values of 0.0030.003 and 0.0770.077.

Table 3 reports the estimates. The multiplier rises from 0.210.21 in year 1 to 0.640.64 in year 4, magnitudes comparable to those Manuel (2026) obtains once he controls for his targeting rule. It stays below one in every year, and it lies below each of the single-confounder estimates, which suggests that aggregate channels beyond the interest rate contribute to the conventional multiplier. These point estimates are closer to those of the Neoclassical model of Nakamura and Steinsson (2014), whose relative multiplier lies below 0.50.5, than to those of their New Keynesian model with consumption–labor complementarity. The relative multiplier of the latter model, about 1.51.5, matches the conventional estimate.

6.2.  Regional effects of stock-wealth shocks

The second application revisits CNS, a design with multiple two-way confounders. The object of interest is the response of county employment and payroll to a stock-market gain when the paths of the other aggregates that move with the market are held fixed. To identify the target, CNS exploit variation in lagged county stock wealth relative to local labor income and estimate the following equation:

Δa,t−1,t+h​y\displaystyle\Delta_{a,t-1,t+h}y =βh​(Sa,t−1​Ra,t−1,t)+Γh​Xa,t−1+ϵa,t−1,t+h.\displaystyle=\beta_{h}\left(S_{a,t-1}R_{a,t-1,t}\right)+\Gamma_{h}X_{a,t-1}+\epsilon_{a,t-1,t+h}. (63)

Here, Δa,t−1,t+h​y\Delta_{a,t-1,t+h}y is the change in log county employment or payroll between t−1t-1 and t+ht+h, Sa,t−1S_{a,t-1} is stock wealth relative to local labor income, and Ra,t−1,tR_{a,t-1,t} is the county portfolio return. Xa,t−1X_{a,t-1} includes county fixed effects, state-by-quarter fixed effects, eight lags of the wealth-return interaction, a Bartik industry control, and interactions of Sa,t−1S_{a,t-1} with four aggregate confounders.

These four aggregate confounders are the holding return on a five-year zero-coupon Treasury bond, national house-price growth, and the present-value growth of aggregate labor income and of non-corporate business income. CNS include them because they regard differential responses to aggregates that co-move with the market as the main threat to identification, and the interactions are intended to absorb those responses through a control function. Such controls leave the paths of the four confounders unrestricted both in the outcome equation and in the stock-return first stage, so we re-estimate the specification with composite HELP-IV.1717 17 We adopt composite HELP-IV rather than multiple-confounder HELP-IV because the multiple-confounder first stage is large relative to the sample, which is the case in which composite HELP-IV is preferable, as Section 3.2.2 explains. At the two-year horizon, multiple-confounder HELP-IV would instrument the stock return together with each of the four confounders over eight quarters. Its first stage would therefore estimate 3333 coefficients from 9696 quarters of aggregate variation.

We estimate the model on the same sample as CNS, 19911991Q33 through 20152015Q22.1818 18 The county panel and the aggregate series are taken from the replication package of Chodorow-Reich et al. (2021), available at https://www.openicpsr.org/openicpsr/project/123521/version/V1/view. Composite HELP-IV holds the paths of the four confounders fixed through its instrument rather than through controls. Accordingly, we estimate (63) without the four interactions and instrument Sa,t−1​Ra,t−1,tS_{a,t-1}R_{a,t-1,t} with the product of the composite shock and the county’s stock-wealth exposure, averaged over 19901990–19931993. The composite shock is constructed as in Proposition 3 from the shock to the aggregate market return, the shocks to the four confounders, and the offset weights. We estimate the shocks from a five-variable national SVAR in the aggregate market return and the four confounders, identified by a Cholesky decomposition with the market return ordered first. We then construct the weights by extending the construction of Sims and Zha (2006) to the joint path of the four confounders. The composite shock therefore moves the market return while leaving those paths through t+ht+h unchanged.1919 19 Ordering the market return last lets it respond on impact to the four confounder shocks, so that the market-return shock no longer moves the confounders on impact. This ordering leaves the estimates little changed. The ordering within the confounder block is irrelevant, because the estimator depends only on the space spanned by those shocks. Inference follows Appendix B.3 and accounts for the estimation of the SVAR.

Table 4 reports the estimated labor market responses of employment and payroll, βhP\beta_{h}^{P} at h=7h=7, two years after the shock, as in CNS, who focus on this horizon because the labor market response starts to stabilize there. The row CNS benchmark reproduces Table 1 of CNS. To isolate the role of the confounder controls, the row No confounder controls drops the four interactions while keeping the remaining controls, and the row Composite HELP-IV applies the estimator described above. No confounder controls is the common reference point for both corrections: comparing it with CNS benchmark isolates the contribution of the control function, and comparing it with Composite HELP-IV shows the effect of holding the four confounder paths fixed under the maintained identification assumptions. Because composite HELP-IV also uses shocks estimated from an SVAR and an exposure measure averaged over a fixed period, the second comparison reflects these design choices as well as the holding of the confounder paths fixed.

We highlight two main findings. First, in every column, composite HELP-IV moves the estimates by more than dropping the confounder controls does. Consider the nontradable payroll coefficient in Column (4), which in the CNS model measures the local income that the additional spending generates. It equals 3.243.24 basis points per one percent of local annual labor income in the benchmark specification and 2.622.62 once the confounder controls are omitted, but only 0.830.83 once the confounder paths are held fixed. Similarly, except for tradable employment, the composite HELP-IV estimates lie between 3131 and 8181 percent below the CNS benchmark for the remaining coefficients. Under the maintained assumptions, the partial-equilibrium effect that CNS seek to measure is therefore considerably smaller than their benchmark estimate.

Second, the difference between the nontradable and the tradable responses is much smaller under composite HELP-IV than in the CNS benchmark. In the CNS benchmark the nontradable industries respond strongly while the tradable industries do not respond, with employment coefficients of 2.022.02 and −0.11-0.11 and payroll coefficients of 3.243.24 and 0.710.71. CNS interpret this difference as evidence that the response operates through local consumption demand, because news about productivity or a change in the cost of capital would raise activity in both sectors. Under composite HELP-IV, the two sectors respond by similar amounts, with employment coefficients of 0.390.39 and 0.430.43 and payroll coefficients of 0.830.83 and 0.490.49. These estimates therefore give weaker support to the consumption wealth effect on which the remainder of the CNS analysis rests.

CNS carry the estimated nontradable payroll coefficient, bNTb_{\mathrm{NT}}, into their model of consumption wealth effects with geographic heterogeneity, an exercise that rests on the portability of the estimated effect. In that model, bNTb_{\mathrm{NT}} is the product of the household marginal propensity to consume (MPC) out of stock wealth, the labor share 1−α1-\alpha, and the local spending multiplier MM, so the MPC equals bNT/[(1−α)​M]b_{\mathrm{NT}}/[(1-\alpha)M]. The same coefficient also scales the aggregate responses to a twenty percent increase in stock valuations that monetary policy does not counter. The aggregate labor bill rises by λL​bNT\lambda_{L}b_{\mathrm{NT}}, where λL\lambda_{L} scales the valuation shock by the aggregate ratio of stock wealth to the labor bill, because the model equates the proportional response of the aggregate labor bill with that of the local nontradable labor bill. Aggregate hours rise by λL​bNT/(1+κA)\lambda_{L}b_{\mathrm{NT}}/(1+\kappa^{A}), because the aggregate degree of wage adjustment κA\kappa^{A} divides that response between wages and hours.

Table 5 compares the three economic magnitudes implied by composite HELP-IV with those implied by the CNS benchmark. All three are substantially smaller under composite HELP-IV. The implied MPC declines from 3.23.2 to 0.80.8 cents per dollar per year. CNS note that their estimate of 3.23.2 cents is close to the annual discount rates commonly assumed in the literature and is therefore consistent with the permanent-income benchmark. The composite HELP-IV estimate falls well below that benchmark and is closer to the small stock-wealth effects estimated from regional variation by Case et al. (2005).

The implied responses of the aggregate labor bill and aggregate hours to a twenty-percent increase in stock valuations likewise decline, from 1.71.7 to 0.440.44 percent and from 0.770.77 to 0.270.27 percent, respectively, which implies a smaller demand-stabilization role for policy after a stock-valuation shock. Holding the confounder paths fixed thus changes not only the estimated coefficient but also the model-based implications that CNS draw from it.

7.  Conclusion

TWFE-IV regressions in exposure designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects, on the assumption that their time effects absorb aggregate confounders. We show that time effects generally suffice to recover these effects only under two conditions, namely that exposures to the treatment and to the confounders are uncorrelated and that the confounders do not feed back into the treatment. When either condition fails, the TWFE-IV estimate suffers from the HEDGE bias. We then develop the HELP-IV framework, which corrects for the HEDGE bias by augmenting the panel IV regression with confounder-path controls and proxy instruments, and adapt it to four more general environments (multiple exposure margins, multiple confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and transformed treatments and outcomes). Our simulations show that, in finite samples, HELP-IV is centered on the target effect and the inference developed in this paper delivers coverage generally close to the nominal level. Our applications show that HELP-IV can deliver estimates of the state-level fiscal multiplier and of stock-wealth effects on the labor market that differ from previous TWFE-IV estimates, with distinct implications for structural models.

This paper opens avenues for future research in the following directions. First, the core idea of HELP-IV is that the moment conditions of a panel IV regression can implicitly deliver the policy counterfactuals of Sims and Zha (2006) and McKay and Wolf (2023). This idea can be extended to models with heterogeneous treatment effects, spatial or production linkages across units, and state-dependent dynamics. Second, HELP-IV is a simple yet general regression-based design. As granular panel data and exposure measures become increasingly available, including those constructed from firm and transaction records with machine-learning and text-based methods, it can be used to study causal relationships with exposure designs in macro-finance (Ottonello and Winberry, 2020; Jeenas, 2026), international economics (Amiti et al., 2022), household finance (Mian and Sufi, 2014; Guren et al., 2021), and labor economics (Autor et al., 2013), as well as in related business research, such as pricing and marketing.

The solution is unique and bhHELP=βhPb_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP}}=\beta_{h}^{P}. ∎

Appendix B Estimation and inference with shocks estimated from an SVAR

This appendix extends the results of Section 4 to instruments that are shocks estimated from a structural vector autoregression (SVAR), as in both applications. In population, each structural shock is a proxy in the sense of (8) or (12), with κ=1\kappa=1 and no measurement error, so the identification results of Sections 2 and 3 apply. The estimated shocks, however, depend on the SVAR estimates, whose sampling error enters the coefficient at first order through the instruments and, for composite HELP-IV, also through the offset weights. The covariance is therefore the sandwich of the moment conditions that stack the panel IV moment with the SVAR estimating equations.

B.1.  The SVAR first step

For estimation in this appendix, we assume that the aggregate process admits a correctly specified, stable SVAR of fixed order pAp_{A},

𝐖t=∑j=1pAAj​𝐖t−j+Ψ0​ϵt,\mathbf{W}_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{p_{A}}A_{j}\mathbf{W}_{t-j}+\Psi_{0}\bm{\epsilon}_{t}, (B.1)

where 𝐖t=(Gt,𝐑t′)′\mathbf{W}_{t}=(G_{t},\mathbf{R}_{t}^{\prime})^{\prime} and ϵt=(ϵg,t,ϵr,t′)′\bm{\epsilon}_{t}=(\epsilon_{g,t},\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{\prime})^{\prime} with KK confounders. This finite-order specification is an additional estimation assumption; the identification results of Sections 2 and 3 do not require it. In this appendix, we normalize the shocks so that each moves its own variable one for one on impact; their variances can differ from one. The estimated shocks are ϵ^t=Ψ^0−1​(𝐖t−∑j=1pAA^j​𝐖t−j)\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t}=\widehat{\Psi}_{0}^{-1}(\mathbf{W}_{t}-\sum_{j=1}^{p_{A}}\widehat{A}_{j}\mathbf{W}_{t-j}).

Let θ\theta collect the VAR coefficients, the impact matrix, and any proxy moments used for identification, in a smooth, locally identified parameterization. The estimator θ^\widehat{\theta} solves exactly identified estimating equations T−1​∑tkt​(θ^)=𝟎T^{-1}\sum_{t}k_{t}(\widehat{\theta})=\mathbf{0}, which stack the VAR normal equations, the equations for the residual covariance matrix, the proxy moments, and the identifying restrictions, as written out in (C.21); the restrictions do not vary over time. In a proxy-SVAR, a proxy identifies a shock through its covariance with the reduced-form residuals; the proxy then enters only through θ\theta, and the panel IV uses the estimated shock. Let Aθ=𝔼⁡[∂kt/∂θ′]A_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}[\partial k_{t}/\partial\theta^{\prime}] be the Jacobian of these equations and Ωk=limT→∞Var(T−1/2∑tkt)\Omega^{k}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\operatorname{Var}(T^{-1/2}\sum_{t}k_{t}) their long-run variance at the population parameters; Appendix C.4 gives both. Lemma C.3 shows that

T(θ^−θ)→𝑑N(𝟎,Aθ−1ΩkAθ−1′).\sqrt{T}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(\mathbf{0},\ A_{\theta}^{-1}\Omega^{k}A_{\theta}^{-1\prime}\bigr). (B.2)

B.2.  Benchmark HELP-IV

For the single-confounder baseline of Section 4.1, the population and sample instrument vectors, marked by the superscript S\mathrm{S} for SVAR shocks, are

𝐙i​t,hS=si​g​(ϵg,t,ϵr,t,…,ϵr,t+h)′,𝐙^i​t,hS=si​g​(ϵ^g,t,ϵ^r,t,…,ϵ^r,t+h)′,\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h}=s_{ig}(\epsilon_{g,t},\epsilon_{r,t},\ldots,\epsilon_{r,t+h})^{\prime},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h}=s_{ig}(\widehat{\epsilon}_{g,t},\widehat{\epsilon}_{r,t},\ldots,\widehat{\epsilon}_{r,t+h})^{\prime}, (B.3)

and b^hHELP,S\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP},\mathrm{S}} is the estimator (49) with 𝐙^i​t,hS\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h} in place of 𝐙i​t,h\mathbf{Z}_{it,h}. Let Σh\Sigma_{h} be (50) evaluated at 𝐙i​t,hS\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h}. The derivative of the IV moment with respect to the SVAR parameters is

Dh=𝔼⁡[limN→∞1N​∑i∂𝐙~i​t,hS∂θ′​ξ~i,t,h],D_{h}=\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h}}{\partial\theta^{\prime}}\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h}\right], (B.4)

evaluated at the population coefficient, holding the observed data fixed. The derivative of each estimated shock is given by (C.26). The multiple-confounder case stacks the shock blocks as in Section 4.1.

The coefficients and the SVAR parameters jointly solve the exactly identified moment conditions that stack the IV moment with ktk_{t}. Their Jacobian with respect to (ϑh′,θ′)(\bm{\vartheta}_{h}^{\prime},\theta^{\prime}) is block triangular,

𝐉hS=(−ΣhDh𝟎Aθ),\mathbf{J}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}=\begin{pmatrix}-\Sigma_{h}&D_{h}\\ \mathbf{0}&A_{\theta}\end{pmatrix}, (B.5)

and their long-run variance is

ΩhS=limN,T→∞Var⁡(1T​∑t(N−1​∑i𝐙~i​t,hS​ξ~i,t,hkt)).\Omega_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}=\lim_{N,T\to\infty}\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t}\begin{pmatrix}N^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{it,h}\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h}\\ k_{t}\end{pmatrix}\right). (B.6)

Let 𝐉^hS\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}} denote (B.5) with the population moments replaced by their sample analogues at the estimates.

Proposition B.1 (Inference for HELP-IV with SVAR shocks).

Under Assumption C.1, the conditions of Proposition 2, and Ω^hS→𝑝ΩhS\widehat{\Omega}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}\xrightarrow{p}\Omega_{h}^{\mathrm{S}},

T(V^hS)−1/2(b^hHELP,S−βhP)→𝑑N(0,1),\sqrt{T}\,(\widehat{V}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}})^{-1/2}\bigl(\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP},\mathrm{S}}-\beta_{h}^{P}\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1), (B.7)

where V^hS=e1′(𝐉^hS)−1Ω^hS(𝐉^hS)−1′e1\widehat{V}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}=e_{1}^{\prime}(\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}})^{-1}\widehat{\Omega}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}(\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}})^{-1\prime}e_{1}, V^hS→𝑝VhS\widehat{V}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}\xrightarrow{p}V_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}, and VhS=e1′(𝐉hS)−1ΩhS(𝐉hS)−1′e1V_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}=e_{1}^{\prime}(\mathbf{J}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}})^{-1}\Omega_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}(\mathbf{J}_{h}^{\mathrm{S}})^{-1\prime}e_{1}.

Partitioning ΩhS\Omega_{h}^{\mathrm{S}} into the IV-moment block Ωg​g\Omega_{gg}, the cross block Ωg​k\Omega_{gk}, and the SVAR block Ωk​k\Omega_{kk}, the covariance VhSV_{h}^{\mathrm{S}} is the panel term e1′Σh−1Ωg​gΣh−1′e1e_{1}^{\prime}\Sigma_{h}^{-1}\Omega_{gg}\Sigma_{h}^{-1\prime}e_{1}, plus a first-step term from Ωk​k\Omega_{kk}, plus a cross term from Ωg​k\Omega_{gk} (Appendix C.6). The cross term can be nonzero, because the regression residual can contain omitted aggregate history, on which the estimated VAR coefficients also depend. Treating the estimated shocks as known sets Dh=𝟎D_{h}=\mathbf{0}.

B.3.  Composite HELP-IV

With SVAR shocks, the primitive instruments of the composite are ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and ϵr,t\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}. Under the own-impact normalization, the inputs of the recursion (30) are

𝐯ℓS=𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​ϵg,t]=𝐑ℓg​σg2,Σr​z,ℓS=𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​ϵr,t′]=𝐑ℓr​𝚺r,\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{S}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\epsilon_{g,t}]=\mathbf{R}_{\ell}^{g}\sigma_{g}^{2},\qquad\Sigma_{rz,\ell}^{\mathrm{S}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{\prime}]=\mathbf{R}_{\ell}^{r}\bm{\Sigma}_{r}, (B.8)

where 𝐑ℓg\mathbf{R}_{\ell}^{g} and 𝐑ℓr\mathbf{R}_{\ell}^{r} are the responses of 𝐑t+ℓ\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell} to ϵg,t\epsilon_{g,t} and to ϵr,t\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}, σg2=Var⁡(ϵg,t)\sigma_{g}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{g,t}), and 𝚺r=Var⁡(ϵr,t)\bm{\Sigma}_{r}=\operatorname{Var}(\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}) is diagonal. The population weights 𝒘sS\bm{w}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}} solve (30) with these inputs. They differ from the weights of Section 4.2, because a proxy that equals a multiple of a shock plus noise scales the corresponding covariance blocks by that multiple, but both composites satisfy (29) and identify βhP\beta_{h}^{P}. The population and estimated composites are

zg,t,hC,S=ϵg,t+∑s=0h(𝒘sS)′​ϵr,t+s,z^g,t,hC,S=ϵ^g,t+∑s=0h(𝒘^sS)′​ϵ^r,t+s.\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}=\epsilon_{g,t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}(\bm{w}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}})^{\prime}\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t+s},\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}=\widehat{\epsilon}_{g,t}+\sum_{s=0}^{h}(\widehat{\bm{w}}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}})^{\prime}\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{r,t+s}. (B.9)

The estimated weights use the fitted SVAR rather than sample cross moments. We calculate the responses recursively, Ψ^ℓ=∑j=1min⁡(pA,ℓ)A^j​Ψ^ℓ−j\widehat{\Psi}_{\ell}=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(p_{A},\ell)}\widehat{A}_{j}\widehat{\Psi}_{\ell-j} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, with Ψ^0\widehat{\Psi}_{0} the estimated impact matrix, and substitute the responses 𝐑^ℓg\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell}^{g} and 𝐑^ℓr\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell}^{r} of 𝐑t+ℓ\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell} and the estimated shock variances into the recursion,

𝒘^ℓS=−(𝐑^0r𝚺^r)−1(𝐑^ℓgσ^g2+∑s=0ℓ−1𝐑^ℓ−sr𝚺^r𝒘^sS),ℓ=0,…,h.\widehat{\bm{w}}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{S}}=-\bigl(\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{0}^{r}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}\bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell}^{g}\widehat{\sigma}_{g}^{2}+\sum_{s=0}^{\ell-1}\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{\ell-s}^{r}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}\widehat{\bm{w}}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}}\Bigr),\qquad\ell=0,\ldots,h. (B.10)

The variance factors arise from the own-impact normalization; under a unit-variance normalization they are identity matrices, and Lemma C.4 maps the two sets of weights into each other. Because the inputs are the responses and variances implied by the fitted SVAR, 𝒘^sS\widehat{\bm{w}}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}} can differ from the result of applying (54) to ϵ^t\widehat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{t}. The estimator b^hHELP​-​C,S\widehat{b}_{h}^{\mathrm{HELP\text{-}C},\mathrm{S}} is (53) with z^g,t,hC,S\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C,\mathrm{S}} in place of z^g,t,hC\widehat{\mathrm{z}}_{g,t,h}^{C}.

Let ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C} and D𝒘s,hD_{\bm{w}_{s},h} be (57) with the structural shocks in place of the proxies and with the weights 𝒘sS\bm{w}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}}. The weights and the shocks are both smooth functions of θ\theta. Let

Dhw=∑s=0hD𝒘s,h​∂𝒘sS∂θ′,D_{h}^{w}=\sum_{s=0}^{h}D_{\bm{w}_{s},h}\frac{\partial\bm{w}_{s}^{\mathrm{S}}}{\partial\theta^{\prime}}, (B.11)
