where V^hC,S=e1′(𝐉^hC,S)−1Ω^hC,S(𝐉^hC,S)−1′e1\widehat{V}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}=e_{1}^{\prime}(\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}})^{-1}\widehat{\Omega}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}(\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}})^{-1\prime}e_{1}, V^hC,S→𝑝VhC,S\widehat{V}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}\xrightarrow{p}V_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}, and VhC,S=e1′(𝐉hC,S)−1ΩhC,S(𝐉hC,S)−1′e1V_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}=e_{1}^{\prime}(\mathbf{J}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}})^{-1}\Omega_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}}(\mathbf{J}_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}})^{-1\prime}e_{1}.

Relative to Proposition 8, the SVAR estimating equations replace the weight equations, and DhS=Dhw+DhϵD_{h}^{\mathrm{S}}=D_{h}^{w}+D_{h}^{\epsilon}. Both parts are functions of the same SVAR estimates, so the sandwich keeps their joint covariance and their covariance with the panel moment. The split between DhwD_{h}^{w} and DhϵD_{h}^{\epsilon} depends on the shock normalization; their sum and VhC,SV_{h}^{C,\mathrm{S}} do not (Lemma C.4).

B.4.  Extensions

Remark B.1 (Extensions with SVAR shocks).

The extensions of Section 4 carry over with SVAR shocks in place of the proxies. Each instrument component determined by the SVAR is a smooth function of θ\theta, so it enters the sandwich through its derivative with respect to θ\theta in the off-diagonal block of the Jacobian; the cross-sectional balance conditions for targeting-rule HELP-IV remain those of Appendix C.8. For HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins and multiple-confounder HELP-IV, the instruments are the exposures times the estimated shocks, and DhD_{h} stacks the shock derivatives over the instrument dates, as in (C.41). For composite HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins, the composite is common to all margins, and DhwD_{h}^{w} and DhϵD_{h}^{\epsilon} have one row per margin.

For E-HELP-IV, the estimated shocks are first put in the unit-covariance normalization of Section 3.3: the treatment instrument is ϵg,t/σg2\epsilon_{g,t}/\sigma_{g}^{2}, and the confounder instruments are 𝚺E−1​ϵr,tE\bm{\Sigma}_{E}^{-1}\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}, where 𝚺E\bm{\Sigma}_{E} is the diagonal covariance matrix of the date-tt shocks in ϵr,tE\bm{\epsilon}_{r,t}^{E}. In these coordinates, 𝐫Hg\mathbf{r}_{H}^{g} and 𝐑HE\mathbf{R}_{H}^{E} are the responses of (Rt,…,Rt+H)′(R_{t},\ldots,R_{t+H})^{\prime} implied by the fitted SVAR, and the weights are (40). The derivatives include the estimated variance factors; (C.45) and (C.46) give them in the equivalent unit-variance coordinates, including the residual-path term under incomplete spanning.

For targeting-rule HELP-IV implemented through the characteristic–instrument controls of Appendix C.8, these controls contain the estimated shocks, so the derivative is that of the complete concentrated moment, (C.9) with the projection derivative (C.62). For transformed treatments and outcomes, the derivatives are formed from the residuals of the transformed regression.

Appendix C Estimation and inference: derivations and proofs

This appendix proves the results of Section 4 and Appendix B. Each estimator solves exactly identified estimating equations that stack the panel IV moment with the moments of its first step, if any, and its asymptotic covariance is the corresponding sandwich, whose middle term keeps all covariances between the panel and first-step moments.

C.1.  Common notation and identification

Let 𝐬i​g=(si​g,1,…,si​g,M)′\mathbf{s}_{ig}=(s_{ig,1},\ldots,s_{ig,M})^{\prime} collect MM time-invariant treatment exposures, with MM fixed. The single-exposure model of Section 2 has M=1M=1 and si​g,1=si​gs_{ig,1}=s_{ig}. Let 𝐑t∈ℝK\mathbf{R}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} collect the confounders and set

ft,h=(Gt,𝐑t′,…,𝐑t+h′)′,pt,h=(zg,t,𝒛r,t′,…,𝒛r,t+h′)′.f_{t,h}=(G_{t},\mathbf{R}_{t}^{\prime},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{t+h}^{\prime})^{\prime},\qquad p_{t,h}=(z_{g,t},\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime},\ldots,\bm{z}_{r,t+h}^{\prime})^{\prime}. (C.1)

Designs without a superscript use the instruments of Section 4. The superscript S\mathrm{S} labels designs whose instruments are shocks estimated from the SVAR of Appendix C.4; in these, zg,tz_{g,t} and 𝒛r,t\bm{z}_{r,t} are replaced by the selected estimated shocks. Instrument validity includes the maintained lead–lag exclusion restrictions.

Write 𝜷hP=(β1,hP,…,βM,hP)′\bm{\beta}_{h}^{P}=(\beta_{1,h}^{P},\ldots,\beta_{M,h}^{P})^{\prime}. For stationary vector series, use Ωx​y=∑ℓ∈ℤCov⁡(xt,yt−ℓ)\Omega_{xy}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t},y_{t-\ell}) and LRV⁡(xt)=Ωx​x\operatorname{LRV}(x_{t})=\Omega_{xx}; Ωy​x=Ωx​y′\Omega_{yx}=\Omega_{xy}^{\prime}. In the scalar case, write Ω⁡(x,y)=∑ℓ∈ℤCov⁡(xt,yt−ℓ)\Omega(x,y)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t},y_{t-\ell}).

C.1.1.  Full-path design with multiple exposures

We refer to HELP-IV with instrumented path controls (Sections 2.3, 3.1, and 3.2.1) as the full-path design, to distinguish it from composite HELP-IV. The common-exposure-basis specification is

Yi,t+h=(𝐬i​g⊗ft,h)′​ϑh+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h,Y_{i,t+h}=(\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes f_{t,h})^{\prime}\vartheta_{h}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}, (C.2)

with regressors Xi​t,hF=𝐬i​g⊗ft,hX^{F}_{it,h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes f_{t,h} and instruments Zi​t,hF=𝐬i​g⊗pt,hZ^{F}_{it,h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes p_{t,h}. The selector Lh=IM⊗e1′L_{h}=I_{M}\otimes e_{1}^{\prime} picks the MM treatment coefficients. The projections of the confounder exposures on 𝐬i​g\mathbf{s}_{ig} enter the path coefficients, and their orthogonal remainders enter ξi,t,h\xi_{i,t,h}.

With only two-way fixed effects, independence of the exposure vector and the aggregate process gives

ΣhF=S⊗𝖠h,\Sigma_{h}^{F}=S\otimes\mathsf{A}_{h}, (C.3)

where S=𝔼⁡[(𝐬i​g−𝔼​𝐬i​g)​(𝐬i​g−𝔼​𝐬i​g)′]S=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\mathbb{E}\mathbf{s}_{ig})(\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\mathbb{E}\mathbf{s}_{ig})^{\prime}] is the exposure covariance matrix, 𝖠h=𝔼⁡[pt,h​ft,h′]\mathsf{A}_{h}=\mathbb{E}[p_{t,h}f_{t,h}^{\prime}], and aggregate variables are centered. Rank therefore requires both SS and 𝖠h\mathsf{A}_{h} to be nonsingular. With additional controls, the residualized ΣhF\Sigma_{h}^{F} gives the rank condition.

C.1.2.  Composite instruments

For a scalar aggregate composite zg,t,hC\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}, use

Xi​t,hC=𝐬i​g​Gt,Zi​t,hC=𝐬i​g​zg,t,hC.X^{C}_{it,h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}G_{t},\qquad Z^{C}_{it,h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}. (C.4)

If 𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​zg,t,hC]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}]=0 for ℓ=0,…,h\ell=0,\ldots,h, the omitted path terms in (C.2) vanish from the population moment, provided the exposures are independent of the aggregate process and the structural exclusion holds. With only two-way effects, ΣhC=S​𝔼​[zg,t,hC​Gt]\Sigma_{h}^{C}=S\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}G_{t}], which path neutrality alone does not bound away from zero.

For multiple exposures the derivative block for 𝒘s\bm{w}_{s} is the M×KM\times K matrix D𝒘s,hD_{\bm{w}_{s},h} of (57) with 𝐬i​g\mathbf{s}_{ig} in place of si​gs_{ig}, where the residual uCu^{C} includes the omitted confounder paths and is therefore correlated with the confounder proxies.

C.1.3.  Residualization and effective sample

Joint inference uses a common effective date set of size TT; fixed leads and lags change sums by finitely many endpoint terms. Let MCM_{C} denote the sample residual-maker for all included controls and fixed effects, applied jointly to Y,X,ZY,X,Z; all panel moments use that operator. With nonseparable controls, path neutrality is imposed on the residualized panel cross moments.

Proposition C.1 (Path neutrality and exposure rank).

Suppose only unit and date effects are included, exposure moments factor from the aggregate process, the primitive instruments satisfy exclusion for ξi,t,h\xi_{i,t,h}, and, with 𝖢h,ℓ∈ℝM×K\mathsf{C}_{h,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K},

Yi,t+h=𝐬i​g′​𝜷hP​Gt+∑ℓ=0h𝐬i​g′​𝖢h,ℓ​𝐑t+ℓ+μi,h+λt,h+ξi,t,h.Y_{i,t+h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\prime}\bm{\beta}_{h}^{P}G_{t}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{h}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\prime}\mathsf{C}_{h,\ell}\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}+\mu_{i,h}+\lambda_{t,h}+\xi_{i,t,h}.
  1. (i)

    ΣhF\Sigma_{h}^{F} is given by (C.3), and ΣhC=S​𝔼​[zg,t,hC​Gt]\Sigma_{h}^{C}=S\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}G_{t}].

    If 𝔼⁡[𝐑t+ℓ​zg,t,hC]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}]=0 for ℓ=0,…,h\ell=0,\ldots,h and S​𝔼​[zg,t,hC​Gt]S\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}G_{t}] is nonsingular, the composite moment identifies 𝜷hP\bm{\beta}_{h}^{P}.

Put 𝐬˙i​g=𝐬i​g−𝔼​𝐬i​g\dot{\mathbf{s}}_{ig}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\mathbb{E}\mathbf{s}_{ig}. Two-way demeaning gives 𝐬i​g⊗ft,h~=(𝐬i​g−𝐬¯g)⊗(ft,h−f¯h)\widetilde{\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes f_{t,h}}=(\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\overline{\mathbf{s}}_{g})\otimes(f_{t,h}-\bar{f}_{h}), so independence implies (C.3) and, in the same way, ΣhC=S​𝔼​[zg,t,hC​Gt]\Sigma_{h}^{C}=S\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}G_{t}]. Thus rank⁡(ΣhF)=rank⁡(S)​rank⁡(𝔼⁡[pt,h​ft,h′])\rank(\Sigma_{h}^{F})=\rank(S)\rank(\mathbb{E}[p_{t,h}f_{t,h}^{\prime}]). At the target,

𝔼⁡[Z~i​t,hC​ui,t,hC]=S​∑ℓ=0h𝖢h,ℓ​𝔼​[𝐑t+ℓ​zg,t,hC]+𝔼⁡[Z~i​t,hC​ξ~i,t,h]=0.\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}^{C}_{it,h}u^{C}_{i,t,h}]=S\sum_{\ell=0}^{h}\mathsf{C}_{h,\ell}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell}\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}]+\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}^{C}_{it,h}\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h}]=0. (C.6)

Let d∈{F,C}d\in\{\mathrm{F},\mathrm{C}\} index the full-path or composite regression; a further superscript S\mathrm{S}, as in uS,Cu^{\mathrm{S,C}}, marks designs with SVAR shocks as instruments. With η\eta collecting its first-step parameters, define

ui,t,hd​(ϑ)\displaystyle u^{d}_{i,t,h}(\vartheta) =Y~i,t+h−X~i​t,hd′ϑ,\displaystyle=\widetilde{Y}_{i,t+h}-\widetilde{X}_{it,h}^{d\prime}\vartheta,

C.2.  Stacked moments and the sandwich covariance

Use gt,h​(ϑ,η)g_{t,h}(\vartheta,\eta) for a stationary population version of the oracle moment in (C.7), where η\eta collects the first-step parameters that enter the instruments, outcomes, regressors, or controls. The approximation from exact sample residualization and finite NN to this process is stated below. The Jacobian with respect to ϑ\vartheta is Σh=−𝔼⁡[∂ϑ′gt,h]\Sigma_{h}=-\mathbb{E}[\partial_{\vartheta^{\prime}}g_{t,h}], which for the designs of Section 4 is (50), and the derivative with respect to the first-step parameters is

Dh=∂η′𝔼⁡[gt,h​(ϑh,η)]|η=η0.D_{h}=\left.\partial_{\eta^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}[g_{t,h}(\vartheta_{h},\eta)]\right|_{\eta=\eta_{0}}. (C.8)

If only ZZ depends on η\eta and the residualization operator is fixed, DhD_{h} takes the form (B.4), with η\eta in place of θ\theta and the residual u~i,t,h\widetilde{u}_{i,t,h} in place of ξ~i,t,h\widetilde{\xi}_{i,t,h}. If YY, XX, or the controls are generated, differentiate the entire concentrated moment instead. In particular,

with Γ^W=T−1​∑t𝐖¯t−1​𝐖¯t−1′\widehat{\Gamma}_{W}=T^{-1}\sum_{t}\underline{\mathbf{W}}_{t-1}\underline{\mathbf{W}}_{t-1}^{\prime}, and the subtracted term is Op​(T−1)O_{p}(T^{-1}); the effect of 𝒜^\widehat{\mathcal{A}} on the sample proxy moment is captured by the block −ℒW​z-\mathcal{L}_{Wz} of AθA_{\theta}. The equations are smooth in θ\theta, and the sample Jacobian converges to AθA_{\theta}, which is nonsingular on the locally identified branch. A mean-value expansion of the exactly identified equations and the CLT for ktk_{t} therefore give (B.2), with the restriction rows contributing no sampling variation. ∎

C.4.6.  Covariance of the aggregate estimates

By Lemma C.3, the covariance of the SVAR estimates is Vθ=Aθ−1ΩkAθ−1′V_{\theta}=A_{\theta}^{-1}\Omega^{k}A_{\theta}^{-1\prime}; write Ωk​k=Ωk\Omega_{kk}=\Omega^{k}. Both blocks are obtained from a single joint covariance estimate of the observed residual products. This includes uncertainty in any estimated proxy-identification moments.

For recursive identification, BB is the lower-triangular Cholesky factor, there is no proxy moment, and θ=(vec⁡(𝒜)′,vech⁡(B)′)′\theta=(\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal{A})^{\prime},\operatorname{vech}(B)^{\prime})^{\prime}. The Jacobian is then block diagonal with blocks

−ΓW⊗In,−En(In2+Kn​n)(B⊗In)En′,-\Gamma_{W}\otimes I_{n},\qquad-E_{n}(I_{n^{2}}+K_{nn})(B\otimes I_{n})E_{n}^{\prime},

where DnD_{n} is the duplication matrix and Dn+=(Dn′​Dn)−1​Dn′D_{n}^{+}=(D_{n}^{\prime}D_{n})^{-1}D_{n}^{\prime}.

C.5.  Regularity conditions and proofs of the inference results

Assumption C.1 (Time-dimension inference).

For a fixed finite collection of horizons:

  1. (i)

    𝔼⁡[gt,h​(ϑh,η0)]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[g_{t,h}(\vartheta_{h},\eta_{0})]=\mathbf{0}, Σh\Sigma_{h} has full column rank, and 𝒲h\mathcal{W}_{h} is positive definite; MM, KK, pAp_{A}, and the horizons are fixed.

  2. (ii)

    The first-step estimator solves T−1​∑tmη,t​(η^)=𝟎T^{-1}\sum_{t}m_{\eta,t}(\widehat{\eta})=\mathbf{0} with AηA_{\eta} nonsingular, or is a smooth function of such a solution, and the composite weight maps have locally constant rank. With SVAR shocks as instruments, the VAR is stable and θ\theta is locally identified under a fixed normalization.

  3. (iii)

    (ϑ^h,η^)→𝑝(ϑh,η0)(\widehat{\vartheta}_{h},\widehat{\eta})\xrightarrow{p}(\vartheta_{h},\eta_{0}). The sample moments are differentiable on a neighborhood of (ϑh,η0)(\vartheta_{h},\eta_{0}), their Jacobians converge in probability to −Σh-\Sigma_{h} and DhD_{h} uniformly on that neighborhood, and the remainders of their first-order expansions are op(T−1/2)o_{p}(T^{-1/2}).

  4. (iv)

    T−1/2∑t𝐦t,h→𝑑N(𝟎,𝛀h)T^{-1/2}\sum_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t,h}\xrightarrow{d}N(\mathbf{0},\bm{\Omega}_{h}) jointly across the reported horizons, where 𝐦t,h\mathbf{m}_{t,h} is (C.10), 𝛀h=∑ℓ∈ℤΓh​(ℓ)\bm{\Omega}_{h}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}\Gamma_{h}(\ell) with Γh​(ℓ)=𝔼⁡[𝐦t,h​𝐦t−ℓ,h′]\Gamma_{h}(\ell)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{m}_{t,h}\mathbf{m}_{t-\ell,h}^{\prime}], and ∑ℓ‖Γh​(ℓ)‖<∞\sum_{\ell}\|\Gamma_{h}(\ell)\|<\infty. For the series and bootstrap results, the corresponding functional CLT holds.

  5. (v)

    After the exact sample residualization,

    1T​∑t{gN,t,h​(ϑh,η0)−gt,h}=op​(1).\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t}\{g_{N,t,h}(\vartheta_{h},\eta_{0})-g_{t,h}\}=o_{p}(1). (C.48)
  6. (vi)

    Lh𝐉h−1𝛀h𝐉h−1′Lh′L_{h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1}\bm{\Omega}_{h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime} is positive definite, and the first step and the panel moments use the same effective dates up to a fixed number of endpoints.

Stationarity, strong mixing with summable coefficients, and finite moments of sufficiently high order are sufficient for (iv). A sufficient condition for (C.48) is that the cross-sectional approximation error, conditional on aggregate history, has zero mean and absolutely summable temporal covariances of total order O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}). A persistent Op(N−1/2)O_{p}(N^{-1/2}) conditional mean, such as targeting imbalance, violates it; Proposition C.4 then replaces the time-only limit.

C.5.1.  Applications with a fixed cross section

For a fixed number of units, condition on the exposures and apply the time-series CLT to the date-level moment itself, which retains the cross-sectional noise; the same sandwich applies. With two regions, at most one centered exposure margin remains after differencing.

C.6.  Cross-covariance and iid structural shocks

This subsection concerns SVAR shocks as instruments. Partition the long-run variance (B.6) into the IV-moment block Ωg​g\Omega_{gg}, the cross block Ωg​k=Ωk​g′\Omega_{gk}=\Omega_{kg}^{\prime}, and the SVAR block Ωk​k\Omega_{kk}, and let Vθ=Aθ−1Ωk​kAθ−1′V_{\theta}=A_{\theta}^{-1}\Omega_{kk}A_{\theta}^{-1\prime}. where

Proposition C.3 (An iid Gaussian counterexample).

There exists a stable model satisfying the baseline HELP-IV exclusions, with iid independent Gaussian structural shocks and strongly relevant instruments, for which C0S=−1C_{0}^{\mathrm{S}}=-1. The corrected limiting variance is strictly positive and smaller than the variance V0regV_{0}^{\mathrm{reg}} that treats the shocks as known.

Let (ϵg,t,ϵr,t)′∼iidN⁡(0,I2)(\epsilon_{g,t},\epsilon_{r,t})^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}N(0,I_{2}), Gt=ϵg,tG_{t}=\epsilon_{g,t}, and Rt=ϵr,tR_{t}=\epsilon_{r,t}. Let the exposure be independent of the aggregate process, with mean zero and variance one. For 0<|ρ|<10<|\rho|<1, set

C.7.  Lead alignment and what it changes

C.7.1.  Composites built from SVAR shocks

Decompose zg,t,hC=∑s=0hvt,h(s)\mathrm{z}_{g,t,h}^{C}=\sum_{s=0}^{h}v^{(s)}_{t,h} with

vt,h(0)=(eg′+𝒘0′Jr)𝜺t,vt,h(s)=𝒘s′Jr𝜺t+s(s≥1).v^{(0)}_{t,h}=(e_{g}^{\prime}+\bm{w}_{0}^{\prime}J_{r})\bm{\varepsilon}_{t},\qquad v^{(s)}_{t,h}=\bm{w}_{s}^{\prime}J_{r}\bm{\varepsilon}_{t+s}\quad(s\geq 1). (C.55)

Let Dh,sD_{h,s} be (B.4) with ZZ replaced by 𝐬i​g​vt,h(s)\mathbf{s}_{ig}v^{(s)}_{t,h}. Each component includes both the shock derivative and the corresponding weight derivative, and Dh=∑sDh,sD_{h}=\sum_{s}D_{h,s}. The SVAR equations may then be aligned with each lead: treat the first step as h+1h+1 copies of the same estimating equations, dated t,…,t+ht,\ldots,t+h, each with its own copy of θ\theta that enters the panel moment through Dh,sD_{h,s}. The stacked moment becomes

𝐦t,hal=(gt,h′,kt′,kt+1′,…,kt+h′)′,\mathbf{m}^{\mathrm{al}}_{t,h}=(g_{t,h}^{\prime},k_{t}^{\prime},k_{t+1}^{\prime},\ldots,k_{t+h}^{\prime})^{\prime}, (C.56)

and its Jacobian has −Σh-\Sigma_{h} and h+1h+1 copies of AθA_{\theta} on the diagonal and Dh,0,…,Dh,hD_{h,0},\ldots,D_{h,h} in the first block row. In population the copies coincide, and in the sample they differ only through endpoint terms. A similar decomposition is available for full-path instruments built from SVAR shocks. It is unnecessary for a composite containing only date-tt news shocks.

C.7.2.  Composites with weights from sample cross moments

In block ℓ\ell of the weight equations (56), the date-tt summand of Σ^r​z,ℓ−s​𝒘s\widehat{\Sigma}_{rz,\ell-s}\bm{w}_{s} is 𝐑t+ℓ−s​𝒛r,t′​𝒘s\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell-s}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}\bm{w}_{s}. It can be re-dated to t−st-s, the base date of the panel moment in which the proxy 𝒛r,t\bm{z}_{r,t} carries the weight 𝒘s\bm{w}_{s}, while the summand of 𝐯^ℓ\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\ell} keeps date tt. The recursion propagates these shifts into later weights, and the Jacobian remains (C.15).

Lemma C.7 (Invariance of the first-order sum).

Let 𝐦t,hal\mathbf{m}^{\mathrm{al}}_{t,h} denote (C.56) or the stacked moment with the aligned weight equations. For fixed hh, under stationarity and finite second moments, T−1/2∑t(𝐦t,hal−𝐦t,h)=Op(T−1/2)T^{-1/2}\sum_{t}(\mathbf{m}^{\mathrm{al}}_{t,h}-\mathbf{m}_{t,h})=O_{p}(T^{-1/2}). If the autocovariances of both are absolutely summable, their long-run variances, and hence the sandwich covariances, coincide.

For each fixed ss and stationary square-integrable ktk_{t},

∑t=1T(kt+s−kt)=∑t=T+1T+skt−∑t=1skt=Op​(1).\sum_{t=1}^{T}(k_{t+s}-k_{t})=\sum_{t=T+1}^{T+s}k_{t}-\sum_{t=1}^{s}k_{t}=O_{p}(1).

This identity proves the claim for SVAR shocks. For weights built from sample cross moments, the aligned and unaligned summands differ in block ℓ\ell only by the terms 𝐑t+ℓ−s​𝒛r,t′​𝒘s\mathbf{R}_{t+\ell-s}\bm{z}_{r,t}^{\prime}\bm{w}_{s} dated t−st-s rather than tt; each of their sums over tt changes by Op​(1)O_{p}(1) by the same identity; premultiplication by a fixed matrix preserves this order. Dividing these sums by T\sqrt{T} gives op​(1)o_{p}(1). The endpoint terms have bounded second moments, so the normalized differences also converge in L2L^{2}. Under covariance summability, the coefficient blocks of the two sandwiches therefore coincide. ∎

Alignment changes only how a finite-bandwidth or finite-series estimator weights offsetting covariances.

C.8.  Targeting rules: estimation, exact balance, and finite-sample uncertainty

Partition confounders into a two-way block 𝐑t(1)\mathbf{R}_{t}^{(1)} of dimension K1K_{1} and a one-way block. Let 𝐚i∈ℝd\mathbf{a}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} contain observed targeting characteristics and a constant, and define the residual exposure

𝐬i​g⟂=𝐬i​g−Π′​𝐚i,\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\Pi^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{i}, (C.57)

where Π=𝔼​[𝐚i​𝐚i′]−1​𝔼​[𝐚i​𝐬i​g′]\Pi=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\prime}] is the population projection coefficient. Its sample analogue Π^=(∑i𝐚i​𝐚i′)−1​∑i𝐚i​𝐬i​g′\widehat{\Pi}=(\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime})^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\prime} gives 𝐬^i​g⟂=𝐬i​g−Π^′​𝐚i\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{ig}^{\perp}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\widehat{\Pi}^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{i}. With ft,h(1)=(Gt,𝐑t(1)′,…,𝐑t+h(1)′)′f^{(1)}_{t,h}=(G_{t},\mathbf{R}_{t}^{(1)\prime},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{t+h}^{(1)\prime})^{\prime} and the corresponding proxy vector pt,h(1)p^{(1)}_{t,h}, the direct implementation is

Xi​t,hT=𝐬i​g⊗ft,h(1),Z^i​t,hT=𝐬^i​g⟂⊗pt,h(1).X^{T}_{it,h}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes f^{(1)}_{t,h},\qquad\widehat{Z}^{T}_{it,h}=\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{ig}^{\perp}\otimes p^{(1)}_{t,h}. (C.58)

Use the joint IV estimator in the main text. With multiple exposures, all columns of Π\Pi are estimated jointly and every margin uses its own residual exposure. The exposure relevance matrix is now S⟂=𝔼⁡[𝐬i​g⟂​𝐬i​g⟂⁣′]S_{\perp}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp\prime}], which must have full rank in the separable case.

C.8.1.  Identification through exposure balance

Suppose the omitted one-way component has the form

Ui,t,how=∑q>K1∑s=0hcq,h,s​si​rq​Rq,t+s.U^{\mathrm{ow}}_{i,t,h}=\sum_{q>K_{1}}\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{q,h,s}s_{ir_{q}}R_{q,t+s}. (C.59)

The targeting restriction is 𝔼⁡[𝐬i​g⟂​si​rq]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}s_{ir_{q}}]=0 for every omitted exposure, together with independence of exposure characteristics from the aggregate process and instrument exclusion for the remaining error conditional on those characteristics. In the two-way-effects case it implies

𝔼⁡[Zi​t,hT​Ui,t,how]=∑q>K1𝔼⁡[𝐬i​g⟂​si​rq]⊗{∑s=0hcq,h,s​𝔼​[pt,h(1)​Rq,t+s]}=0.\mathbb{E}[Z^{T}_{it,h}U^{\mathrm{ow}}_{i,t,h}]=\sum_{q>K_{1}}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}s_{ir_{q}}]\otimes\left\{\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{q,h,s}\mathbb{E}[p^{(1)}_{t,h}R_{q,t+s}]\right\}=0. (C.60)

Centering is implicit after fixed effects. With additional controls this condition must hold for the concentrated moment as well.

C.8.2.  Implementation through characteristic–instrument controls

In a balanced panel with common date weights and only two-way effects, adding Wi​t,h=𝐚i⊗pt,h(1)W_{it,h}=\mathbf{a}_{i}\otimes p^{(1)}_{t,h} as included controls and using 𝐬i​g⊗pt,h(1)\mathbf{s}_{ig}\otimes p^{(1)}_{t,h} as instruments is equivalent to using (C.58). Redundant constant interactions are dropped after time demeaning. For every pair of primitive instruments pj,tp_{j,t} and pk,tp_{k,t} and every residual exposure margin s^i​ℓ⟂\widehat{s}^{\perp}_{i\ell},

∑i,t𝐚i​pj,t​s^i​ℓ⟂​pk,t=(∑i𝐚i​s^i​ℓ⟂)​(∑tpj,t​pk,t)=0.\sum_{i,t}\mathbf{a}_{i}p_{j,t}\widehat{s}^{\perp}_{i\ell}p_{k,t}=\Big(\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\widehat{s}^{\perp}_{i\ell}\Big)\Big(\sum_{t}p_{j,t}p_{k,t}\Big)=0. (C.61)

With additional controls CC, the exact Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) implementation projects on [W,C][W,C] jointly, and irregular panels require the weighted projection. When the instruments are SVAR shocks, WW is generated, so (C.9) is used with the projection rebuilt at each θ\theta.

The derivative of the generated projection has a closed form. Stack all included control columns, after dropping redundant columns, in a full-column-rank matrix 𝒞⁡(θ)\mathcal{C}(\theta), and set M⁡(θ)=I−𝒞⁡(θ)​(𝒞​(θ)′​𝒞​(θ))−1​𝒞​(θ)′M(\theta)=I-\mathcal{C}(\theta)(\mathcal{C}(\theta)^{\prime}\mathcal{C}(\theta))^{-1}\mathcal{C}(\theta)^{\prime}. Differentiating the projector gives

d​M=−M⁡(d​𝒞)​(𝒞′​𝒞)−1​𝒞′−𝒞​(𝒞′​𝒞)−1​(d​𝒞)′​M.dM=-M(d\mathcal{C})(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\mathcal{C})^{-1}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}-\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\mathcal{C})^{-1}(d\mathcal{C})^{\prime}M. (C.62)

For any stacked variable v⁡(θ)v(\theta), d​v~=(d​M)​v+M​d​vd\widetilde{v}=(dM)v+M\,dv. Inserting these derivatives for Y,X,ZY,X,Z into (C.9) accounts for the dependence of the targeting controls on the estimated shocks. Formula (C.62) follows by differentiating 𝒞​(𝒞′​𝒞)−1​𝒞′\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\mathcal{C})^{-1}\mathcal{C}^{\prime} and collecting the terms using M​𝒞=0M\mathcal{C}=0. It requires a locally fixed control rank, as does the concentrated-moment expansion.

C.8.3.  Cross-sectional sampling uncertainty

Population exposure balance can fail in the sample. For each one-way confounder q>K1q>K_{1}, define the sample imbalance

δ^q=1N​∑i𝐬^i​g⟂​si​rq.\widehat{\delta}_{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{ig}^{\perp}s_{ir_{q}}. (C.63)

Let γq=𝔼​[𝐚i​𝐚i′]−1​𝔼​[𝐚i​si​rq]\gamma_{q}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}s_{ir_{q}}] and let χq,i=𝐬i​g⟂​(si​rq−𝐚i′​γq)\chi_{q,i}=\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}(s_{ir_{q}}-\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\gamma_{q}) be the product of the two projection residuals. The pair (Π^,δ^q)(\widehat{\Pi},\widehat{\delta}_{q}) solves an exactly identified cross-sectional system that stacks the projection equations 𝐚i​(𝐬i​g′−𝐚i′​Π)\mathbf{a}_{i}(\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\prime}-\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\Pi) and the balance moment (𝐬i​g−Π′​𝐚i)​si​rq−δq(\mathbf{s}_{ig}-\Pi^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{i})s_{ir_{q}}-\delta_{q}. Under population balance and a cross-sectional CLT, the sandwich covariance of this system gives

N​δ^q→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,𝔼⁡[χq,i​χq,i′]).\sqrt{N}\,\widehat{\delta}_{q}\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(\mathbf{0},\ \mathbb{E}[\chi_{q,i}\chi_{q,i}^{\prime}]\bigr).

The Jacobian block for Π\Pi replaces si​rqs_{ir_{q}} by its projection residual in χq,i\chi_{q,i}, so this covariance already accounts for the estimation of Π\Pi.

Set

mq,h=∑s=0hcq,h,s​𝔼​[pt,h(1)​Rq,t+s],κi,h=∑q>K1χq,i⊗mq,h.m_{q,h}=\sum_{s=0}^{h}c_{q,h,s}\mathbb{E}[p^{(1)}_{t,h}R_{q,t+s}],\qquad\kappa_{i,h}=\sum_{q>K_{1}}\chi_{q,i}\otimes m_{q,h}. (C.64)

The time-averaged omitted-path moment contains ∑qδ^q⊗mq,h\sum_{q}\widehat{\delta}_{q}\otimes m_{q,h}, which can survive averaging over time. In the separable model just described, assuming that the remaining finite-NN approximation is negligible and T/NT/N is bounded, the coefficient therefore acquires a cross-sectional term of order T/N\sqrt{T/N} in addition to the time-series sandwich of Proposition C.2; Proposition C.4 gives the joint limit. The time component includes any aggregate first-step moments.

Three regimes arise. If each omitted exposure lies exactly in the span of 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i}, then δ^q=0\widehat{\delta}_{q}=0 in every sample and the displayed imbalance term is absent. If balance holds only in population, root-NN balance and T/N→0T/N\to 0 suffice to make it negligible. If T/N→τ>0T/N\to\tau>0, it generally contributes at first order. Under independence of the leading aggregate time component and the cross-sectional sampling component,

Var(𝜷^h)≃Lh𝐉h−1(1TΩT,h+1NEgΩN,hEg′)𝐉h−1′Lh′,\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{h})\simeq L_{h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1}\Bigl(\frac{1}{T}\Omega_{T,h}+\frac{1}{N}E_{g}\Omega_{N,h}E_{g}^{\prime}\Bigr)\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime}, (C.65)

where ΩT,h=𝛀h\Omega_{T,h}=\bm{\Omega}_{h} is the long-run variance of the stacked moment in (C.10), EgE_{g} embeds the panel-moment block in the stacked moment, and ΩN,h\Omega_{N,h} is the limit of Var(N−1/2∑iκi,h)\operatorname{Var}(N^{-1/2}\sum_{i}\kappa_{i,h}). The cross-sectional term enters through the panel moment only. Without independence, the covariance also includes the cross covariance of the two components (Proposition C.4).

Proposition C.4 (Joint time and cross-sectional targeting limit).

Suppose (C.59) holds, the structural remainder satisfies conditional instrument exclusion, Assumption C.1 holds for the remaining moments, 𝔼⁡[𝐚i​𝐚i′]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}] is nonsingular, T/N→τ∈[0,∞)T/N\to\tau\in[0,\infty), and

(T−1/2∑t𝐦t,hN−1/2∑iκi,h)→𝑑N⁡(0,(ΩT,hΩT​N,hΩT​N,h′ΩN,h)).\begin{pmatrix}T^{-1/2}\sum_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t,h}\\ N^{-1/2}\sum_{i}\kappa_{i,h}\end{pmatrix}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N\!\left(0,\begin{pmatrix}\Omega_{T,h}&\Omega_{TN,h}\\ \Omega_{TN,h}^{\prime}&\Omega_{N,h}\end{pmatrix}\right). (C.66)

Then

T​(𝜷^h−𝜷hP)→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,VhT),\sqrt{T}(\widehat{\bm{\beta}}_{h}-\bm{\beta}_{h}^{P})\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(\mathbf{0},\ V_{h}^{\mathrm{T}}\bigr), (C.67)

where VhT=Lh𝐉h−1{ΩT,h+τEgΩN,hEg′+τ(ΩT​N,hEg′+EgΩT​N,h′)}𝐉h−1′Lh′V_{h}^{\mathrm{T}}=L_{h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1}\{\Omega_{T,h}+\tau E_{g}\Omega_{N,h}E_{g}^{\prime}+\sqrt{\tau}(\Omega_{TN,h}E_{g}^{\prime}+E_{g}\Omega_{TN,h}^{\prime})\}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime}. Under exact sample balance, VhT=Lh𝐉h−1ΩT,h𝐉h−1′Lh′V_{h}^{\mathrm{T}}=L_{h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1}\Omega_{T,h}\mathbf{J}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime}.

Let Aa=𝔼⁡[𝐚i​𝐚i′]A_{a}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}] and A^a=N−1​∑i𝐚i​𝐚i′\widehat{A}_{a}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}. The normal equations imply

Π^−Π=A^a−1N−1∑i𝐚i𝐬i​g⟂⁣′=Aa−1N−1∑i𝐚i𝐬i​g⟂⁣′+op(N−1/2).\widehat{\Pi}-\Pi=\widehat{A}_{a}^{-1}N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp\prime}=A_{a}^{-1}N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp\prime}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). (C.68)

Consequently,

δ^q\displaystyle\widehat{\delta}_{q} =N−1​∑i𝐬i​g⟂​si​rq−(Π^−Π)′​N−1​∑i𝐚i​si​rq\displaystyle=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}s_{ir_{q}}-(\widehat{\Pi}-\Pi)^{\prime}N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}s_{ir_{q}}
=N−1∑i𝐬i​g⟂(si​rq−𝐚i′γq)+op(N−1/2)=N−1∑iχq,i+op(N−1/2).\displaystyle=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{s}_{ig}^{\perp}(s_{ir_{q}}-\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\gamma_{q})+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\chi_{q,i}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). (C.69)

Here 𝔼​χq,i=0\mathbb{E}\chi_{q,i}=0 by population balance and projection orthogonality. Since m^q,h=mq,h+Op(T−1/2)\widehat{m}_{q,h}=m_{q,h}+O_{p}(T^{-1/2}),

∑qδ^q⊗m^q,h=N−1∑iκi,h+Op((NT)−1/2)+op(N−1/2).\sum_{q}\widehat{\delta}_{q}\otimes\widehat{m}_{q,h}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\kappa_{i,h}+O_{p}((NT)^{-1/2})+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}).

Hence, with bounded T/NT/N, the normalized stacked sample moment at the population parameters equals

T−1/2∑t𝐦t,h+T/NEgN−1/2∑iκi,h+op(1).T^{-1/2}\sum_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t,h}+\sqrt{T/N}\,E_{g}N^{-1/2}\sum_{i}\kappa_{i,h}+o_{p}(1). (C.70)

Its joint CLT gives a normal limit with covariance ΩT,h+τ​Eg​ΩN,h​Eg′+τ​(ΩT​N,h​Eg′+Eg​ΩT​N,h′)\Omega_{T,h}+\tau E_{g}\Omega_{N,h}E_{g}^{\prime}+\sqrt{\tau}(\Omega_{TN,h}E_{g}^{\prime}+E_{g}\Omega_{TN,h}^{\prime}), and the argument of Proposition C.2 then gives (C.67). If si​rq=𝐚i′​γqs_{ir_{q}}=\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\gamma_{q}, then

δ^q=N−1​∑i𝐬^i​g⟂​𝐚i′​γq=0\widehat{\delta}_{q}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{ig}^{\perp}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\prime}\gamma_{q}=0

by the sample normal equations. This proves the exact-balance claim. ∎

When ΩN,h\Omega_{N,h} is estimable and units are independently sampled, a covariance estimator is

Ω^N,h=1N​∑i(κ^i,h−κ^¯h)​(κ^i,h−κ^¯h)′,\widehat{\Omega}_{N,h}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}(\widehat{\kappa}_{i,h}-\overline{\widehat{\kappa}}_{h})(\widehat{\kappa}_{i,h}-\overline{\widehat{\kappa}}_{h})^{\prime}, (C.71)

with consistently estimated projections, omitted-path coefficients, and aggregate moments in κi,h\kappa_{i,h}; clustered units require the corresponding cluster covariance. The variance added to the coefficient covariance is N−1Lh𝐉^h−1EgΩ^N,hEg′𝐉^h−1′Lh′N^{-1}L_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1}E_{g}\widehat{\Omega}_{N,h}E_{g}^{\prime}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime}.

If the omitted exposures or the coefficients in mq,hm_{q,h} are not identified, (C.65) has no sample analogue, and one must maintain a negligible-imbalance condition or retain the relevant path controls. Time-only heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC), equal-weighted cosine (EWC), and time-block bootstrap estimators do not recover the imbalance term, which time centering removes.

C.9.  Feasible covariance estimates and simultaneous inference

Compute the sample Jacobian 𝐉^h\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h} of the stacked moments: Σ^h\widehat{\Sigma}_{h}, the sample derivative D^h\widehat{D}_{h} of the concentrated moment at (ϑ^h,η^)(\widehat{\vartheta}_{h},\widehat{\eta}), holding ϑ^h\widehat{\vartheta}_{h} fixed, and the first-step Jacobian A^η\widehat{A}_{\eta}. V^h=Lh𝐉^h−1𝛀^h𝐉^h−1′Lh′,\widehat{V}_{h}=L_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1}\widehat{\bm{\Omega}}_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime}, (C.72)

Numerical derivatives of the entire moment reconstruct shocks, responses, weights, and any generated controls at each perturbation.

C.9.3.  Joint restrictions and horizon bands

Stack all desired coefficients and their date-level moments on the same sample, and form the joint sandwich covariance V^\widehat{V}. If RR defines rr linearly independent restrictions, consistent HAC gives

T​(R​β^−r0)′​(R​V^​R′)−1​(R​β^−r0)→𝑑χr2.T(R\widehat{\beta}-r_{0})^{\prime}(R\widehat{V}R^{\prime})^{-1}(R\widehat{\beta}-r_{0})\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \chi_{r}^{2}. (C.80)

Under the fixed-ν\nu EWC conditions and ν≥r\nu\geq r, the corrected statistic (ν−r+1)/(ν​r)(\nu-r+1)/(\nu r) times the left-hand side of (C.80), with EWC in place of HAC, converges to Fr,ν−r+1F_{r,\nu-r+1}. This follows because ν​R​V^EWC​R′\nu R\widehat{V}^{\mathrm{EWC}}R^{\prime}, with V^EWC\widehat{V}^{\mathrm{EWC}} the sandwich formed with 𝛀^EWC\widehat{\bm{\Omega}}^{\mathrm{EWC}}, has an independent Wishart limit. Marginal intervals are pointwise; simultaneous bands can be calibrated from the maximum absolute studentized statistic in the joint bootstrap below.

C.10.  Resampling inference

The time-dimension bootstrap resamples contiguous time blocks jointly across the aggregate data, the proxies, and the panel cross section, keeping unit labels and exposures fixed and using the same draws across horizons. With block length ℓT→∞\ell_{T}\to\infty and ℓT/T→0\ell_{T}/T\to 0, joint blocks preserve the cross covariance between the panel and first-step moments; independent aggregate and panel draws remove it. We resample circular blocks of preassembled date records, each containing all lags, leads, and panel outcomes needed at its base date, with block length larger than the lag–lead span.

Full re-estimation reruns every estimated component, namely the aggregate moments or the VAR, the proxy restrictions, the normalization, the estimated shocks, the offset weights, the generated controls, the residualization, and the panel IV, on the identified branch of the original sample. Alternatively, a centered one-step block bootstrap resamples blocks of 𝐦ˇt\check{\mathbf{m}}_{t} and takes one Newton step from the original estimate,

β∗=β^−L​𝐉^−1​1T​∑t=1T𝐦ˇt∗,\beta^{*}=\widehat{\beta}-L\widehat{\mathbf{J}}^{-1}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\check{\mathbf{m}}_{t}^{*}, (C.81)

which reproduces the first-order distribution under a valid block-bootstrap approximation [Künsch, 1989, Gonçalves, 2011].

When the targeting component of Proposition C.4 matters, the time draw is supplemented, under the independence used in (C.65), by a centered cross-sectional draw of Lh​𝐉^h−1​Eg​κ^iL_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1}E_{g}\widehat{\kappa}_{i} at scale N−1/2N^{-1/2}.

C.11.  Weak controlled treatment relevance

For HELP-IV with the instruments of Section 4.1, write ϑ=(b,c′)′\vartheta=(b,c^{\prime})^{\prime} and partition the sample moments as g¯​(ϑ)=(g¯g​(ϑ),g¯r​(ϑ)′)′\bar{g}(\vartheta)=(\bar{g}_{g}(\vartheta),\bar{g}_{r}(\vartheta)^{\prime})^{\prime}. If the nuisance path block Σr​c\Sigma_{rc} is strongly identified, solve g¯r​(b,c^​(b))=0\bar{g}_{r}(b,\widehat{c}(b))=0 at each candidate bb and form

ζt​(b)=gg,t​(b,c⁡(b))−Σg​c​Σr​c−1​gr,t​(b,c⁡(b)).\zeta_{t}(b)=g_{g,t}(b,c(b))-\Sigma_{gc}\Sigma_{rc}^{-1}g_{r,t}(b,c(b)).

With a consistent HAC estimate of its long-run variance,

𝒞1−α={b:T​g¯g​(b,c^​(b))2Ω^ζ​(b)≤χ1,1−α2}.\mathcal{C}_{1-\alpha}=\left\{b:\frac{T\bar{g}_{g}(b,\widehat{c}(b))^{2}}{\widehat{\Omega}_{\zeta}(b)}\leq\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\right\}. (C.82)

The denominator accounts for estimation of c⁡(b)c(b), and the null moment has a regular limit without dividing by the controlled first stage. If the path block is weak, the joint moment test over (b,c)(b,c) is inverted and projected onto bb [Dufour and Taamouti, 2005]. With SVAR shocks or estimated offset weights, the first-step moments are stacked into ζt​(b)\zeta_{t}(b).

Appendix D Monte Carlo details

This appendix reports the designs and results summarized in Section 5, in the order of the main text.

D.1.  Weak proxies

Table D.1 raises the standard deviation of the measurement error of one proxy in the backward-looking environment from 0.50.5 to 22 and 33, and keeps that of the other proxy at 0.50.5. The structural shock then accounts for 20 and 10 percent of the variance of the weakened proxy, against 80 percent in Section 5.1.

The table also reports the median first-stage FF statistic of HELP-IV. The statistic is the squared ratio of the sample covariance between the treatment and the effective instrument, which is the denominator of HELP-IV, to the standard error of that covariance. The effective instrument is the combination of instruments that is uncorrelated in the sample with every path control, and the standard error uses the long-run variance estimator of the HELP-IV standard errors. Because the statistic divides the covariance by its own standard error, it does not depend on the units of the instruments or of the confounders.

Besides the measures of the main text, this table and the following ones report the range of the estimates, which is the difference between their 95th and 5th percentiles. Unlike the RMSE, the range is not dominated by the few replications with extreme estimates, which occur because a just-identified IV estimator has no finite moments [Kinal, 1980]. Comparing the median length of the intervals with the range shows whether the standard errors track the dispersion of the estimates.

Table D.1 delivers two results. First, the median bias of HELP-IV stays at most 0.040.04 in absolute value although the median first-stage FF statistic falls from 3939–4848 with the proxies of the main text to 88 or 99 with the noisiest treatment proxy, and its intervals cover the target in 89–94 percent of replications in every cell with a weakened proxy. These designs do not establish uniform validity of the Wald intervals under weak identification. Second, weak proxies cost precision. When the noise of the treatment proxy is 33, the range of HELP-IV at h=2h=2 and h=4h=4 is 2.32.3 to 2.52.5 times that of the first block. When the noise of the confounder proxy is 33, the range is up to 3.63.6 times as large, and 1212 of the 2,0002{,}000 replications have errors above 1010 in absolute value at h=4h=4. Because these replications dominate the RMSE, the RMSE equals 7.317.31 and exceeds the range of 1.911.91.

D.2.  Exact identification and the first step in the forward-looking environment

Table D.2 reports the exactly identified case, in which the researcher observes proxies for all six news shocks instead of two.2020 20 In the forward-looking environment, the first step of E-HELP-IV and the time-series step of the decomposition method control for two lags of GtG_{t} and RtR_{t}. The proxies of the seven date-tt shocks that move RR, namely zr,tz_{r,t} and the six news proxies, then span the confounder path through t+6t+6. The composite instrument therefore holds the whole expected path fixed, and the unabsorbed share of Section 3.3 is zero, against 2.0 percent with two news proxies. TWFE-IV and the decomposition method are biased with the same signs as in Table 1. E-HELP-IV has a median bias of at most 0.040.04 in absolute value and an RMSE of 0.170.17 to 0.470.47, and its intervals cover the target in 92–94 percent of replications, slightly more often than the nominal 90 percent.

To locate the source of this over-coverage, Table D.3 compares the intervals of Panel B of Table 1 and of Table D.2 with two alternatives. The first alternative uses the population weights, which need no first-step term. The second omits the first-step term from the standard error. The first step sets the weights from the sample covariances between the confounder path and the date-tt proxies. The composite instrument therefore has zero sample covariance with every combination of Rt,…,Rt+6R_{t},\ldots,R_{t+6} that the proxies can offset. As a result, the estimated weights lower the range of the estimates by about 45 to 65 percent relative to the population weights. With the population weights, the intervals cover the target in 87–88 percent of replications. Without the first-step term, the standard error ignores the lower dispersion, and the intervals cover the target in 96–100 percent of replications. With the first-step term, the median length of the intervals is close to the range of the estimates, but the tt-statistic remains less dispersed than a standard normal variable, so coverage is 92--95 percent.2121 21 The simulations use Student-tνt_{\nu} critical values for designs whose simulated tt-statistic is more dispersed than a standard normal variable and normal critical values for the other designs, including E-HELP-IV. This calibration depends on the design and differs from the prespecified EWC procedure of Appendix C.9.

D.3.  Shocks estimated from an SVAR

This subsection uses as instruments the shocks estimated from an SVAR, as in Appendix B, instead of the proxies. The researcher fits a VAR(2) to (Gt,Rt)(G_{t},R_{t}), which is correctly specified. The impact column of the treatment shock is identified by the covariance between the reduced-form residuals and the treatment proxy, and the confounder shock is the remaining structural shock. HELP-IV then uses the estimated shocks as instruments, and composite HELP-IV uses a single instrument whose weights come from the impulse responses of the fitted SVAR. The sandwich covariance stacks the SVAR estimating equations with the IV moment, and for composite HELP-IV these first-step moments are aligned with the lead of the instrument that they offset (Appendix C.7).

Table D.4 shows that HELP-IV and composite HELP-IV with SVAR shocks both have a median bias of at most 0.020.02 in absolute value. Their intervals cover the target in 87–90 percent of replications, against 88–89 percent with the proxies as instruments. The median length of the intervals is within 0.020.02 of the range of the estimates at every horizon, so the standard errors with the first-step term track the dispersion of the estimates.

D.4.  One-way general equilibrium

To show that the bias of the decomposition method in Panel A of Table 1 comes from two-way general equilibrium on impact (Section 2.4), Table D.5 removes RtR_{t} and Rt−1R_{t-1} from the equation for GtG_{t}, so that general equilibrium is one-way. Because the impact response of the treatment under the fixed path then equals its unrestricted impact response, the decomposition method recovers βhP\beta_{h}^{P} in population.2222 22 Donaldson [2026, Appendix C.4] considers a specification similar to that of our cross-sectional step, which adds exposure times the lagged treatment and the lagged confounder shock. TWFE-IV is biased by the exposure-correlation component alone, which is −0.18-0.18 on impact and at most 0.040.04 in absolute value thereafter. HELP-IV and the decomposition method both have a median bias of at most 0.020.02 in absolute value, and their RMSEs differ by at most 0.020.02.

The two methods differ in the coverage of their intervals. The intervals of HELP-IV cover the target in 87–88 percent of replications, whereas those of the decomposition method cover it in 97 percent at h=0h=0 but in only 84 and 80 percent at h=2h=2 and h=4h=4. The difference comes from the covariance estimator of the decomposition method. Donaldson [2026, Appendix A.7] writes her estimator as a just-identified system of generalized method of moments (GMM) conditions that stacks the panel and the time-series moments over all horizons. The baseline covariance estimator, specification (ii) of that appendix, sets to zero the covariances between the panel and the time-series moments and the covariances across horizons. The resulting standard error is distorted in both directions: the baseline intervals are longer than the range of the estimates at h=0h=0 and about 10 to 20 percent shorter at h=2h=2 and h=4h=4.

D.5.  Two exposure margins

To evaluate HELP-IV with multiple exposure margins (Section 3.1), this subsection lets the treatment reach each unit through two exposure margins. The first margin is the exposure si​gs_{ig} of Section 5.1.1. The second, si​g,2s_{ig,2}, equals 0.5​si​g0.5\,s_{ig} plus an independent normal term with standard deviation 0.80.8, so that the two margins have a correlation of 0.530.53. The outcome depends on the second margin through si​g,2​(0.35​Gt−0.12​Gt−1+0.08​Gt−2)s_{ig,2}(0.35\,G_{t}-0.12\,G_{t-1}+0.08\,G_{t-2}). Confounder exposure is si​r=0.65​si​g+0.30​si​g,2s_{ir}=0.65\,s_{ig}+0.30\,s_{ig,2} plus an independent standard normal term, so it rises with both margins. Because 0.65+0.30×0.5=0.80.65+0.30\times 0.5=0.8, the projection of si​rs_{ir} on si​gs_{ig} alone keeps the coefficient 0.80.8 of Section 5.1.1. HELP-IV interacts the treatment, the path controls, and the instruments with both margins, whereas TWFE-IV is estimated margin by margin. Both panel regressions control for the lags of GtG_{t} and RtR_{t} interacted with both margins.

Table D.6 shows that HELP-IV recovers both margin-specific partial-equilibrium effects, β1,hP\beta_{1,h}^{P} and β2,hP\beta_{2,h}^{P}. Its median bias is at most 0.030.03 in absolute value, and its intervals cover the target in 85–89 percent of replications on both margins. TWFE-IV is biased on both margins, because confounder exposure rises with both. On the second margin, its bias reaches 0.220.22 against a target of 0.100.10.

D.6.  The two-region model

This subsection describes the two-region model of Donaldson [2026, Appendix D], its calibration, and the design of the simulations. Symbols specific to her model follow her paper and are local to this subsection and the next.

The model is a monetary union of two regions, Home (HH) and Foreign (FF), each of size 0.50.5. The model extends Nakamura and Steinsson [2014] by letting the regions differ in their exposure to the aggregate spending shock and in their intertemporal elasticity of substitution. We log-linearize the model around the symmetric zero-inflation steady state and solve the linear model with Dynare. Lower-case variables are log deviations from the steady state, and spending is measured in units of steady-state output, so a spending shock of one is one percent of steady-state output.

Households in each region consume both goods, with a share ϕj\phi_{j} of the good of their own region j∈{H,F}j\in\{H,F\}. Home and Foreign consumer-price inflation are therefore πH,tC=ϕH​πH,t+(1−ϕH)​πF,t\pi^{C}_{H,t}=\phi_{H}\pi_{H,t}+(1-\phi_{H})\pi_{F,t} and πF,tC=ϕF​πF,t+(1−ϕF)​πH,t\pi^{C}_{F,t}=\phi_{F}\pi_{F,t}+(1-\phi_{F})\pi_{H,t}, where πH,t\pi_{H,t} and πF,t\pi_{F,t} are the producer-price inflation rates. The Home household satisfies the Euler equation

cH,t=𝔼t​cH,t+1−σH​(it−𝔼t​πH,t+1C),c_{H,t}=\mathbb{E}_{t}c_{H,t+1}-\sigma_{H}\bigl(i_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{t}\pi^{C}_{H,t+1}\bigr),

where iti_{t} is the nominal interest rate of the union and σH\sigma_{H} is the Home elasticity of intertemporal substitution. Complete markets link consumption across regions through cH,t/σH−cF,t/σF=(ϕH+ϕF−1)​τtc_{H,t}/\sigma_{H}-c_{F,t}/\sigma_{F}=(\phi_{H}+\phi_{F}-1)\tau_{t}, where τt=τt−1+πF,t−πH,t\tau_{t}=\tau_{t-1}+\pi_{F,t}-\pi_{H,t} is the relative price of Foreign goods. The Foreign Euler equation follows from the Home Euler equation and the risk-sharing condition. With a steady-state spending share of 0.20.2 and a trade elasticity η\eta, goods markets clear when

yH,t\displaystyle y_{H,t} =0.8​[ϕH​(cH,t+η⁡(1−ϕH)​τt)+(1−ϕF)​(cF,t+η​ϕF​τt)]+gH,t,\displaystyle=0.8\Bigl[\phi_{H}\bigl(c_{H,t}+\eta(1-\phi_{H})\tau_{t}\bigr)+(1-\phi_{F})\bigl(c_{F,t}+\eta\phi_{F}\tau_{t}\bigr)\Bigr]+g_{H,t},
yF,t\displaystyle y_{F,t} =0.8​[(1−ϕH)​(cH,t−η​ϕH​τt)+ϕF​(cF,t−η⁡(1−ϕF)​τt)]+gF,t,\displaystyle=0.8\Bigl[(1-\phi_{H})\bigl(c_{H,t}-\eta\phi_{H}\tau_{t}\bigr)+\phi_{F}\bigl(c_{F,t}-\eta(1-\phi_{F})\tau_{t}\bigr)\Bigr]+g_{F,t},

where gH,tg_{H,t} and gF,tg_{F,t} are regional government purchases.

Firms keep their price with probability α\alpha in each quarter, so each region has the Phillips curve πj,t=ϰ​m​cj,t+β​𝔼t​πj,t+1\pi_{j,t}=\varkappa\,mc_{j,t}+\beta\mathbb{E}_{t}\pi_{j,t+1}, with real marginal cost

m​cH,t\displaystyle mc_{H,t} =1/ν+1−aa​yH,t+cH,tσH+(1−ϕH)​τt,\displaystyle=\frac{1/\nu+1-a}{a}\,y_{H,t}+\frac{c_{H,t}}{\sigma_{H}}+(1-\phi_{H})\tau_{t},
m​cF,t\displaystyle mc_{F,t} =1/ν+1−aa​yF,t+cF,tσF−(1−ϕF)​τt,\displaystyle=\frac{1/\nu+1-a}{a}\,y_{F,t}+\frac{c_{F,t}}{\sigma_{F}}-(1-\phi_{F})\tau_{t},

where β\beta is the discount factor, ν\nu is the Frisch elasticity of labor supply, and aa is the elasticity of output with respect to labor. The slope is ϰ=ζ⁡(1−α)​(1−α​β)/α\varkappa=\zeta(1-\alpha)(1-\alpha\beta)/\alpha, where ζ=1/[1+((1+1/ν)/a−1)​ϑ]\zeta=1/[1+((1+1/\nu)/a-1)\vartheta] is the strategic-complementarity factor of Nakamura and Steinsson [2014] and ϑ=7\vartheta=7 is the elasticity of substitution between varieties.

The nominal rate follows the policy rule

it=ρi​it−1+(1−ρi)​(ϕπ​πta​g​g+ϕy​yta​g​g)+ut,i_{t}=\rho_{i}\,i_{t-1}+(1-\rho_{i})\bigl(\phi_{\pi}\pi^{agg}_{t}+\phi_{y}\,y^{agg}_{t}\bigr)+u_{t},

where πta​g​g=0.5​(πH,tC+πF,tC)\pi^{agg}_{t}=0.5\,(\pi^{C}_{H,t}+\pi^{C}_{F,t}) and yta​g​g=0.5​(yH,t+yF,t)y^{agg}_{t}=0.5\,(y_{H,t}+y_{F,t}) are inflation and output in the union. The policy shock ut=ρu​ut−1+ϵi,t+∑k≥1ϵk,t−knu_{t}=\rho_{u}u_{t-1}+\epsilon_{i,t}+\sum_{k\geq 1}\epsilon^{n}_{k,t-k} combines a contemporaneous shock ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t} with news shocks ϵk,tn\epsilon^{n}_{k,t}, which are announced at tt about date t+kt+k. The confounder is the real rate rt=it−𝔼t​πt+1a​g​gr_{t}=i_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{t}\pi^{agg}_{t+1}, and the regressions use its annualized value Rt=4​rtR_{t}=4r_{t}.

The persistence ρu\rho_{u} of the policy shock defines the two scenarios of her paper. In the aligned scenario, ρu=0.85\rho_{u}=0.85, so a policy shock moves the real rate persistently, as a spending shock does, and a few date-tt policy shocks can reproduce the path of the real rate that a spending shock generates. In the misaligned scenario, ρu=0\rho_{u}=0, so a policy shock moves the real rate only briefly, as the last rows of Table D.7 show. Our simulations use the aligned scenario, and the misaligned scenario serves only to check our implementation against her figures.

Regional spending follows gj,t=ρg​gj,t−1+ℓj​xt+ej,tg_{j,t}=\rho_{g}g_{j,t-1}+\ell_{j}x_{t}+e_{j,t}, where xtx_{t} is the common spending impulse, the loading ℓj\ell_{j} is the exposure of region jj, and ej,te_{j,t} is a regional shock. The loadings satisfy 0.5​ℓH+0.5​ℓF=10.5\,\ell_{H}+0.5\,\ell_{F}=1, so aggregate spending Gt=0.5​(gH,t+gF,t)G_{t}=0.5\,(g_{H,t}+g_{F,t}) moves one for one with the impulse. In her model, xt=ϵg,tx_{t}=\epsilon_{g,t}, the spending shock, so spending does not respond to the real rate and general equilibrium is one-way. In our two-way version, xt=ϵg,t−ψ​rt−1x_{t}=\epsilon_{g,t}-\psi\,r_{t-1}, so spending responds to the real rate with a one-quarter lag. Because of the lag, GtG_{t} contains no contemporaneous policy shock, as Proposition 6 requires.

The calibration follows Table A12 of Donaldson [2026], with β=0.99\beta=0.99, ν=1\nu=1, η=2\eta=2, a=0.63a=0.63, ϕH=ϕF=0.85\phi_{H}=\phi_{F}=0.85, α=0.75\alpha=0.75, ρi=0.8\rho_{i}=0.8, ϕπ=1.5\phi_{\pi}=1.5, ρg=0.85\rho_{g}=0.85, and no hand-to-mouth households. Four settings depart from that table, because its printed values do not reproduce her Figures 3 and A3. First, the slope includes the factor ζ\zeta, which gives ϰ=0.0053\varkappa=0.0053. Second, the output coefficient inside the bracket of the policy rule is ϕy=0.5\phi_{y}=0.5, so its effective value is 0.10.1. Third, the elasticities σH=1.2\sigma_{H}=1.2 and σF=0.8\sigma_{F}=0.8 and the loadings ℓH=0.8\ell_{H}=0.8 and ℓF=1.2\ell_{F}=1.2 are the values of her Table 3. The region more exposed to spending thus has the lower elasticity of intertemporal substitution, so its consumption responds less to the real rate, and exposure to the treatment and exposure to the real rate are negatively correlated. Fourth, we choose ρu=0.85\rho_{u}=0.85 and ρu=0\rho_{u}=0 to reproduce her figures, because she does not report the values behind them.2323 23 Her Table 3, which serves another exercise, sets ρu=0.75\rho_{u}=0.75 and a hand-to-mouth share of 0.20.2. Table D.7 shows that our implementation reproduces her Figures 3 and A3 with the four settings.

We set the feedback coefficient ψ\psi from a statistic of annual US data. We estimate local projections of the federal funds rate and of the annual change in national defense spending relative to GDP on the monetary policy shock of Romer and Romer [2004] over 1971 to 2007. The projections control for two lags of the two variables and of the shock. The statistic divides the cumulative spending response over years 0 to 4 by the cumulative funds-rate response. The statistic equals −0.21-0.21, so the point estimate implies that spending falls after a monetary tightening. We compute the same statistic on annual averages of a long simulation of the model, with the spending shock and the contemporaneous policy shock as the only shocks, and ψ=0.456\psi=0.456 reproduces it.

Each replication simulates T=200T=200 quarters after a burn-in of 200 quarters. The regressions use 194 of the 200 quarters, because the first two quarters provide the lagged controls and the last four provide the leads up to h=4h=4. The spending shock has standard deviation 11. The contemporaneous policy shock and the news shocks about the policy shock one, two, and three quarters ahead have standard deviation 0.250.25, and the regional spending shocks have standard deviation 0.50.5. The other news shocks serve only to compute population values. The researcher observes the spending shock, the contemporaneous policy shock, and the three news shocks without error, as in the simulations of Donaldson [2026, Section 3.3].2424 24 Her text does not state whether the shocks in her simulations carry measurement error.

With two regions, the panel regressions with unit and time effects reduce to time-series regressions on the difference between the regions, so exposure enters only through the difference ℓH−ℓF=−0.4\ell_{H}-\ell_{F}=-0.4. The outcome and the treatment are the cumulative variables

𝒴j,t+h=∑k=0hyj,t+k−yj,t−1100+yj,t−1,𝒢j,t+h=∑k=0hgj,t+k−gj,t−1100+yj,t−1,\mathcal{Y}_{j,t+h}=\sum_{k=0}^{h}\frac{y_{j,t+k}-y_{j,t-1}}{100+y_{j,t-1}},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{j,t+h}=\sum_{k=0}^{h}\frac{g_{j,t+k}-g_{j,t-1}}{100+y_{j,t-1}},

where 100+yj,t100+y_{j,t} is the output of region jj in levels. The regressions of the outcome on the treatment control for the lagged growth of the output difference, as in Donaldson [2026]. The first step of E-HELP-IV controls for two lags of GtG_{t} and RtR_{t}, whereas the time-series step of the decomposition has no controls and uses Newey–West standard errors with four lags.

D.7.  The cumulative fiscal multiplier in the two-region model

This subsection evaluates E-HELP-IV for the transformed target of Section 3.4 in the model of Appendix D.6. The target ℬhP\mathcal{B}_{h}^{P} is the partial-equilibrium multiplier, the cumulative fiscal multiplier when the expected path of the real rate is held fixed; Donaldson [2026] calls it the portable multiplier. Because the model is forward-looking, the exercise draws on Sections 3.3 and 3.4. The experiment behind the target combines the spending shock with the sequence of date-tt policy shocks, the contemporaneous shock and 40 news shocks, that holds the path of the real rate fixed over quarters 0 to 40. The target divides the cumulative response of the output difference to the experiment by the cumulative response of the spending difference. Under two-way general equilibrium, the spending response itself changes when the path of the real rate is held fixed, so the denominator of the target differs from the unrestricted spending response.

We compare three estimators. The benchmark is the shift-share design of Section 3.4, which instruments the cumulative treatment by exposure times the one-quarter change in aggregate spending relative to lagged output, as in her fiscal application. The decomposition is her ex ante decomposition with the four date-tt policy shocks. E-HELP-IV is the transformed design of Section 3.4 with the composite instrument of Section 3.3, built from the same four shocks. The decomposition and E-HELP-IV thus use the four shocks to offset the path of the real rate over quarters 0 to 4 as closely as possible. The standard error of E-HELP-IV includes the first-step term for the estimated weights, and the decomposition uses her baseline covariance estimator.

Table D.8 delivers three results. First, the shift-share design, which corrects neither for the HEDGE bias nor for the omitted-history bias of Proposition 6, is biased by 0.480.48 to 0.660.66 in both panels. Second, under one-way general equilibrium (Panel A), the decomposition method and E-HELP-IV both have a median bias of at most 0.030.03 in absolute value, which replicates the finding of Donaldson [2026] that her ex ante decomposition with four shocks recovers the partial-equilibrium multiplier in the aligned scenario. E-HELP-IV is more precise, with a range 19–22 percent narrower and intervals 32–39 percent shorter.

Third, under two-way general equilibrium (Panel B), E-HELP-IV keeps a median bias of at most 0.010.01 in absolute value, and its intervals cover the target in 92–93 percent of replications. The bias of the decomposition method grows with the horizon and reaches 0.070.07 at h=4h=4, 8 percent of the target. Its intervals nevertheless cover the target in 93–98 percent of replications, because they are 1.5 to 1.8 times as long as those of E-HELP-IV; coverage does not reveal the bias.

In both panels, single replications dominate the RMSE at long horizons. In Panel A, a single replication accounts for 46 and 90 percent of the sum of squared errors of E-HELP-IV at h=2h=2 and h=4h=4, so its RMSE exceeds that of the decomposition method at these horizons although its range is narrower. In Panel B, the largest error at h=4h=4 accounts for 61 percent of the sum of squared errors of E-HELP-IV and for 55 percent of that of the decomposition method, while the range of E-HELP-IV is 19 percent narrower.

The population limits, which we compute from the impulse responses of the model, show that the bias of the decomposition method in Panel B is not a finite-sample effect. The limit of E-HELP-IV stays within 0.0020.002 of the target, whereas the limit of the decomposition method exceeds the target by 1 to 8 percent at h=1h=1 to 44. Because the fall in spending that the higher real rate causes accumulates, the excess keeps growing beyond h=4h=4 and reaches 19 percent at h=8h=8, two years after the shock.

D.8.  Multiple aggregate confounders

To support the comparison of the three HELP-IV designs in Section 5.2.2, Table D.9 reports the median bias and the range of each design.2525 25 Because the outcome equation of Section 5.2.1 contains no lags of the aggregates, the panel regressions of Section 5.2 control only for the lagged outcome. In Panel A, the range of multiple-confounder HELP-IV does not exceed that of composite HELP-IV up to h=6h=6 but is larger at h=8h=8, 2.742.74 against 1.931.93. In Panel B, by contrast, the range of composite HELP-IV is 1.41.4 to 1.51.5 times that of multiple-confounder HELP-IV at every horizon. In the same panel, the median length of the intervals of multiple-confounder HELP-IV falls from 96 percent of the range of its estimates at h=2h=2 to 79 percent at h=8h=8, whereas the ratio for composite HELP-IV stays between 93 and 102 percent. The standard error of multiple-confounder HELP-IV thus understates the dispersion of its estimates at long horizons.

In Panel A, the extreme estimates of multiple-confounder HELP-IV come from the replications with a weak first stage. Its first-stage FF statistic is below one in 0.80.8 and 4.24.2 percent of replications at h=6h=6 and 88. Without these replications, its median bias changes by at most 0.020.02, and its RMSE falls from 1.381.38 to 0.490.49 at h=6h=6 and from above 900900 to 0.780.78 at h=8h=8. In Panel B, by contrast, the statistic is never below one.

Table D.10 reports the other two combinations of measurement error and within-period response, which Section 5.2.2 summarizes. With a small measurement error and no within-period response, the first-stage FF statistic of multiple-confounder HELP-IV is never below one, and the RMSE of composite HELP-IV is 1.11.1 to 1.21.2 times that of multiple-confounder HELP-IV. With a large measurement error and a within-period response, the statistic is below one in 0.70.7 and 5.85.8 percent of replications at h=6h=6 and 88. The errors of multiple-confounder HELP-IV then exceed 1010 in absolute value in 1818 replications at h=8h=8, whereas the largest error of composite HELP-IV is only 6.66.6.

The standard error of targeting-rule HELP-IV adds the cross-sectional part of Section 4, because the orthogonality of Assumption 2 holds in a sample of NN units only up to an error of order N−1/2N^{-1/2}. With N=T=200N=T=200, this part raises the coverage of targeting-rule HELP-IV by at most 0.80.8 percentage points at the reported horizons.

Appendix E Inference for the empirical applications

This appendix describes the standard errors in Tables 3 and 4. The HELP-IV instruments are generated from an estimated aggregate model, so inference accounts jointly for the estimation of that model and for the panel regression. The HELP-IV rows use the covariance formulas for SVAR shocks in Propositions B.1 and B.2 (Appendix B), with the transformed outcome and treatment in the fiscal application. The decomposition row uses the covariance estimator described in Appendix E.2, and the shift-share IV row uses a time-block bootstrap (Appendix E.3). The targeting-rule entries contain only the time-series component of uncertainty (Appendix E.1.1).

E.1.  Analytic standard errors

For a common effective sample, the analytic variance is the coefficient element of the sample sandwich,

Var^(β^h)=1TLh𝐉^h−1𝛀^h𝐉^h−1′Lh′,\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_{h})=\frac{1}{T}\,L_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1}\widehat{\bm{\Omega}}_{h}\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h}^{-1\prime}L_{h}^{\prime},

where 𝐉^h\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{h} is the sample Jacobian (B.5) or (B.12) and 𝛀^h\widehat{\bm{\Omega}}_{h} is the long-run covariance of the stacked date-level moments, the panel IV moment and the SVAR estimating equations (Appendix B). For full-path estimation the treatment selector picks the coefficient on the treatment from the full parameter vector. The derivative holds the panel coefficient fixed, differentiates the complete concentrated moment, and is evaluated analytically (Appendix C.4).

E.1.1.  Fiscal multipliers

Backward-looking HELP-IV uses the bivariate proxy-SVAR described in Section 6.1. Its first-step moments cover the VAR coefficients, residual covariance, proxy-identification moments, and shock normalizations, as in (C.21) and Lemma C.3. For targeting-rule HELP-IV, interactions between targeting characteristics and estimated shocks are generated controls. Their derivatives enter through (C.9) and (C.62). For E-HELP-IV, the four-variable SVAR also determines the news offset. Its derivative includes the residual-path term in (C.45), because the path is not exactly spanned. We use Bartlett weights with bandwidth ⌊4​(T/100)2/9⌋=3\lfloor 4(T/100)^{2/9}\rfloor=3.

The targeting-rule standard errors in Tables 3 and E.1 contain the time-series component only. They are complete standard errors under exact sample balance or under imbalance that is negligible at the time-series scale. Balance in the population alone adds the term in (C.65), and with 46 states and 39 annual observations, the approximation T/N→0T/N\to 0 does not justify omitting it. The sample analogue (C.71) requires the omitted exposures and their path loadings; when these are not identified, the formula cannot be evaluated. The entries therefore do not establish coverage under population balance alone, which would require an estimable augmented model or a justified joint sampling procedure. The controlled first stages of the targeting-rule specifications are strong, with first-stage FF statistics above 4848 at every reported horizon.

E.1.2.  Stock-wealth responses

The five-variable SVAR is common to all six outcome specifications. County observations are population weighted; county effects, state-by-quarter effects, lagged interactions, and the Bartik control are projected out jointly. The relevant ΣhC\Sigma_{h}^{C} and DhD_{h} are those of this weighted, residualized design. Path neutrality of the composite in the aggregate data implies orthogonality of these panel moments only if the residualized county exposures are independent of the aggregate process; we maintain this condition, which does not follow from aggregate covariances alone.

For the dated composite, decompose the complete derivative as Dh=∑s=0hDh,sD_{h}=\sum_{s=0}^{h}D_{h,s}, including both shock and weight derivatives in each component, and use the aligned stacked moment and Jacobian of (C.56). They give the same sandwich covariance as the unaligned version, up to fixed endpoint terms, but their finite-bandwidth estimates can differ, in either direction. We use bandwidth h+1=8h+1=8 quarters at h=7h=7. A difference between two outcome coefficients stacks the moments of both outcome regressions and uses the difference of their coefficient rows of the inverse Jacobian.

If the panel and SVAR use different date sets ℐP\mathcal{I}_{P} and ℐA\mathcal{I}_{A}, with sizes TPT_{P} and TAT_{A}, the panel moment is averaged over ℐP\mathcal{I}_{P} and the SVAR estimating equations over ℐA\mathcal{I}_{A}, and the sandwich must retain the covariance of the two averages over their overlap. On a common calendar of length T∗T_{*}, the two summands receive weights (T∗/TP)𝟏{t∈ℐP}(T_{*}/T_{P}){\bf 1}\{t\in\mathcal{I}_{P}\} and (T∗/TA)𝟏{t∈ℐA}(T_{*}/T_{A}){\bf 1}\{t\in\mathcal{I}_{A}\} before their joint covariance is formed, with normalization T∗−1T_{*}^{-1}. The common-sample formulas apply directly when the date sets agree up to fixed endpoints; other overlap patterns require their corresponding joint limit.

The CNS benchmark and No confounder controls rows retain the county-and-quarter clustered standard errors of the original specification. They do not estimate structural shocks or offset weights.

E.1.3.  Direction of the first-step correction

The cross-covariances in (C.50) and (C.52) can be negative. For backward-looking HELP-IV in the fiscal application, treating the estimated shocks as known gives standard errors of 0.350.35, 0.500.50, 0.520.52, and 0.670.67, against 0.380.38, 0.400.40, 0.360.36, and 0.530.53 after the joint correction. For nontradable payroll, the corresponding values are 1.091.09 and 0.740.74. Accounting for the first step lowers the standard error in four of these five cases.

E.2.  The decomposition method

We implement the procedure of Donaldson [2026]. Her aggregate local projection of the federal funds rate controls for lagged realizations of the funds rate and of both shocks, log real per capita output, the average federal tax rate, CPI inflation, and log real per capita defense spending. Her correction cumulates the effects of the offsetting monetary policy shocks from the impact date onward.

The decomposition row uses the baseline covariance estimator, specification (ii) of Donaldson [2026, Appendix A.7]. At each horizon k=0,…,hk=0,\ldots,h, her estimator combines two sets of moments. The panel moments come from the regressions of the outcome and of spending on si​g​Gts_{ig}G_{t} and si​g​R​Rts_{ig}RR_{t}. The time-series moments come from the local projection of the federal funds rate at lead kk. The baseline estimator treats the moments of different horizons as uncorrelated and sets to zero the covariance between the panel and the time-series moments. Within a horizon, the panel moments are clustered by year, and the time-series moments use Newey–West weights with bandwidth 33. The standard error of the multiplier follows by the delta method. With bandwidth 44 or h+1h+1 instead, the standard errors change by at most 0.010.01. The block bootstrap of Appendix E.3 gives standard errors that are 18 to 46 percent larger, because the baseline estimator omits the covariances across horizons (Appendix D.4).

E.3.  Block bootstrap

A circular block draw reweights every panel observation dated in the corresponding period. Let ctc_{t} denote the number of sampled blocks containing date tt. All panel observations at date tt receive weight ctc_{t}, and dates with ct=0c_{t}=0 are omitted. We use circular blocks of four annual observations, which cover the longest reported response window, and 1,0001{,}000 replications.

Within each replication, we:

  1. (i)

    re-estimate the panel regressions using the block weights; and

  2. (ii)

    recompute the ratio that defines the shift-share IV multiplier.

The bootstrap standard error is the interquartile range of the replication estimates divided by 1.3491.349, which is robust to draws in which the estimated first-stage denominator is close to zero.

The shift-share IV row contains no generated shock. A Bartlett HAC estimator based on the cross-sectionally averaged IV moment gives standard errors slightly smaller than the block bootstrap. Three- or six-year blocks instead of four-year blocks change the bootstrap standard errors little.

For the HELP-IV rows, Table E.1 compares the analytic standard errors with block-bootstrap standard errors. The block draw is applied to the stacked date-level moments of the analytic sandwich, mapped through the inverse sample Jacobian, so the panel moment and the first-step moments of the same dates are drawn together. The block length is the bandwidth plus one, four years in the fiscal application and nine quarters in the stock-wealth application, which matches the triangular Bartlett weights asymptotically, up to circular and endpoint conventions [Künsch, 1989]. The standard error is the standard deviation of 10,00010{,}000 draws. The two sets of standard errors differ by less than four percent in the fiscal application and by less than three percent in the stock-wealth application. Because both use the same sample Jacobian and stacked moments, the comparison checks the long-run variance estimator.

E.4.  Scope of the reported inference

The standard errors and intervals are pointwise in the response horizon. The analytic construction accounts for the estimation of the aggregate model and of the generated HELP-IV objects, with the targeting qualification above. It does not address weak identification, for which Appendix C.11 applies; the controlled first stages reported here do not indicate weakness.
